units.title: Task-Oriented Approach to Stroke Rehabilitation
units.summary: Experience-Dependent Neural Plasticity Model of Motor Behavior Motor Control Motor Development Motor Learning Task-Oriented Evaluation Framework Task-Oriented Treatment Strategies After completing this chapter, the reader will be able to accom-plish the following: 1. Describe the motor behavior (i.e., motor control, motor learning, and motor development) theories and model that support the occupational therapy (OT) task-oriented ap-proach to persons after stroke. Describe the evaluation framework for the OT task-oriented approach and identify specific assessments that are con-sistent with the approach. Describe general treatment principles for the OT task- oriented approach and their application to persons after stroke. In the past 30 to 35 years, new models of motor con-trol have evolved from the ecological approach to per-ception and action 31,87 and from the study of complex, dynamical systems in mathematics and the sciences.

units.title: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living
section_path: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living
units.summary: Driving Community Mobility Alternative Transportation Driver Evaluation and Rehabilitation Driver Rehabilitation Specialist Generalist Framework Spectrum of Driver Services On-Road Evaluation Screening and Assessment Tools Comprehensive Driving Evaluation After completing this chapter, the reader will be able to accom-plish the following: 1. Understand the instrumental activity of daily living (IADL) of driving and community mobility as a highly valued but complex occupation. Identify the risk factors for the IADL of driving and com-munity mobility and appropriately implement evaluation and intervention strategies. Addressing this IADL either through interventions to prepare for the resumption of driving, make an appropriate referral to a driver rehabilitation specialist, or assist with a compre-hensive community mobility plan. For most individuals, the world becomes a larger place when one acquires a driver’s license.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Somehow, I thought it would never happen; cancer, yes, but not this. My right arm lay lifeless at my side, and my right leg was too weak to lift from the sheet. For the sec-ond time in a week, I was in a hospital bed. My left arm was hooked up to a plastic bottle suspended from an intra-venous (IV) pole, and a slender tube was relaying medica-tion via my veins to the rest of my system.

units.title: PREVALENCE AND IMPACT OF STROKE
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Globally, stroke remains the second leading cause of mor-tality behind heart disease, accounting for nearly 12% of all deaths in 2015. Here in the United States, stroke mor-tality has declined over the past decade, but stroke remains prevalent and an important cause of serious long-term dis-ability. Nearly 800,000 people in the United States will have a new or recurrent stroke each year which amounts to a stroke every 40 seconds. 7 The United States has an esti-mated 7 million stroke survivors today, which is double the number of survivors 25 years ago.

units.title: EPIDEMIOLOGY OF STROKE
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Stroke is largely a preventable disease with known, modifi-able risk factors. 11 The established modifiable risk factors for stroke include hypertension, hyperlipidemia, cigarette smoking, obesity, elevated serum fibrinogen levels, diabetes, a sedentary lifestyle, and the use of contraceptives with high doses of estrogen. 110 The most important and easily treated of these risk factors is systolic hypertension. In the Multiple Risk Factor Intervention Trial, 40% of strokes were attrib-uted to systolic blood pressures greater than 140 mm Hg.

units.title: PATHOGENESIS AND PATHOLOGY OF STROKE
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Definition and Description of Stroke Syndromes Stroke Stroke is essentially a disease of the cerebral vasculature in which a failure to supply oxygen to brain cells, which are the most susceptible to ischemic damage, leads to their death. Strokes are comprised of two broad categories: ischemic and hemorrhagic. Ischemic strokes account for approximately 80% of strokes, and hemorrhagic strokes account for the remainder. Transient Ischemic Attack Symptoms of a transient ischemic attack (TIA) include the focal deficits of an ischemic stroke within a clearly vascular distribution, but in the case of TIAs patients return to base-line without noticeable clinical deficits within a few minutes to hours.

units.title: STROKE DIAGNOSIS
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: The main tool used in the initial stroke diagnostic evalua-tions is cerebral imaging. A CT of the brain is the initial and immediate test of choice with other modalities such CT angi-ography and MRI to follow based on the results of the CT. Computed Tomography CT is a readily available and useful technique that has become the standard for the evaluation of a patient expe-riencing an acute onset of stroke. The most important functions of a CT scan in an acute patient are identify-ing the presence of a hemorrhage (best seen on CT) and ruling out other conditions (e.g., tumor or abscess). In the acute phase of stroke, most CT scans are actually negative with no clear evidence of abnormalities.

units.title: DISCHARGE PLANNING
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Ischemic Stroke: Management of Acute Case and Complications with Workup G.H. is a 76-year-old woman who has a history of hyper-tension and diabetes mellitus and had an MI 2 years ago. She arrives at her local ED 4 hours after an acute onset of weakness in her left arm and leg. She fell at home after try-ing to get up, and it was only after her neighbors heard her calls for help that the emergency services rescue team came to her aid. As part of the multidisciplinary team, the occupational therapist should assist and provide input for the patient’s discharge plan.

units.title: CONCEPTS CENTRAL TO ENABLING PARTICIPATION
section_path: Improving Participation and Quality of Life through Occupation
units.summary: In the Occupational Therapy Practice Framework, 3rd Edition (OTPF), the definition of “participation” is adopted from the World Health Organization (WHO) definition in the International Classification of Func-tioning, Disability, and Health (ICF) and is said to be “involvement in a life situation.” 2,74 The term participation encompasses the concepts of personal independence and social and community integration. 74 Participation must also be considered across the life span. A child plays with friends, engages in sports, goes to school, and is a member of a family; an adult participates in family, work, leisure, and community activities; an older adult may want to con-tinue to work, travel, do volunteer work, and spend time with family. These activities reflect the individual’s desire to participate fully in society, performing the occupations that are meaningful and important to them.

units.title: OCCUPATION
section_path: Improving Participation and Quality of Life through Occupation
units.summary: To participate fully in a life that has meaning, indepen-dence, and choice, the individual engages in “occupa-tions.” Occupation has been defined as the “ordinary and familiar things that persons do every day.” 22 Occupations have purpose, and perhaps most importantly, they have meaning for the person engaged in them. When individu-als engage in occupations, they are engaged in activities that are directed by goals or are purposeful, are per-formed in situations or contexts that influence them, can be identified by the doer and others, and are meaning-ful. 20 Occupations should be considered neutral, that is, they are neither positive nor negative; for some individu-als, smoking cigarettes or other risky or illness producing activities are valued occupations. 62 Occupations usually are classified into general cat-egories, the most common classifications fall into the domains of work (or productivity), play or leisure, and self-maintenance (also referred to as self-care and instru-mental tasks). Work contributes significantly to life satisfaction, well-being, self-worth, and social identity following stroke.

units.title: CLIENT-CENTEREDCARE
section_path: Improving Participation and Quality of Life through Occupation
units.summary: Clients who have had strokes need support to return to their lives as they lived them before the stroke. They require services that help them build endurance, increase movement and strength, increase awareness, obtain assistive devices such as wheelchairs and self-care tools, acquire accessible housing, and gain access to barrier-free workplaces and communities. 12 These needs challenge rehabilitation professionals to extend their interventions beyond the clients’ immediate impairments to focus on their long-term health needs by helping them develop healthy behaviors to improve their health and well-being and to minimize long-term health care costs associated with dysfunction.

units.title: QUALITY OF LIFE
section_path: Improving Participation and Quality of Life through Occupation
units.summary: The client’s perceived quality of life is increasingly being used as a determinant of outcome in health care. Qual-ity is not achieved with strength, range, coordination, and balance. Quality is achieved by having meaningful rela-tionships, having a job, being a good parent, and engaging in leisure interests, all which depend on having cognitive capacity, strength, endurance, and mobility, which may require new skills and new ways of doing things. The WHO Quality of Life Group defines quality of life as an individual’s perceptions of their position in life in the con-text of the culture and value systems in which they live and in relation to their goals, expectations, standards, and con-cerns.
summary_sentences: The client’s perceived quality of life is increasingly being used as a determinant of outcome in health care.

BARRIERS TO PARTICIPATION AND QUALITY OF LIFE
units.summary: BARRIERS TO PARTICIPATION AND QUALITY OF LIFE Once the practitioners identify problems with partici-pation and quality of life, they must address barriers to resumption of activities. Such barriers can be divided into several subgroups, including disability in basic and com-plex IADLs, decreased cognition, impaired motor func-tion and balance, limited mobility, urinary incontinence, poor speech and language function, depression, decreased resource utilization, environmental inaccessibility, and diminishing social and community support. Each is dis-cussed to highlight how rehabilitation can address the issues that may limit an individual’s participation after stroke. HOW TO FOSTER PARTICIPATION THROUGHOUT THE CONTINUUM OF CARE No one method of treatment fosters participation in all avenues of rehabilitative care. The stroke team requires commitment and creativity to address the issue.

units.title: THEORETICAL ASSUMPTIONS AND MODEL UNDERLYING THE OT-TOA
section_path: THEORETICAL ASSUMPTIONS AND MODEL UNDERLYING THE OT-TOA
units.summary: In the past 30 to 35 years, new models of motor con-trol have evolved from the ecological approach to per-ception and action 31,87 and from the study of complex, dynamical systems in mathematics and the sciences. 35 The new models emphasize the interaction between persons and their environments and suggest that motor behavior emerges from persons’ multiple systems interacting with unique tasks and environmental con-texts. 65 “Thus, the systems model of motor control is more interactive or heterarchical and emphasizes the role of the environment more than the earlier reflex- hierarchical model.” 57 In the systems model, the nervous system is viewed dif-ferently from earlier reflex-hierarchical models. Instead of being the primary system controlling movement, the nervous system now is considered only one system among many systems that affect motor behavior. units.title: SYSTEMS VIEW OF MOTOR DEVELOPMENT
units.summary: A systems view of motor development suggests that changes over time are caused by multiple factors or sys-tems such as maturation of the nervous system, biome-chanical constraints and resources, and the impact of the physical and social environment. 40,54,57 For example, Thelen and Fisher 86 reported that the disappearance of the stepping reflex at 4 to 5 months old is due to multiple factors internal and external to the child. Internal factors include the strength of the leg muscles, weight of the legs, and arousal level of the child. External factors include the varying effects of gravity in different environments.

units.title: CONTEMPORARY VIEW OF MOTOR LEARNING
units.summary: Schmidt 81 defined motor learning as “a set of processes associated with practice or experience leading to rela-tively permanent changes in the capabilities of respond-ing.” Thus, recent motor learning theories acknowledge that behavior changes observed during practice may be As a result, contemporary motor learning research evaluates learning not only after the acquisition phase (i.e., immediate effects) but also after a retention phase (i.e., short- or long-term effects) or a transfer test (i.e., ability to generalize to new task) and, thus, new ways of thinking about motor learning have emerged. Motor learning research supports the idea that random practice (i.e., repetitive practice of several tasks in a varied sequence within a practice session) is better than blocked practice (i.e., repetitive practice of the same task within a practice session). 82 Similarly, practicing variations of the same tasks in varied contexts is better than practicing the same task in the same context.

units.title: SUMMARY
units.summary: This chapter describes an OT- TOA for persons after stroke and describes the theoretical basis for and assump-tions of the approach, based on contemporary motor con-trol, motor learning, and motor development literature. The chapter also provides a top-down evaluation frame-work that emphasizes the importance of evaluating role and occupational performance tasks first and then the selective assessment of personal and environmental fac-tors. In addition, the chapter describes the application of treatment principles to various patient problems and, finally, includes a case study describing the application of the OT-TOA to a specific person after stroke. In addition to his son who farms, he has another son and daughter, who are married and live within a 2-hour drive. Their bedroom, bathroom, kitchen, living room, and dining room are on the main floor.

units.title: INTRODUCTION*
units.summary: Client-centered practice is an approach to providing reha-bilitation services that … embraces a philosophy of respect for, and partnership with, people receiving services. Client-centered practice recognizes the autonomy of individuals, the need for client choice in making decisions about occupational needs, the strengths clients bring to a therapy encounter, the benefits of client-therapist partnership, and the need to ensure that services are accessible and fit the context in which a client lives. 2 and Pollock 5 suggest that the therapist implementing this approach to evaluation include the fol-lowing concepts: 1.

units.title: THE EVENT
units.summary: It happened during breakfast, on a bright December morning, unannounced, almost gently, and absolutely painlessly. I was wearing a thick terry cloth robe, which buffered my slumping to the floor and gave it (at least in my visual memory) a slow-motion appearance. I ended up on my left side on the parquet floor, reject-ing my father-in-law’s offers of help, thrashing my right leg, holding onto the seat of my chair with my right hand, a little embarrassed and miffed that I did not seem able to stand up. I also remember distinctly my irritation at my mother-in-law’s plaintive demands that her husband remove a piece of bread I was chewing on when the stroke hit.

units.title: THERAPY
units.summary: When the editor of this book, who had been my occupa-tional therapist, asked me to write about my experiences as a patient recovering from stroke and suggested the title “Notes of a Survivor,” I asked him whether he meant sur-vivor of the stroke or survivor of physical and occupational therapy. Lest my later comments sound too enthusiastic or be considered self-serving on the part of the editor, let me start with a few negatives. Both physical therapy and occupational therapy are boring, consisting as they must of highly repetitive exer-cises and activities: the patient soon learns to count “reps,” longing to reach the magic number (usually 10—do thera-pists have a functional rationale for this quota?) requested by the therapist. And no cheating is tolerated; therapists have mastered a secret way of keeping track of reps auto-matically and privately even as they keep up a conversa-tion with you, and they will not be defrauded of even a few reps.

units.title: GOING HOME
units.summary: I had fallen once in my hospital room, and I fell once again a few days after my return home. wall, I went through the steps my therapists had so care-fully rehearsed with me in the hospital gym, and on both occasions, I got up on my own. However, after my rela-tives left, I had nightmares about falling in the middle of a room and not being able to get up and reach the phone or the intercom. The problem was solved by the acquisition of a portable phone, which I slipped into my pocket every night as soon as I entered my house.

units.title: CONCLUDING REMARKS
units.summary: Although I cannot run, I can walk without a cane, I am independent in my daily activities, I have been able to resume my (fortunately sedentary) job, and I travel around the world. To be sure, this is not the typical outcome of stroke. Every patient is different, and I have been unusu-ally lucky in that I was spared speech impediments and spasticity. This in turn has made my rehabilitation easier and more effective.

units.title: P.S.
units.summary: Just as Alexandre Dumas père felt obliged to write “Twenty Years Later,” a follow-up to The Three Muske-teers, so 10 years after my stroke, I also feel obliged to offer a follow-up. The good news is that I still walk inde-pendently, work full-time, and travel extensively. The bad news is that I never ran again—although running remains a recurrent subject of my dreams—and I still have par-esthesia in the left side of my body, mostly in the hand. Additional problems are due to two situations, one of which is totally outside my will, while for the other, I have to take full responsibility.

units.title: EPILOGUE
units.summary: In my “Concluding Remarks,” I optimistically stated that I was unusually lucky from my first right brain stroke, when I was spared speech impediment and spasticity. I was unusually unlucky 4 months ago, on a Saturday before Easter, when I was hit again by a bad stroke affecting the left hemisphere of my brain, due to my frequent atrial fibrillation (a-fib). Unlike what I remembered happening 20 years ago, I was totally unconscious regarding what happened sud-denly to me, vaguely thinking that I was falling to my right side. Fortunately, my physical therapist wife, my veritable custodian angel, came to my assistance, called an ambu-lance, and paramedics quickly took me to the Allen Pavil-ion, where the neurologist on call had the premonition to send me promptly to Columbia University Medical Center, where a providentially clever radioneurologist/interventionist inserted a line into my femoral artery, all the way into my cerebral left middle artery, from which he removed the offending embolus.

units.summary: As the intervention process progresses, different types of evaluation methods are used to gather information from and about the client during each step of the pro-cess. As we already noted, occupation-focused inter-view guides such as COPM 25, OPHI-I I, 23 or the ADL Taxonomy 28,40,41 can be used to facilitate the client’s self-report and prioritization of strengths and prob-lems with occupational performance, including ADL task performance. When the occupational therapist progresses to the step in which he or she implements performance analyses and defines and describes the task actions the client did and did not perform effec-tively, either standardized or nonstandardized per-formance analyses can be used. 15 If the client reports problems with ADL task performance or social inter-action, existing standardized observational tools such as the AMPS 16,17 or the Evaluation of Social Inter-action 14 can be used.

units.title: INTRODUCTION
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis
units.summary: Occupational therapy (OT) intervention in stroke reha-bilitation is focused on increasing functional indepen-dence and participation and can vary greatly from one patient to the next. Limited return of upper and lower extremity function can make participation in activities of daily living (ADLs) quite challenging, and interventions must be tailored to meet the unique needs of each per-son. One study found that even 4 years following a stroke, stroke survivors continued to report high levels of activ-ity limitation and participation restriction. 6 Loss of func-tion and disuse of the paretic limb are common, and these upper extremity impairments have been shown to have a negative impact on activity and participation.

units.summary: The World Health Organization’s 2001 International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health 23 provides a useful framework for assessment of health and disability at individual and population levels. units.title: GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis
units.summary: Generally speaking, there are various approaches a thera-pist can employ to increase functional participation. Some clients will improve participation through remediation of their impairments. Other clients will need to rely on com-pensatory techniques to achieve independence in ADLs. In addition to hemiparesis after stroke, any neurobehav-ioral deficits (see Chapter 25) that might be present will affect treatment choice and intervention method.

units.title: DRESSING
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis
units.summary: There are a number of different techniques and approaches for dressing with hemiparesis. The indi-vidual needs of each patient should be considered as well as the presence of caregivers who may be assist-ing the patient. Regular practice with dressing during OT intervention has been shown to lead to significant improvements in performance. 21 Resources such as the Occupational Therapy Toolkit™ 7 provide handouts for one-handed dressing techniques that can be helpful for patients and caregivers to carryover techniques learned in therapy. Use the shirt tags to identify the front and back of the shirt.

units.title: SUMMARY
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis
units.summary: This chapter describes equipment recommendations as well as practical and creative solutions that the occu-pational therapist can incorporate to assist patients in becoming more independent when performing ADLs and IADLs. For individuals with limited functional return of the involved upper extremity, compensatory techniques are crucial during the rehabilitation process and can maxi-mize the potential to reach meaningful goals. As always, the therapist should focus on activities that the patient finds most meaningful in order to make the biggest impact on participation. For individuals with extensive paralysis resulting from stroke, family members or hired outside help may be required to assist with ADLs.

units.title: TERMINOLOGY
units.summary: Many terms have been used in occupational therapy (OT) practice to describe an individual’s ability to change the position of his or her body in space and move within the environment. Mobility broadly refers to movements that result in a change of body position or location. The term bed mobility has been used interchangeably with gross mobility within the rehabilitation setting and traditionally has included tasks such as rolling to both sides, rolling to side lying, moving from a sitting to a supine position and vice versa, and moving from sitting to standing. Transfer refers to movement from one surface to another such as from a bed to a wheelchair, from a wheelchair to a toilet, or from a wheelchair to a car and involves varied methods of achievement.

units.title: FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY: RELATIONSHIP TO ACTIVITIES AND PARTICIPATION
section_path: FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY: RELATIONSHIP TO ACTIVITIES AND PARTICIPATION
units.summary: FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY: RELATIONSHIP TO ACTIVITIES AND PARTICIPATION Occupational therapists have always approached functional mobility from the perspective that individual elements involved in changing the position of the body were necessary to achieve competency in broad areas of occupation. Improve-ment in activities of daily living (ADLs), instrumental activi-ties of daily living (IADLs), education, work, play, leisure, and social participation has always been the ultimate goal of OT. The American Occupational Therapy Association, in “Practice Framework: Domain and Process,” describes functional mobility as “moving from one position or place to another (during performance of everyday activities), such as in-bed mobility, wheelchair mobility, transfers (wheelchair, bed, car, tub, toilet, tub/shower, chair, floor).

units.summary: INFLUENCE OF CONTEXTUAL FACTORS ON FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY Contextual factors represent a variety of interrelated con-ditions and situations that may influence an individual’s ability to become proficient in performing mobility tasks. Personal factors are unique to the individual’s life and living situation and influence the selection of mobility interventions.

units.title: FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY: THE OUTCOME OF MULTIPLE PROCESSES
section_path: FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY: THE OUTCOME OF MULTIPLE PROCESSES
units.summary: FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY: THE OUTCOME OF MULTIPLE PROCESSES Functional mobility requires the successful interaction of a number of systems. Carrying out skilled rolling, sitting, and standing does not depend solely on the integrity of the neuromusculoskeletal system. Occupational therapists must be mindful of the interdependence of various sen-sory, perceptual, and cognitive functions in the execution of these tasks and create evaluation tools that respect this relationship, such as the Árnadóttir Occupational Ther-apy Neurobehavioral Evaluation (see Chapter 25).

units.title: FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY TASKS
units.summary: Functional mobility tasks occur throughout the daily routine under varying circumstances within changeable environ-ments. Each task requires the individual to stabilize his or her body in space or exhibit dynamic postural control. Das and McCollum 26 identified three major requirements for loco-motion that can be applied to all functional mobility tasks: 1. Progression or movement in a desired direction 2.

units.title: ACTIVITIES IN THE SUPINE POSITION
units.summary: The performance of supine activities is often associated with the acute stages of the rehabilitation process. Bridg-ing, rolling, and movement from side lying to sit are basic functional mobility tasks that are necessary to the provi-sion of nursing care and movement of the client from a bed to a wheelchair. However, these mobility sequences are also important in enabling the client to participate in a wide range of life areas. For example, consider the indi-vidual who chooses to lie on a beach to enjoy the sun and surf. Analysis of Movement In the functional mobility task of bridging, the back and hip extensors support the body against the forces of gravity.

As the patient begins to rise from the seated position, the somatosensory system pro-vides information about the forces exerted and the ongoing changes in limb position. On completion of this task, the results of the sequence provide additional feedback. ADJUNCT TECHNIQUES TO ENHANCE SKILL ACQUISITION

units.title: EVALUATION TOOLS
units.summary: Many therapists perform a subjective assessment of func-tional mobility based on clinical observation. However, it is advantageous to use a recognized evaluation tool to sup-port the need for services, document progress, and assess treatment efficacy. Table 7.2 includes a list of relevant tools for evaluating mobility functions. Currently, the only standardized evaluation for mobility skills is Carr and Shepherd’s Motor Assessment Scale for Stroke Patients.

units.title: ANTICIPATING CHANGING ENVIRONMENTS
units.summary: The ultimate goal of functional mobility retraining is to have the patient resume the roles and activities associated with his or her lifestyle before the stroke. This goal pre-sumes that the patient needs to transfer reacquired mobil-ity skills to environments unique to his or her individual The treatment setting presents a predictable environment where the physical aspects of therapeutic equipment and furnishings remain unchanged from one treatment session to another. The patient’s home environment also may be viewed as predict-able because of the patient’s familiarity with the surround-ings. The research examining normal movement sequences has found great variety in the movement patterns used to perform each mobility task. A single pattern may be identified as occurring more frequently during rolling, although many subjects use alternative patterns that are equally effective.

units.title: TERMINOLOGY
units.summary: Physical therapists must first familiarize themselves with the components of the typical gait cycle and with the ter-minology used to describe these components before they can analyze the gait of a person who has had a stroke. A cycle begins when the heel of one foot touches the ground and ends after the leg and body have advanced through space and time and the heel of that same foot hits the ground again. The cycle includes a period when the leg is in contact with the ground, which is followed by a period when it is advancing through space. Thus the gait cycle of one leg can be divided into two phases: the stance phase (in which the leg is in contact with the ground) and the swing phase (in which the leg is off the ground).

units.title: RELIABLE GAIT PARAMETERS
units.summary: Cadence is the number of steps or strides per unit of time. Walking velocity equals speed: the distance walked divided by time. Because time–distance variables are the compo-nents of gait that can be measured most reliably, thera-pists can use them in assessing improvement in patients after stroke. 56,113,114 For example, persons who have had a stroke with a resulting hemiparesis typically walk with a slower-than-typical gait.

units.title: HEMIPLEGIC GAITS
units.summary: The type of gait of a person who has had a stroke depends on where in the brain the insult has occurred and which systems are affected, such as motor, sensory, balance, coordination, perceptual, and visual systems. If a motor area in the cortex or a motor track is involved, hemiple-gia or hemiparesis is manifested in the contralateral limbs. The location of the infarction within these areas deter-mines whether the arm or the leg is more impaired. Not all patients after stroke are hemiplegic or hemiparetic, nor do all hemiparetic patients have the same degree of motor deficits. BOX 8.1 Modified Functional Walking Categories*

units.title: OSTEOPOROSIS
units.summary: Stroke survivors have an increased risk of falling through-out their hospitalization (acute stroke unit and inpatient stroke rehabilitation), which continues to be elevated even after discharge back into the community. 133,124 While fall rates (13% to 36%) and risk factors vary across settings (Perrson 2016), 5,32,108,109,138,106 this population has an increased fracture risk. From 1.2% to 6% of falls result in fractures to the distal radius, humeral head, and hip. 23,111,135 Fractures occur predominantly on the paretic side, and hip fractures in particular accelerate the downward spiral toward increased morbidity and mortality.

units.title: TREATMENT INTERVENTIONS
units.summary: The physical therapist first addresses deficits identified during the physical assessment that are contributing to the atypical gait, such as decreased ROM and strength. Interventions can include basic modalities and therapeutic exercise and a variety of approaches to address the lack of movement and voluntary control. Many interventions are based on theories that advocate facilitation of typical movement and sensory stimulation of the patient by the therapist. In this context, the patient is a passive recipi-ent of the therapist’s efforts. The list of abnormal gait patterns that can appear after stroke is too extensive to be covered completely in a single chapter.

units.title: ASSISTIVE DEVICES
units.summary: The assistive devices most commonly used with patients after stroke are canes, walkers, and occasionally two crutches. Hemiparetic patients whose balance is impaired minimally and who have functional strength in the oppo-site UE may use a cane. Two crutches or a walker requires at least some functional use of both upper extremities. Both devices provide more external stability, with the walker providing more stability than the crutches. Two-Point Contralateral Gait Pattern Using One Device Hemiparetic patients with a nonfunctional arm often are taught a two-point contralateral gait pattern using one assistive device.

units.title: IS RETURN TO WORK AN OPTION?
section_path: IS RETURN TO WORK AN OPTION?
units.summary: Other chapters in this book have described the sequelae of impairments, functional limitations, and performance and participation problems common after stroke (see Chapters 1, 17, 18, 20, 24, 25, and 28). The client must be medically stable before considering return to work, but the treatment team should not assume that return to work is not possible in clients with hemiparesis, expressive speech deficits, or impaired mobility. For example, a large study of 2500 working-age individuals with stroke found that 74% returned to work 1 year poststroke. In cases of mild stroke, the vast majority of stroke survivors easily passed motor, cognitive, and functional screens, so it was assumed that they could return to their prestroke activities; however, nearly 40% of clients presenting to the emergency department with mild stroke never returned to work, and another 15% remained unemployed 6 months later.

units.title: UNDERSTANDING THE JOB AND WORKPLACE
units.summary: Rehabilitation professionals understand the requirements of most daily living tasks and are well equipped to design assessments and interventions for these areas. Physical therapists know how to assess and rehabilitate an ath-lete with a shoulder injury, occupational therapists rou-tinely help people resume their ADLs and manage their home responsibilities, and speech pathologists are experts at helping people communicate and manage cognitive impairments. The motion necessary to swing a tennis racket, the requirements of getting bathed and dressed, and the oral motor control necessary to speak are well known to these rehabilitation professionals. With more than 867 detailed occupations in the U.S.

units.title: ASSESSING THE CLIENT’S WORK ABILITIES AND LIMITATIONS
section_path: ASSESSING THE CLIENT’S WORK ABILITIES AND LIMITATIONS
units.summary: ASSESSING THE CLIENT’S WORK ABILITIES AND LIMITATIONS Employment tests must be derived from a job analysis and physical demands analysis that targets critical or impor-tant job duties, work behaviors, or work outcomes. 31 Evaluations used to make work decisions must possess the following characteristics in this hierarchical order: (1) it must be safe to administer; (2) it must give reliable val-ues that are quantifiable; (3) it must predict risk of future injury or illness; and (4) it must be practical. Predicting risk of future injury is a type of validity, which means that the test measures what it claims to measure. If the client does not possess the ability to return to work after the assessment but wants to return to work and there is potential to do so, a treatment plan can be initiated. The profession of OT defines the occupation of work as (1) employment interests and pursuits, (2) employment seeking and acquisition, (3) job performance, (4) retire-ment preparation and adjustment, (5) volunteer explora-tion, and (6) volunteer participation.

units.title: DESIGNING TREATMENT TO ADDRESS RETURN TO WORK AFTER STROKE
section_path: DESIGNING TREATMENT TO ADDRESS RETURN TO WORK AFTER STROKE
units.summary: DESIGNING TREATMENT TO ADDRESS RETURN TO WORK AFTER STROKE Stroke can impair a wide range of functions that result in limitations in a client’s ability to meet these generic worker requirements. This may be directly tied to physical, physi-ological, cognitive, emotional, social, sensory, or motiva-tional changes after stroke, or it could be a combination of a constellation of limitations. Interventions to address some of these generic worker requirements may be novel to clinicians who treat in traditional outpatient settings. WHERE CAN OT ADDRESS RETURN TO WORK AFTER STROKE? When the client is medically stable, discussions regard-ing return to work may be appropriate.

units.title: INTRODUCTION
section_path: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living
units.summary: For most individuals, the world becomes a larger place when one acquires a driver’s license. Driving a motor vehicle allows people to move beyond their neighborhood, community, state, province, or country to visit, explore, and join activities outside the home and immediate envi-ronment. Although public transportation in communities provide some of the same destinations, driving a motor vehicle allows for the spontaneity and freedom to move beyond the boundaries of train, subway, or bus stations. After a driver’s license has been acquired, there is an expectation that a person will be always be able to drive, and although there may be other methods of transport available, driving is the most accepted form of community mobility in the United States. The generation born between 1945 and 1964 is affection-ately known as the Baby Boomers.

units.title: VISUAL HISTORY
units.summary: TLG has emphasized the use of videotaping in both research and intervention because of the lack of images of parenting by individuals with physical disabilities, which affects diverse professionals, including occupational therapists, and parents and their family members. The occupational therapy (OT) team coined the term visual history to refer to the mental image that most people have of the way a task is accomplished. 12 For example, when people imagine holding a baby, they think of a baby in someone’s arms. Such limited visual histories may inter-fere with the goal of learning to accomplish a task in a new way.

units.title: NORMAL HUMAN SEXUAL RESPONSE
units.summary: One must have an understanding of the normal human sexual response cycle before one can explore the relation-ship between sexuality and disability. Masters and John-son 49 divided the human sexual response cycle into four segments: (1) excitement, (2) plateau, (3) orgasm, and (4) resolution. In each phase, definite physical changes occur in both sexes. During the excitement phase, physiologi-cal reactions occur because of somatosensory or psycho-genic stimulation. In normal human development, changes in the sexual response cycle occur during the aging process.

units.title: SEXUALITY AND NEUROLOGIC FUNCTION
units.summary: Sexual function is controlled by the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves, and control of libido and sexual pleasure is mediated by several areas in the cortex, mid-brain, and brainstem. 57 Men experience reflexogenic and psychogenic erections. Reflexogenic erections are caused by direct stimulation to the penis and may occur without conscious awareness, even in the absence of penile sensa-tion. Psychogenic erections originate from mental activity such as sexual fantasies and stimulating visual input and do not require direct penile stimulation.

units.title: EFFECTS OF STROKE ON SEXUAL FUNCTION
section_path: EFFECTS OF STROKE ON SEXUAL FUNCTION
units.summary: The literature shows that common effects of stroke on sexual function are decreased libido, impaired erectile and ejaculatory function, decreased vaginal lubrication, impaired ego and self-esteem, and depression. The motor, sensory, cognitive, and physiological effects of stroke have been shown to affect the desire and ability to engage in sexual activities in many ways. 78 Some research has been focused on relating sexual dysfunction to the location of the lesion. counseling for patients after stroke but does not pro-vide specific interventions.* As a result, therapists are left with insufficient information to treat sexual dysfunction adequately. Attitudes on the part of the public or the patient’s family members also may affect the patient emotionally or psy-chologically.

units.title: SUMMARY
units.summary: All persons are sexual, and sexual activity is important to most persons throughout their lives. Interest in or desire for sexual activity does not necessarily diminish as persons grow older. Stroke may interfere with sexual expression by affecting the survivor’s desire; libido; erectile or lubrication response; orgasm or ejaculation; and sensorimotor, cognitive, psychoso-cial, ADL, and role function. Stroke also may affect the part-ner’s response or the patient’s ability to find a sexual partner.

units.title: SUMMARY
units.summary: A review of the litera-ture reveals that leisure may be defined in various ways. Many factors influence an individual’s participation in lei-sure activities, such as roles, attitudes, satisfaction, stage in the life cycle, and intrinsic and extrinsic barriers. The role of the occupational therapist is multifaceted, including assessment, intervention through techniques and adap-tive equipment, and patient and family education, with an emphasis on community resources. Leisure activities may be used to improve a patient’s motivation, quality of life, and self-esteem and as means to treat impairment.

units.title: OVERVIEW OF CAREGIVING INTHE UNITED STATES
section_path: OVERVIEW OF CAREGIVING INTHE UNITED STATES
units.summary: Characteristics of Caregivers in the United States The typical caregiver may be described as a married woman with some post–high school education or a college degree and a full-time employee earning less than $50,000 per year. The median age of a caregiver is 48 years old and of a care recipient is 79 years old 26 (see Table 14.1). On the other hand, spousal caregivers are split evenly between male and female, with a median age of 64 years. It has been estimated that 43.5 million Americans (19.2%) are informal caregivers and 39.8 million Americans (16.6%) are informal caregivers for adults (18 and older). 65 Informal caregivers are defined as individuals who assist others with self-care, home care, and medical tasks with-out receiving additional time, pay, or other resources.

units.title: OT ROLE WITH CAREGIVERS OF PERSONS WITH STROKE
section_path: OT ROLE WITH CAREGIVERS OF PERSONS WITH STROKE
units.summary: Caregiver assessment is an essential first step in acknowl-edging, valuing, and understanding the caregiver. It has been defined as a “systematic process of gathering infor-mation about a caregiving situation to identify the specific problems, needs, strengths, and resources of the family caregiver, as well as the caregiver’s ability to contribute to the needs of the care recipient.” 36 Among leaders in care-giving research, there is a consensus on the fundamental principles to guide caregiver assessment policy and prac-tice (Box 14.1). 34 There are differing opinions on when a caregiver assessment is warranted. Adelman and colleagues 1 sug-gested that caregivers receive a referral for assessment of burden if they have around-the-clock responsibilities for recipients with high health needs or if they are dealing with an impending care setting transition. BOX 14.1 Seven Fundamental Principles for Caregiver Assessment Because caregivers are a core part of health care and long-term care, it is important to recognize, respect, assess, and address their needs.

units.title: PSYCHOLOGICAL FACTORS AS PREDICTORS OF STROKE
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
PSYCHOLOGICAL FACTORS AS PREDICTORS OF STROKE
units.summary: PSYCHOLOGICAL FACTORS AS PREDICTORS OF STROKE Physiological, behavioral, family history, and genetics are risk factors for stroke. The examination of psychologi-cal factors as predictors of stroke has warranted attention because evidence indicates that personality traits may also be associated with increased risk. One study identifies it as a risk factor for younger study participants and for those with high high-density lipopro-tein cholesterol values 157; another found that participants with a pattern of outward expression of anger were twice as likely to sustain a stroke compared with even-tempered individuals.

units.title: EMOTIONAL REACTION TO STROKE
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: For any individual hospitalized after a traumatic event, a barrage of emotion is likely to develop. Being faced with an acute illness with chronic consequences, compounded by being acutely aware of the physical changes occurring and by being surrounded by a foreign and controlling environment, adds to one’s emotional reaction. 44 During an acute phase of the illness, one is concerned with sur-vival, is often confused with what is happening, and may be the recipient of poor communication from hospital staff. This results in feelings of being overwhelmed; in experi-ence of loss of control over personal care, which affects one’s sense of dignity; and in experiences of the hospital environment being dissatisfying, inadequate, and insensi-tive.

units.summary: Among the most significant considerations in understand-ing the characteristics and consequences of stroke is the relationship of depression to onset, recovery, and reha-bilitation. Because of the neurophysiological changes and reaction to the consequences of stroke, depression has major implications for the course of recovery. Despite the causes of depression, assessment and treatment of depres-sion affect psychological, functional, and medical health. The relationship between cerebrovascular disease and depression has long been studied. A significant comorbidity exists between poststroke depression and anxiety.

units.title: SUMMARY
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: From the initial onset of a stroke through the process of recovery, one follows an unpredictable path. The indi-vidual is faced with a plethora of choices and challenges that are as unexpected as they are difficult. One is asked to relearn the activities one has always taken for granted, to assume new roles that may be unfamiliar or that chal-lenge one’s self-worth, and to rewrite the future. Although patients aspire to return to their prestroke existence, their struggles are compounded by the emotional reactions to the loss of activities, abilities, and independence; by the potential of social stigma; and for some, by the real pres-ence of psychiatric conditions.

units.summary: The Bobath approach has been one of the more influential approaches within the traditional paradigm. Some of the elements of this approach are as follows 4: i. The central nervous system is organized hierarchically, in which higher centers, such as the cerebral cortex, influ-ence control over the lower centers such as the spinal cord. When there is damage to higher centers, primitive forms of movements (e.g., reflex postures and move-ments), controlled by the spinal cord and brainstem, are released from the normal inhibition from higher centers. Evidence-based practice is an important aspect of education, clinical practice, and research in occupational and physi-cal therapy.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

units.summary: 43 reviewed 44 RCTs to examine the effects of RT on UL motor control, UL capacity, ADL, muscle strength, and muscle tone in comparison with nonrobotic therapy. The review separately examined the effectiveness of two different types of robotic systems: exoskeletons, defined as external structural devices that are designed to apply assistive forces on one or more joints, and end- effectors, defined as systems with a single attachment designed to guide the most distal part of the UL. The total number of participants in this review was 1362, making this one of the most comprehensive reviews. Most studies included participants who were more than 3 months of their stroke event. The application of robotic technology to stroke reha-bilitation began in the 1990s.

units.summary: The past 5 years have been an exciting period for stroke rehabilitation. Occupational and physical therapists are being asked to provide intervention based on sound sci-entific principles and with demonstrated effectiveness. The lack of effectiveness of traditional approaches, such as the Bobath approach, urges therapists to abandon such approaches in favor of more recent and effective func-tional approaches. Recent advances in understanding of motor control and motor impairments after stroke and emerging diagnos-tic and therapeutic technologies have clearly facilitated a paradigm shift toward functional TOT.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

AN OVERVIEW OF COMMON TRUNK IMPAIRMENTS THAT MAY INTERFERE WITH DAILY FUNCTION
units.summary: AN OVERVIEW OF COMMON TRUNK IMPAIRMENTS THAT MAY INTERFERE WITH DAILY FUNCTION While motor control studies after stroke focus primarily on upper extremity function and/or gait, there is a body of descriptive evidence that aims to give clinicians insight into the various specific trunk impairments observed after stroke. Dickstein and colleagues 21 examined anticipatory pos-tural adjustment in trunk muscles during the performance of upper and lower limb flexion tasks in patients with hemiparesis secondary to stroke. The researchers recorded electromyographic activity of the lumbar erector spinae and of the latissimus dorsi muscles bilaterally during flex-ion of either arm and from the two rectus abdominis and obliquus externus muscles during flexion of either hip.

units.summary: Therapists should question patients about their perceived stability limits. Stability limits have been defined as the “boundaries of an area of space in which the body can maintain its position without changing the base of sup-port.” 50 Patients’ perceived stability limits may or may not be consistent with their actual limits. If patients’ perceived lim-its of stability are greater than their actual limits, they are at risk for falls. If their perceived limits of stability are less than their actual limits, they may be reluctant to attempt tasks with progressively greater demands on their postural system (e.g., lower extremity dressing without assistive devices and picking up objects from the floor without a reacher). The use of valid and reliable tools is always recommended.

units.title: INTRODUCTION
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Standing Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Our ability to maintain an upright standing posture and to control our posture while standing is instrumental to almost everything we do during daily life. For example, when cooking a meal, our ability to walk around the kitchen or retrieve needed items from cabinets, drawers, and the refrigerator is, in part, dependent on our ability to control our body’s position in space (aka postural control). Unfortunately, impairments in postural control (aka balance) are common after stroke and they have a sig-nificant impact on function. 6,38,48,54,66,76 For example, evi-dence suggests that balance impairment is an independent predictor of independent toileting 38 and that impairments in balance are associated with falls in the community.

units.title: POSTURAL CONTROL
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Standing Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: In the literature, various terms (e.g., postural control, bal-ance, equilibrium, postural reactions, balance reactions, etc.) are used interchangeably to describe a person’s abil-ity to control their body’s position in space in order to maintain postural orientation and stability. 60,66 Accord-ing to Shumway-Cook and Woollacott, “postural control involves controlling the body’s position in space for the dual purposes of stability and orientation.” They further define postural stability as the ability to control the cen-ter of mass (COM) with respect to the base of support (BOS), and postural orientation as the ability to maintain appropriate relationships between body segments and between the body and the environment for task perfor-mance. 60 Postural control responses can be reactive (i.e., in response to an external threat to balance) or anticipa-tory (i.e., planned in advance of a movement that may destabilize balance. 60 Many theories have been proposed to explain the abil-ity to maintain postural control.

units.summary: The integration of information from three sensory modalities is used for maintaining balance. The systems of importance are the 6,60 (1) visual system; (2) vestibular system; (3) somatosensory system. Visual System The visual system (see Chapter 24) provides information regarding vertical orientation and visual flow. Visual or optical flow information, which describes movement of an image on the retina, is important input that aids detection of personal and environmental movement. Information provided by the visual system can be ambiguous and must be compared with other sensory information to determine accuracy.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Standing Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: When conducting a subjective interview, the clinician must keep in mind that patients who have had an acute stroke may not be able to provide accurate information during the interview process due to cognitive and/or language impairments. Clinicians may need to use other sources of information, including family members, signifi-cant others, and information from the medical chart, to supplement, clarify, or verify information that a patient provides. Patients may improve in their ability to provide information as cognitive and language deficits improve. Patients often also demonstrate a greater awareness of their situation and surroundings as they improve and become more fully integrated into the home and commu-nity environments. A comprehensive evaluation is crucial in helping the therapist understand specific balance problems that a patient may be experiencing.

units.title: STROKE SYNDROMES
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The most common stroke of the vestibular system, first reported in the late 19th century, 31 is lateral medullary syndrome, also known as Wallenberg syndrome. 3 This syndrome is caused by a stroke of either the PICA or AICA. Because both arteries that supply the vestibular nuclei also supply other areas, lateral medullary syndrome is manifested by mixed sensory and motor loss, including vertigo, latero-pulsion, disequilibrium, ataxia, contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the trunk and limbs, and the following ipsilateral signs: facial numbness, Horner syn-drome (drooping of the upper eyelid, constriction of the pupil, and decreased sweating), and dysphagia. Involve-ment of the PICA also includes hoarseness and skew devi-ation of the eyes. In approximately 20% of patients who complain of ver-tigo, in general, the cause is vascular in nature (stroke, vertebrobasilar migraine headache, or transient ischemic attack).

For therapists to assist patients with meeting this goal, a thorough understanding of the various prob-lems associated with upper extremity dysfunction after stroke is required. The therapist has the responsibility to stay informed of (and contribute to) the new develop-ments in and information about upper extremity function.

units.title: RATIONALE FOR DEVELOPMENT
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Rehabilitation Technologies to Promote Upper Limb Recovery After Stroke
units.summary: Rehabilitation scientists are concerned about the lack of empirical evidence on treatment efficacy and its impact on motor recovery and functional outcomes after stroke. At present, they do not have the necessary knowledge to predict which treatment interventions, dose, or intensity elicit the best functional outcomes for an individual patient. Rehabilitation scientists are working diligently to quantify the “active ingredients” of various treatments so they can recommend use of the most effective and efficient therapy methods for patient care.

units.title: THEORIES GUIDING TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Rehabilitation Technologies to Promote Upper Limb Recovery After Stroke
units.summary: Rehabilitation technology is a relatively new and growing field, experiencing some of the same developmental chal-lenges seen during the history of conventional rehabilita-tion practice. Its development has been strongly influenced by motor learning principles, specifically massed practice and explicit learning paradigms. For example, rehabilita-tion robotics is designed to produce highly intensive upper limb training that is quantifiable, easily graded, cognitively challenging, and goal-directed. Motor learning principles guide their delivery of feedback regarding knowledge of performance (e.g., via haptics), and knowledge of results, by way of graphs, changes in the virtual tasks and environ-ment, and other forms of feedback.

units.summary: ROBOTS FOR DISTAL TRAINING FOCUSED ON THE HAND The development of robots to assist with wrist and hand retraining has lagged behind that of shoulder and elbow devices, largely due to the complexity of control needed to assist with grasp and release motions. Although the num-ber of robots designed for hand rehabilitation after stroke has grown significantly in recent years, few are commer-cially available. 2 The subsequent sections will focus on two empirically tested devices that are available for clinical use: the Hand Mentor and the Amadeo robots. units.title: SUMMARY
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Rehabilitation Technologies to Promote Upper Limb Recovery After Stroke
units.summary: The focus of conventional therapies has shifted from ana-lytical training methods directed at impairments in motor function to an emphasis on TOT for the upper limb. The development of rehabilitation technologies is following a similar trend. Potential benefits of these devices include controllable treatment intensity, high repetition, task- specific practice, and sensory-motor feedback to enhance knowledge of performance and results. The research presented in this chapter generally supports the use of rehabilitation technologies to improve upper limb motor functions after stroke.

units.title: ETIOLOGY OF STROKE HAND EDEMA
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The edema that therapists treat is defined as an excess accumulation of fluid in the interstitium. It occurs on the capillary level (microcirculation level) when there is an imbalance of pressure between the arterioles, venules, and interstitium or an obstruction of the lymphatic sys-tem. 17,51 This is also known as an imbalance in Starling equilibrium. It is important to note the vascular system refers not only to the venous and arterial capillaries but also to the lymphatic capillaries. Anatomic Overview of the Venous and Lymphatic Systems Related to Stroke Hand Edema and Its Etiology The venous congestion and limb dependency theory is most relevant to the treatment techniques this chapter will present.

units.title: HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Neuhaus and colleagues have published a review of the orthotic devices literature covering a 100-year period. 31 Their review has documented two different approaches to orthotic devices: the biomechanical approach and the neurophysiological approach. The biomechanical perspective considers issues such as soft-tissue lengthening, prevention of contracture and deformity, maintenance of biomechanical alignment, and effects on the nonneural components of spasticity. In con-trast, the neurophysiological perspective considers reflex inhibition, effects on the neural basis of spasticity, facilita-tion through sensory input, and inhibition through posi-tioning and sensory input.

units.title: REVIEW OF ORTHOSES COMMONLY USED FOR PATIENTS AFTER STROKE
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
REVIEW OF ORTHOSES COMMONLY USED FOR PATIENTS AFTER STROKE
units.summary: The finger spreader (finger abduction orthosis) is fabri-cated of foam rubber and positions the fingers and thumb in abduction. According to Bobath the purpose of the orthosis is to “obtain extension of wrist and fingers.… Abduction not only facilitates extension of the fingers, but also reduces flexor spasticity throughout the whole arm.… It has a better and more dynamic effect than the use of a (standard) orthosis and reduces the possibility of edema.” 2 One should note that Bobath’s rationale is not consistent with the current understanding of motor control and related neurologic principles. A sturdier version of this orthosis (fabricated of low- temperature plastic) was proposed by Doubilet and Polkow. 8 They recommended wearing the orthosis only during the day. units.title: GENERAL FABRICATION GUIDELINES
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Many materials to fabricate orthotic devices are com-mercially available today. They are thermoplastic materi-als; some have more rubber content base than others do. The rubber content base materials tend to have increased conformability and drape compared with pure thermo-plastic materials, but they may be more difficult to handle because of their draping quality. Thermoplastic materials generally have a greater memory capacity than the rubber-based thermoplas-tics. If the orthosis prescribed for a patient includes a forearm trough, basic principles call for the trough to cover two- thirds of the forearm.

units.summary: VISUAL PROCESSING DURING FUNCTIONAL ACTIVITIES The visual system is commonly impaired after acquired brain damage (also known as stroke). It is estimated that two-thirds of all stroke survivors have a visual impairment. 19 Typical visual impairments include visual field deficits, loss of ocular alignment or control, diplopia, convergence insufficiency, spatial relations deficits, and changes in visual acuity.

units.summary: Assessment of visual acuity has been described in Box 24.1. Visual acuity refers to clarity and sharpness of sight. It is commonly measured using the Snellen chart (or text cards for near acuity) and noted, for example, as 20/20, 20/60, 20/200, and so on. Modifications such as using LEA Symbols (picture charts) or a “tumbling E” chart are available for those with aphasia. MANAGING VISUAL FIELD DEFICITS WITH AN EMPHASIS ON HEMIANOPSIA The visual fields extend approximately 65 degrees upward, 75 degrees downward, 60 degrees inward, and 95 degrees outward when the eye is in the forward position.

units.title: THE A-ONEINSTRUMENT
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Impact of Neurobehavioral Deficits on Activities of Daily Living
units.summary: The A-ONE is a standardized criterion-based instrument used by occupational therapists to assess persons with neurologic disorders, such as stroke, affecting ADL. It enables occupational therapists to determine the impact of neurobehavioral impairments on ADL performance in natural contexts, that is, the underlying reason for the lack of independence. It consists of two scales, a Functional Independence scale focusing on ADL performance and Neurobehavioral Impairment scale focusing on the type of impairment and severity of impact. Three possible meth-ods of application of the A-ONE and the conceptual back-ground behind it have developed over the years. In this chapter, ADLs are defined as basic daily activities such as eating, grooming, toileting, and dressing, as well as functional mobility.

units.title: DETECTING THE EFFECT OF NEUROBEHAVIORAL DEFICITS ON ACTIVITY PERFORMANCE
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

DETECTING THE EFFECT OF NEUROBEHAVIORAL DEFICITS ON ACTIVITY PERFORMANCE
units.summary: DETECTING THE EFFECT OF NEUROBEHAVIORAL DEFICITS ON ACTIVITY PERFORMANCE The therapist can detect occupational errors through observation of occupational performance, with these errors indicating the effect of neurobehavioral deficits on task performance. Subsequently, the therapist can hypoth-esize about the impaired body functions that caused the error. As neurobehavioral deficits often interfere with independence, therapists can benefit from detecting errors in occupational performance while observing ADL and thereby gain an understanding of the impairments affecting the patient’s activity limitation. FUNCTION OF THE CEREBRAL CORTEX: THE FOUNDATION OF TASK PERFORMANCE Occupational therapists regularly observe the perfor-mance of daily activities as they work with stroke survi-vors. With the use of clinical reasoning combined with task analysis, detection of impaired neurologic body functions is possible.

CLINICAL REASONING INVOLVED IN USING THE A-ONE
units.summary: CLINICAL REASONING INVOLVED IN USING THE A-ONE As mentioned in an earlier section of this chapter, the thera-pist applies different types of clinical reasoning when applying the A-ONE principles to evaluate task performance and dys-functional body functions that limit the performance. Further exploration is necessary in relation to the reasoning that goes into the A-ONE. When observing dressing performance, the therapist may detect a critical cue such as not dressing one arm. Occupational therapists have basically used two evaluation and intervention approaches when working with patients with neu-rologic conditions: the deficit-specific approach, also termed bottom-up, restorative, or remedial approach, and the functional adaptation or compensation approach, also referred to as top- down or adaptive approach. Evaluation tools used when applying the deficit-specific approach are aimed at the impaired body structures and functions, using the ICF terminology.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Treatment of Cognitive-Perceptual Deficits: A Function-Based Approach
units.summary: The functional approach uses repetitive practice in partic-ular activities, usually daily living tasks, to help the patient become more independent. This approach is designed to treat symptoms rather than the cause of the dysfunction. 37 Some occupational therapists believe that their role in cognitive and perceptual rehabilitation lies solely in the realm of a functional approach, involving training in com-pensatory techniques and only with tasks directly related to functional performance. 83 This approach appears most compatible with research, indicating that family members and financial providers rank independence in ADL as the highest priority for rehabilitation. Remediation (or restoration or transfer of training) emphasizes restoration of the function or the skill lost due to stroke.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Treatment of Cognitive-Perceptual Deficits: A Function-Based Approach
units.summary: TREATMENT APPROACHES FOR SPECIFIC NEUROBEHAVIORAL IMPAIRMENTS Therapists rarely observe perceptual or cognitive deficits in isolation. Usually these deficits overlap and are difficult to interpret because of their complexity. Little research has been conducted or published on outcomes of specific treatment approaches for isolated perceptual and cognitive deficits, with the possible exceptions of memory impair-ments and unilateral neglect. There are several models of awareness that can help develop intervention plans. The pyramid model of self-awareness was developed by Crosson et al.

units.summary: SOCIETAL ATTITUDES AND EXPECTAIONS OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES For the past 45 years, individuals with disabilities have been lobbying for their needs and rights and have been relatively successful with the passage of several laws. The Americans with Disabilities Act has played a major role at the International Classification of Functioning, Disabil-ity and Health (ICF) 7 activities and participation level to increase access to transportation and public places. This increase in environmental accessibility has enabled many individuals with disabilities to pursue their education, employment, and leisure interests to become more active, productive members of society.

units.summary: MANUFACTURER PRODUCTION OF DURABLE MEDICAL EQUIPMENT The durable medical equipment industry has grown tre-mendously in the past 45 years to meet the increasing pop-ulation of individuals with disabilities and the increasing demand for more versatile, lighter-weight products. The increase in product options and advancement to lighter- weight materials such as aircraft quality aluminum and titanium have resulted in a vast selection of off-the-shelf products that have the potential to meet a wide array of needs. Manufacturers understand the need for individuals with disabilities to try specific products to ensure they will meet their needs.

units.title: REHABILITATION SERVICES
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The provision of rehabilitation services has changed dra-matically with respect to length of stay on rehabilitation units and knowledge required to appreciate the variety of wheelchair and seating system options. Initially, clients had sufficient time in rehabilitation programs to reach their full potential and adjust to the changes in their bodies before they received a wheelchair and integrated into their discharge environment, preferably home. Today, because of the influence of traditional insurance funding limita-tions, clients are discharged from rehabilitation units once they are medically stable, have demonstrated restoration gains, and have a support system in place to enable them to be relatively safe with their basic ADL. Mountain and colleagues found that 59% of individuals with stroke who were “non-walking,” with a walking Functional Indepen-dence Measure score of 1 to 5, at admission to their reha-bilitation service were using a wheelchair at discharge.

Medicare has specific codes and reimbursement guidelines for durable medical equipment.

units.summary: SYSTEM AND POLICY CHANGES: DEVELOPMENT OF STANDARDS AND ORGANIZATIONS TO MONITOR ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY SERVICES System changes have evolved over the past four decades and include the development of authorities and organi-zations to organize, control, and monitor assistive tech-nology services. The Rehabilitation Engineering and Assistive Technology Society of North America (RESNA), National Registry of Rehabilitation Technology Suppliers (NRRTS), American Academy of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, and Foundation for Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation have been created or to develop or have been active in developing standards to ensure a higher standard of practice with wheelchair service provision. A monumental accomplishment was the American National Standards Institute/RESNA Wheelchair Standards.

units.title: SITTING: BODY FUNCTION AND STRUCTURES
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: To appreciate and evaluate postural alignment, it is impor-tant to have an understanding of body function and struc-tures. A therapist should understand the basic anatomy of skeletal structures and their relationship to one another. The pelvis is the foundation for sitting; thus, knowledge of the anatomy, biomechanical features of the pelvis, and its relationship with the musculature and fascia of the spine and extremities is essential to understand how changes in lower extremity positioning influence the pelvis and sub-sequently the spine and upper extremity alignment. The pelvis moves anteriorly and posteriorly in the sagittal plane around a coronal axis, laterally tilting in a frontal plane around an anteroposterior axis and rotation-ally in a transverse plane around a vertical axis.

IMPACT OF COMMUNICATION IMPAIRMENT FOLLOWING STROKE
units.summary: IMPACT OF COMMUNICATION IMPAIRMENT FOLLOWING STROKE Communication disorders following stroke include not only the impairment itself but also the person’s emotional response to it, adaptations to the disorder, and recogni-tion and possible acceptance that some changes in com-munication may be permanent. The reaction of the stroke survivor to communication impairment is unique to the individual. The alteration of communication in the first few days and weeks following the “brain attack” can result in a range of emotions, from fear of the future to indiffer-ence.

INCIDENCE AND PREVALENCE OF COMMUNICATION DISORDERS
units.summary: INCIDENCE AND PREVALENCE OF COMMUNICATION DISORDERS Valid statistical information about the incidence of speech and language disorders following stroke is not available. However, according to the American Heart Association, 3 in 2006, there were around 6.5 million stroke survivors alive, and “on average, every 40 seconds someone in the United States has a stroke.” 3 In the United States, the incidence of stroke has actually declined over the past 50 years. 12 The percentage of strokes that have initial symptoms of speech and/or language issues is unknown.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

THE MANAGEMENT OF MOTOR SPEECH DISORDERS
units.summary: Normal speech production requires the exquisite coor-dination of the muscle groups that control respiration, phonation (voice production), resonation, and articula-tion. 21,24 The ever-changing automatic adjustments for speech to balance the motor subsystems and integrate the movements require complex motor control. Respiratory weakness, for example, results in reduced loudness, short phrases, and awkward breath groups. Ultimately, it is a major factor in the fatigue associated with speaking and even decreased desire to speak. Unilateral Upper Motor Neuron Dysarthria One of the most common and identifiable dysarthrias is unilateral upper motor neuron dysarthria.

MEDICAL COMPLICATIONS ASSOCIATED WITH DYSPHAGIA IN STROKE
units.summary: Aspiration refers to the penetration of food or liquid into the airway, below the level of the vocal folds, before, dur-ing, or after the swallow. Laryngeal penetration refers to the entrance of food or liquid into the larynx, above the level of the vocal folds. 53 Silent aspiration is defined as the entrance of saliva, food, or liquid below the level of the true vocal folds without a cough or any clinical signs of difficulty. 38 Aspiration and laryngeal penetration occur when the ability of the swallowing mechanism to prevent material from entering the airway is impaired. Aspiration can lead to aspiration pneumonia in patients with stroke, 54,59,63,77,86 which may lead to hospitaliza-tion or death.

units.title: ROLE OF THE SWALLOWING TEAM
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: A tracheostomy is a hole or stoma in the neck that allows breathing to occur either directly through the stoma or through a tracheostomy tube. The stoma or tube is situated below the vocal cords and creates a path for the airway, allowing respiration to occur through the stoma or tube, rather than through the upper airway. The surgical procedure to create the stoma is a tracheotomy, although these two terms are sometimes used interchangeably. Critically ill patients with or without stroke require tracheos-tomy when they cannot breathe normally (respiratory failure), when fluid builds up in the upper airway, and/or when there is a blockage in the airway. In inpatient settings, optimal management of dysphagia is performed by a multidisciplinary team.

units.title: Stroke
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Stroke Stroke is essentially a disease of the cerebral vasculature in which a failure to supply oxygen to brain cells, which are the most susceptible to ischemic damage, leads to their death. Strokes are comprised of two broad categories: ischemic and hemorrhagic. Ischemic strokes account for approximately 80% of strokes, and hemorrhagic strokes account for the remainder.

units.title: Transient Ischemic Attack
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Transient Ischemic Attack Symptoms of a transient ischemic attack (TIA) include the focal deficits of an ischemic stroke within a clearly vascular distribution, but in the case of TIAs patients return to base-line without noticeable clinical deficits within a few minutes to hours. Previously TIAs were thought to be completely reversible without any cerebral infarction; however as the sensitivity of imaging has improved, small areas of infarct frequently can be seen with TIAs. The causes of TIAs are the same as other forms of ischemic stroke. By definition, the clinical symptoms of TIAs must resolve clinically in less than 24 hours.

units.title: Cardiac Sources
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Cardiac Sources Cardiac dysrhythmias, structural anomalies, and acute infarctions are the usual causes of cardiac emboli. The most common source of an embolism is the left atrium of patients with atrial fibrillation. The usual mechanism of thrombus formation in atrial fibrillation is by clot forma-tion in the left atrial appendage. This then breaks off and creates an embolus that can move through the arterial sys-tem.
