units.title: Vascular Sources
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Vascular Sources The sources of vascular emboli are usually atheromatous plaques in the walls of the aorta, carotid arteries, or smaller vessels in the cerebral circulation. Platelet activation and the formation of a fibrin clot can occur rapidly. The most com-mon areas affected by the emboli of the vascular system are the same as those affected by cardiac sources of emboli. The most common areas for ulcerated plaques in the cerebral blood supply are the aorta and the proximal internal carotid artery.

The most common areas for ulcerated plaques in the cerebral blood supply are the aorta and the proximal internal carotid artery.

units.title: Paradoxical Sources
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Paradoxical Sources Congenital atrial septal defects can create the opportunity for emboli to cross from the right-sided (venous) circula-tion to the left-sided (arterial) circulation, an uncommon source of cerebral emboli. Paradoxical embolic material can originate from a deep venous thrombosis (DVT). Transesophageal echocardiography with a “bubble study” helps identify patients at risk for this condition. One of the most common atrial shunting abnormalities is a pat-ent foramen ovale (PFO; the fetal opening between the right and left sides of the heart).

units.title: Unknown Sources
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Unknown Sources Thrombi of unknown source often occur in patients with known hypercoagulability syndromes. These syndromes can result from acquired diseases (e.g., lupus anticoagulant and metastatic tumors) or inborn errors of the coagula-tion system (e.g., protein S and C deficiencies). Surgery or medication therapies such as estrogen replacement can induce iatrogenic causes of hypercoagulable states. Even when the patient is known to be in a hypercoagulable state, the source of the emboli may remain unknown.

units.title: Pathophysiology
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Atherosclerotic plaque formation is greatest at the branching points of major vessels and forms in areas of turbulent flow. Chronic hypertension is a common pre-cursor, and damage to the intimal wall may be followed by lymphocyte infiltration. Foam cells then develop, and the first stage of atherosclerosis is formed. Calcification and narrowing with resultant turbulent flow follow.

units.title: Atherothrombotic Disease
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Atherothrombotic Disease The most common site for the development of atheroscle-rosis and the subsequent development of atherothrombosis that leads to TIAs and stroke in the anterior circulation is the origin of the carotid artery and in the posterior circula-tion is the top of the basilar artery. Other sites of athero-sclerosis include the carotid siphon and the stems (bases) of the middle cerebral artery, anterior cerebral artery, and origin of the basilar artery. 40 The atheromatous plaques are sources of emboli that can cause distal symptoms in a TIA or stroke. These embolic events are similar events from other embolic sources.

units.title: Lacunar Syndrome
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Lacunar Syndrome A lacunar stroke occurs in one of the perforating branches of the circle of Willis, the middle cerebral artery stem, or the vertebral or basilar arteries. The occlusion of these vessels results from the atherothrombotic or lipohyalinotic blockage of one of these arteries. The development of dis-ease in these arteries correlates closely with the presence of chronic hypertension and diabetic microvascular dis-ease. 138,83 These are small vessels, 100 to 300 μm in diam-eter, that branch off the main artery and penetrate into the deep gray or white matter of the cerebrum.

units.title: Hemorrhagic Conversion
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Hemorrhagic Conversion As a sequela of an embolic or ischemic infarction, a purely ischemic infarct may convert into a hemorrhagic lesion. Thrombi can migrate, lyse, and reperfuse into an isch-emic area, leading to small hemorrhages (petechial hem-orrhages) because the damaged capillaries and small blood vessels no longer maintain their integrity. These damaged areas then can coalesce (combine) and form a hemorrhage into ischemic tissue. 90 These conversions are more com-mon in large infarcts, such as an occluded middle cere-bral artery, or in a large infarction in the distribution of a lenticulostriate artery.

units.title: Hypertensive Bleed
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Hypertensive Bleed Hypertensive cerebral hemorrhages usually occur in one of four sites: the putamen and internal capsule, pons, thalamus, and cerebellum. Usually these hemorrhages develop from small penetrating arteries in the deep brain that have had damage from hypertension. The usual hypertensive ICH develops over the span of a few minutes but occasionally can take as long as 60 minutes or longer to reach maximal size. Unlike ischemic infarcts, hemor-rhagic bleeds do not follow the anatomic distribution of blood vessels but dissect through tissue planes spherically.

units.title: Lobar Intracerebral Bleed
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Lobar Intracerebral Bleed Lobar hemorrhages are ICHs that occur outside the basal ganglia and thalamus in the white matter of the cerebral cortex. These types of hemorrhages and hypertension are not correlated clearly; the most common underlying con-dition in patients with this type of ICH is cerebral amyloid angiopathy. 27 Other causes include the presence of AVMs, bleeding diatheses, tumors (e.g., melanoma or glioma), aneurysms in the circle of Willis, and a large number of idiopathic cases. has drawn increased attention in recent years as CAA has shown a clear association with lobar hemorrhage and an increased risk for rebleeding compared to other causes.

units.title: Saccular Aneurysm and Subarachnoid Bleed
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Saccular Aneurysm and Subarachnoid Bleed A saccular aneurysm rupture is the most common cause of a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). 166 Saccular aneurysms occur at the bifurcation (branching) points of the large arteries in the brain and are most commonly found in the anterior portion of the circle of Willis. 11 An estimated 0.5% to 1% of normal individuals harbor saccular aneurysms. 171 Despite the high number, bleeding from them is rare (6 to 16 per 100,000).

units.title: Arteriovenous Malformation
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Arteriovenous Malformation AVMs are found throughout the body and can occur in any part of the brain. They are usually congenital and consist of an abnormal tangle of blood vessels connect-ing arterial and venous systems without an intervening capillary bed. They range from a few millimeters in size to large masses that can increase cardiac output because of the amount of their blood flow. The larger AVMs in the brain tend to be found in the posterior portions of the cerebral hemispheres.

units.title: Posttraumatic Hemorrhagic Stroke
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Posttraumatic Hemorrhagic Stroke A traumatic brain injury commonly results in hemorrhagic damage to the brain in addition to ischemic and other injuries. The four major types of injury caused by trau-matic brain injury include SAH and ICH, diffuse axonal injury, contusions, and anoxic injury from hypoperfusion (decreased flow in the vessels) and hypoxemia (decreased oxygen level). This combination of injuries leads to a con-stellation of findings that mixes the features of a number of individual ischemic and hemorrhagic injuries.

units.title: Stroke-like Syndromes
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Stroke-like Syndromes A number of conditions in addition to TIAs and cerebral infarctions can cause transient paralysis. These condi-tions generally resolve spontaneously with no long-term sequelae. The most common cause of transient hemipa-resis is Todd paralysis, which develops postictally (after a seizure). Todd paralysis results from neurotransmit-ter depletion and neuronal fatigue in focal areas of the brain caused by the extremely high neuronal firing rate during a seizure.

Often the initial symptoms are seizures and ICHs.

units.title: Computed Tomography
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Computed Tomography CT is a readily available and useful technique that has become the standard for the evaluation of a patient expe-riencing an acute onset of stroke. The most important functions of a CT scan in an acute patient are identify-ing the presence of a hemorrhage (best seen on CT) and ruling out other conditions (e.g., tumor or abscess). In the acute phase of stroke, most CT scans are actually negative with no clear evidence of abnormalities. A nega-tive immediate CT scan with an acute neurologic deficit determined by physical examination actually can verify the impression of stroke because it rules out tumors, hem-orrhages, and other brain lesions.

units.title: Unheaded source content
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: The diagnosis of stroke and differentiation of stroke from strokelike syndromes is based on the clinical presentation and physical examination of the patient. The examiner needs to differentiate a true stroke from syndromes that can mimic a stroke, such as Todd paralysis, seizures, multiple sclerosis, tumors, and metabolic syndromes. Most often, the patient’s symptoms in the emergency department (ED) include an acute onset of weakness or other neurologic deficits. The patient history can help identify the risk fac-tors for stroke and the nature of the lesion.

units.title: CT Angiography
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: CT Angiography CT angiography is performed by creating a 3D recon-struction of flow within the blood vessels of the brain after injecting contrast material through a peripheral vein. This helps identify filling defects and any large vessel occlu-sions. As new interventional treatments for acute stroke become more widely accepted, there is a time sensitive need to assess for these large vessel occlusions. When a large vessel is blocked by a thrombus the patient may be eligible for mechanical retrieval of the clot by neuroin-terventionalists.

units.title: Transcranial and Carotid Doppler
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Transcranial and carotid Doppler studies allow for noninva-sive visualization of the cerebral vessels. The advantages are that they provide useful therapeutic information on the state of the cerebral vessels and the blood flow to the brain. Approx-imately one third of patients who have had ischemic strokes that are cardiac in origin have significant cerebrovascular disease. 104 Patients with symptoms or evidence of posterior circulation disease are tested best with a transcranial Doppler study, including examination of the vertebrobasilar system.

units.title: Magnetic Resonance Angiography
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: MRA is used to evaluate patients with stroke symptoms to detect any vascular abnormalities that may have caused the stroke or to look for alterations of cerebral blood flow that may have resulted from an embolic or thrombotic event. This is a very common noninvasive technique and is often done at the time of the MRI scan to assess the extent of cerebral injury; MRA is able to image vessels similarly to classical angiography. 173 The newer techniques of MRA have sensitivity for detection of 86% to 90% 122 for detec-tion of severe stenosis, and the earlier issues of relatively low specificity of 64% 9,86 (because of overdetection by the earlier techniques) is now in the range of 89% to 96% for studies done with contrast-enhanced MRA. 78 Despite these advantages, the spatial resolution is still less than traditional angiography, which may be an issue in patients in whom surgical management is planned.

units.title: Electrocardiography
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Electrocardiography (ECG) is used to evaluate patients with stroke symptoms to detect dysrhythmias (which may be a source of embolism) or MI or other acute cardiac events that may be related to an acute stroke. Given that ECG is just a snapshot in time and arrhythmias are often paroxysmal, new techniques which allow for longer term monitoring for dysrhythmias have been adopted. A Holter monitor is a non-invasive device which is worn for 24-48 hours and records ECG activity with external skin elec-trodes. For patients whose rhythm will need to be moni-tored longer, an implantable loop recorder may be used.

units.title: Blood Work
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: The standard acute evaluation of the stroke patient includes a screening set of blood analyses, including hematologic studies, serum electrolyte levels, and renal (e.g., serum creatinine) and hepatic chemical analyses (liver function tests). The typical hematologic evaluation includes a complete blood count, platelet count, pro-thrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time (PTT). These studies help to rule out other causes of stroke-like symptoms, to diagnose complications, and to allow for a baseline analysis before the initiation of therapies such as anticoagulation. The blood chemistry analyses allow met-abolic abnormalities to be ruled out, as do the renal and hepatic chemistry analyses.

units.title: Acute Stroke Management
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: In management of acute stroke patients, basic medical needs such as airway protection, maintenance of adequate circulation, and the treatment of any acute concurrent medical problems (e.g. myocardial infarction, dysrhyth-mias) are addressed. The neurologic management of the acute stroke focuses on identifying the cause of the stroke, determining if the patient is a candidate for reperfusion therapy, preventing progression of the lesion, and treating acute neurologic complications.

units.title: General Principles
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: The general principles of acute stroke management include attempting to stop progression of the lesion to limit deficits and early reperfusion of ischemic territory, reducing cerebral edema, decreasing the risk of hydro-cephalus, treating seizures, and preventing complications such as DVT or aspiration that may lead to severe illness. Reperfusion remains a fundamen-tal goal of ischemic stroke management when feasible, using either thrombolytics or mechanical thrombectomy, and reduces both mortality and disability after stroke. units.title: Clot Retrieval, Mechanical Thrombectomy
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Clot Retrieval, Mechanical Thrombectomy Although IV tPA has been widely adopted, it comes with a significant risk of subsequent ICH and has a limited suc-cess rate in reestablishing blood flow in large vessel occlu-sions. These facts along with the narrow therapeutic time window for tPA administration led to the development of endovascular clot retrieval devices. The first clot retrieval device, Mechanical Embolus Removal in Cerebral Isch-emia (MERCI), was approved by the FDA in 2004. Since then, there have been major improvements in technology and an explosion of clinical literature investigating this class of devices and optimizing the indications for their use.

units.title: Certified Stroke Centers & Mobile Stroke Units
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
Certified Stroke Centers & Mobile Stroke Units
units.summary: Certified Stroke Centers & Mobile Stroke Units Given the time sensitive nature of interventions such as IV tPA and clot retrieval there has been a push to reduce time to intervention. Part of this effort includes the dilemma of whether or not to bypass a nearby hos-pital in favor of transporting a patient to a more distant hospital with interventional capabilities. Hospitals that have acute stroke teams, stroke protocols, stroke units and the ability to administer tPA can be certified as Pri-mary Stroke Centers by the Joint Commission. Those with interventional capabilities and coverage by neuro-interventionalists can garner the Comprehensive Stroke Center certification.

units.title: Other Treatments for Altering Cerebral Perfusion
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
Other Treatments for Altering Cerebral Perfusion
units.summary: Other Treatments for Altering Cerebral Perfusion A number of different treatments aimed at lowering blood viscosity or cerebral perfusion have been used in the past, including hemodilution with agents such as dextran, albu-min, and hetastarch. None of the 12 studies reviewed by Asplund demonstrated any clear benefit. 5 Similarly, stud-ies of prostacyclins and several different types of cerebral vasodilators have also shown no clear evidence of increased survival rates or improvement in outcomes after treat-ment. 97 Research continues to be active in these areas, but so far none of these alternative treatments for increasing cerebral perfusion has yielded a favorable outcome.

97 Research continues to be active in these areas, but so far none of these alternative treatments for increasing cerebral perfusion has yielded a favorable outcome.

units.title: Agents for Cerebral Edema
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Agents for Cerebral Edema Agents that reduce cerebral edema include corticosteroids, mannitol, glycerol, vinca alkaloids, and piracetam. All the studies done on persons receiving steroids 132 after an acute stroke demonstrated no clear benefits, and steroid use cre-ates a risk of hyperglycemia and DVT. 55 Use of the other agents also has no clear benefit in the treatment of acute stroke, so they are also not routinely used. Interventions for cerebral edema are typically limited to elevating the head of the bed, monitoring serum electrolytes, and neu-rosurgical intervention if cerebral edema is so severe as to necessitate direct reduction of intracranial pressure.

units.title: Cooling Therapy
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Cooling Therapy Another proposed treatment of acute stroke has been the initiation of cooling therapy on presentation with the induction of a medical coma to limit the extent of brain injury after stroke. In most patients who present with stroke, there is a natural tendency for the body temper-ature to be elevated between, which is associated with increased injury and poorer outcomes. 12,29 Induction of hypothermia has shown some promise in post cardiac arrest patients who do not quickly regain consciousness when they achieve return of spontaneous circulation, and is now included in the most recent Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) guidelines. Despite success in post arrest patients, existing studies on the application of mechani-cal or pharmacologic cooling of acute stroke patients do not yet provide convincing evidence that death or long- term disability is significantly reduced.

units.title: Surgical Therapies
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: A carotid endarterectomy (CEA) is the surgical opening of the carotid arteries to remove plaque and restore flow. This therapy has been shown to be use-ful in preventing recurrent strokes or development of stroke in individuals with TIAs, but it has not been used to treat acute stroke. In theory, the opening of the carot-ids could subject ischemic areas and their blood vessels to excessive pressure from restored blood flow and lead to hemorrhage. 118 Concerns about using major anesthesia in a patient with an acute stroke makes this surgery too risky to treat acute stroke.

units.title: Hemorrhagic Stroke
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: In patients who have had a hemorrhagic stroke, the size and location of the lesion determine the overall prognosis; supratentorial lesions larger than 5 cm have a poor prog-nosis, and brainstem lesions larger than 3 cm are usually fatal. 41 In these cases, the control of edema is important, and the techniques previously described can be used. In patients with SAH, the treatment regimen is usually more aggressive and focuses on several issues, which include the control of ICP, prevention of re-bleeding, maintenance of cerebral perfusion, and control of vasospasm.

units.title: Prevention of Re-bleeding
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Prevention of Re-bleeding Before 1980, 6 weeks of bed rest was prescribed routinely for the care of patients with acute SAH to prevent re- bleeding. In 1981, a study demonstrated that bed rest was inferior to surgical treatment, lowering of blood pres-sure, and carotid ligation. 171 Carotid ligation has been largely abandoned because of its surgical risks and the advent of techniques for direct repair of the aneurysm including clipping and endovascular coiling. Only treat-ment of the aneurysm itself has been shown to be effec-tive in preventing re-bleeding.

units.title: Control of Vasospasm
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Control of Vasospasm The treatment of vasospasm is important to pre-vent ischemic stroke as a complication of SAH. Cur-rent treatments include the use of orally administered nimodipine, a calcium channel blocker shown to improve outcomes of patients who have had an SAH with vasospasm. Nimodipine is administered within the first 4 days of SAH and continued for 21 days. The use of hypertension, hypervolemia, and hemodilution was initially recommended by some studies.

units.title: Hypertension
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Hypertension Diastolic and systolic hypertension are each independently and strongly implicated in causing stroke. Hypertension increases the risk of stroke in all age groups of men and women. 180 In fact, no threshold level of blood pressure exists below which the risk curve plateaus. 107 For every 7.5–mm Hg increase in diastolic pressure is a 46% increase in stroke incidence and a 29% increase in coronary heart disease (CHD).

units.title: Hyperlipidemia
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Hyperlipidemia Strokes are a well-established complication of athero-sclerotic disease and the development of atherosclerotic disease in the carotid arteries as well as other vascula-ture has been shown to be related to the levels of serum lipids. 144 The treatment of hyperlipidemia through the use of statins has been used successfully for pri-mary prevention of stroke in patients with risk factors for cerebrovascular disease. 142,62 Low density lipopro-tein (LDL) cholesterol has been specifically targeted as being associated with the development of clinically significant atherosclerotic disease. Recommendations center around the reduction of LDL specifically, with target levels depending on cardiovascular risk.

units.title: Diabetes
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Diabetes The rate of atherosclerosis development in coronary, femoral, and cerebral vessels is increased in patients with diabetes. Stroke is increased 2.5 to 4 times in patients with diabetes compared with those without diabetes. 94 In the Framingham Study, glucose intolerance (blood sugar >150 mg/mL) is only a significant, independent contribu-tor to stroke in older women and is greater for women than men at any age. 87 Because of the associated risk of stroke, careful management of diabetes in addition to all other risk factors is prudent.

units.title: Oral Contraceptives
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Oral Contraceptives In women older than age 35 years who have other stroke risk factors, oral contraceptive use is associated with an increased incidence of stroke. 18 The relative risk for oral contraceptive users is approximately five times greater if they are already in the high-risk group. With the use of lower estrogen oral contraceptives, the risk has decreased substantially in recent years. 159 That the incidence of fatal SAH increased in oral contraceptive-using women with concomitant smoking is noteworthy; in the group older than age 35 years, the incidence is four times higher.

units.title: Lifestyle Modification (Activity, Alcohol Consumption, Smoking)
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Lifestyle Modification (Activity, Alcohol Consumption, Smoking) General lifestyle modification including exercise, limiting alcohol consumption and avoiding or quitting smoking have clear benefits for reducing risk of stroke. Although weight loss and exercise have been clearly associated with a reduction in heart disease morbidity and mortality, the link to stroke is not as well established. Even with limited evi-dence linking these particular behavioral changes to stroke, encouraging a healthier diet and addressing obesity affects other cardiovascular risk factors including hypertension and hyperlipidemia, and is an important part of post-stroke counseling. The AHA and American Stroke Association (ASA) both recommend weight loss for patients who are overweight or obese as a general strategy for health.

units.title: Antiplatelet Medications
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Antiplatelet Medications In patients who have had a TIA or stroke, long-term use of aspirin has been shown to decrease the incidence of death, MI, and recurrent events by up to 23%. 24 The doses of aspirin used across numerous studies have ranged from 30 mg to 600 mg; all doses resulted in a 14% to 18% reduction in recurrent cerebral events, but gastrointesti-nal complications increased with the higher doses. 61,39,63 In general, the standard dosage of one baby aspirin (81 mg/day) is the usual treatment for recurrent ischemic stroke. Multiple other antiplatelet agents have arisen in recent years as alternatives or additions to aspirin.

units.title: Anticoagulation
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Anticoagulation The risk for stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation is approximately 5 fold higher than those without. Those patients who have already had a stroke and remain untreated for atrial fibrillation have an estimated risk of recurrent stroke per year of 2.2% to greater than 10% based on other risk factors. 43 Factors that increased risk in the large Swed-ish Atrial Fibrillation Cohort Study include gender (female), hypertension, diabetes, CHF, and age. For patients who have atrial fibrillation with cardiac sources of emboli, full anticoagulation is the treatment of choice; this is true for pri-mary and secondary prevention.

units.title: Carotid Endarterectomy
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Carotid Endarterectomy Carotid stenosis is often discovered in the evaluation for the cause of a stroke. Routine screening for carotid disease is not recommended, however. The surgical treatment of carotid artery stenosis has been shown to be beneficial in recent studies of stroke recurrence in patients with severely (>70%) stenosed carotid arteries. 25,57 For patients with high-grade stenosis, CEA reduces the range of stroke risk from 22% to 26% down to 8% to 12%.

units.title: Hemorrhagic Stroke
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: The mainstay of ICH prevention is controlling systolic and diastolic hypertension. No clear benefit exists for one group of treatment agents versus another as long as adequate hypertension control is maintained. In patients in whom the ICH follows vasculitis or the use of antico-agulants, the treatment for preventing recurrence includes treating the vasculitis or terminating anticoagulant use. 138 The secondary prevention of recurrent stroke and SAH of AVMs or aneurysms includes surgical management of the lesions (the treatment of choice).

units.title: General Principles
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: To prevent complications and long-term sequelae after a stroke, maximizing function, decreasing morbidity, and preventing rehospitalization from a complication are important. Prevention of these complications begins on the day the patient arrives at the hospital with symptoms of acute stroke. Many complications are associated with bed rest in general, but some are specific to stroke.

units.title: Contractures
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Contractures Contractures are periarticular motion impairments that result from loss of elasticity in the periarticular tissues, which include muscles, tendons, and ligaments. Con-tractures can occur in any immobilized joint but are particularly prevalent in paretic limbs after a stroke. In fact, only 10% of hemiplegic stroke patients recover limb strength and mobility rapidly enough to avoid devel-oping contractures 65 Shoulder pain, contractures, and muscle pain occur in 70% to 80% of patients who have had a hemiplegic stroke. 9 Chapter 20 addresses the man-agement and related issues of the hemiplegic shoulder.

units.title: BOX 1.1 Treatments for Osteoporosis
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: 70 To prevent shortening of the connective tissue in muscles and joints, an active range of motion (ROM) program must be initiated. Because cer-tain muscles span two joints, joints must be positioned to allow full physiological stretch of the muscles involved. When a contracture is present, the mainstay of treatment is gradual, prolonged stretch. The minimal treatment is a sustained stretch greater than 30 minutes.

units.title: Osteoporosis
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Osteoporosis Bone is a metabolically active tissue normally in a state of equilibrium between active bone resorption and deposi-tion. The ratio of bone formation to bone resorption is influenced by the stressors to which the bone is subjected, a relationship known as Wolff’s law. 135 The lack of weight bearing and normal stress on long bones on the hemiple-gic side of a stroke patient leads to a predominance of bone resorption. This loss of bone mass can start as early as 30 hours after the beginning of immobility 170 and with bed rest can be as high as 25% to 45% in 30 to 36 weeks.

units.title: Falls
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Falls Falls are of particular concern in survivors of stroke. These patients are at increased risk of hip fracture because of developed osteoporosis, and the acuity of their balance, visual perceptions, and spatial perceptions are decreased. The increased risk of falls has been documented in several studies and is greater in patients who have had a right hemi-spheric stroke. 130,117,128 Fall prevention should emphasize balance and cognitive training, removing environmental hazards, and using adaptive devices.

units.title: Seizures
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Seizures Seizures after strokes have been documented since the 19th century. Whereas the incidence of late-onset seizures (epi-lepsy) in individuals who have had strokes ranges from 6% to 18%, 52,71,175 the incidence of early seizures is approxi-mately 10%, with reports ranging from 3% to 38%. 10,179 The risk for seizures is highest right after stroke: 57% of seizures occur in the first week, and 88% of all seizures after stroke occur in the first year. 10 Seizures are more common in patients who have had any type of hemorrhagic stroke; 85% of these seizures are early seizures.

units.title: Hydrocephalus
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Hydrocephalus Hydrocephalus can occur acutely, especially in patients with SAH and ICH as discussed previously, or it can develop insidiously later. Hydrocephalus is usually her-alded by the gradual onset of a triad of symptoms, includ-ing lethargy with decreased mental function, ataxia, and urinary incontinence. When hydrocephalus is suspected, one should perform a CT scan promptly, demonstrated ventricular enlargement in this condition. Treatment typ-ically involves surgical placement of a ventricular shunt.

units.title: Spasticity
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Spasticity Spasticity is defined as a motor disorder characterized by a velocity-dependent increase in tonic stretch reflexes with exaggerated tendon jerks. 84 In a typi-cal pattern of recovery after hemiplegic stroke, an initial period occurs with little resistance to passive motion of the muscles and joints. Approximately 48 hours after the stroke, tendon reflexes and muscle resistance to passive motion begin to return. 70 Whereas the lower extremity usually develops extensor spasticity that can assist with function, the upper extremity spasticity is usually in a flexor pattern.

units.title: Post Stroke Pain
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Post Stroke Pain Pain following a stroke can be secondary to musculoskele-tal, mechanical complications as discussed previously or as a result of damage to the central nervous system. Central pain from a stroke typically presents 1-2 months after the event with burning, tingling, radiating pain. This type of pain affects approximately 10% of stroke survivors and is most common in patients whose strokes affected areas of the CNS carrying sensory pathways. Post stroke central pain syndrome (PSCPS) is classically described due to thalamic stroke, but can originate from damage to sensory tracts throughout the CNS.

units.title: Deconditioning
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Deconditioning Physiological deconditioning in patients after a stroke results from the acute medical illness and the associated bed rest and immobility that may result. Table 1.9 lists some of the effects of deconditioning. All of these factors can alter the ability of the patient to recover. Therefore, it is important to get the patient out of bed early post- stroke, and to increase activity steadily.

units.title: Psychological Complications
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Psychological Complications Stroke is a major life event and is associated with signifi-cant alterations in the individual’s well-being and inde-pendence. Negative emotional reactions are common in patients after a stroke 168 and can have a significant effect on the patient’s eventual outcome. After a stroke, patients may go through the four stages of bereavement described by Worden. 85 These include accepting the loss, experienc-ing the pain of the loss, adjusting to a new environment in which previous abilities are missing, and investing in new activities.

units.title: Urinary Tract Dysfunction
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Urinary Tract Dysfunction Urinary incontinence is common after stroke, affecting 51% to 60% of patients, 14 and can cause difficulties with rehabilitation, influence eventual discharge location, and place stress on caregivers. 36 One month and 6 months after stroke, 29% and 14% of patients, respectively, still have urinary incontinence. 31 The usual pathophysiology of incontinence is detrusor hyperreflexia, which is com-mon in patients with cortical lesions. A stroke damages the inhibitory pathways that modulate micturition.

units.title: Skin Breakdown and Decubitus Ulcers
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Skin Breakdown and Decubitus Ulcers Pressure ulcer formation is a serious health problem in debilitated and immobilized patients. After a stroke, patients are at particular risk for pressure ulcers because they have numerous factors contributing to skin break-down. Abnormal sensation, contracture, malnutrition, immobility, and muscle and soft- tissue atrophy often develop and may be complicated by advanced age. Pre-vention of pressure ulcers should be the focus of care.

units.title: Dysphagia
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Dysphagia Swallowing disorders are common after a stroke. Dyspha-gia is more common in elderly patients, with an incidence of 25% to 45%. 52,54 Aspiration can lead to pneumonia, and decreased oral intake can lead to dehydration and malnutrition. Screening for dysphagia should occur within the first 24 hours of hospitalization for patients with acute stroke, before oral feedings or medications are initiated (AHA stroke rehab guidelines).

units.title: Aspiration
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Aspiration Aspiration causes chemical pneumonitis that can lead to a secondary bacterial infection. Because numerous anaero-bic organisms colonize the mouth, aspiration pneumonia can develop into an anaerobic abscess. 116 Such abscesses occur less frequently in edentulous individuals because they have reduced oral flora; abscesses can occur in up to one third of hospitalized patients. 103 The treatment of choice is to reduce the risk of aspiration and to administer antibiotics.

units.title: Deep Venous Thrombosis
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Deep Venous Thrombosis DVT is a common prob-lem after stroke and has an inci-dence of 23% to 75% depending on the severity of the stroke. Most of the morbidity and mortality associated with DVT results from venous thromboembolism (VTE). Pulmonary embolism (PE) after stroke has an incidence of 10% to 29% and a mortality rate of 10%. 13 The forma-tion of DVT is caused by the triad of risk factors outlined by Virchow postulates: altered blood flow, damage to the blood vessel wall, and altered blood coagulability.

units.title: Improved Primary Stroke Prevention
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Primary prevention of stroke remains the most important strategy to decrease morbidity and mortality from stroke. With a good understanding of the risk factors for stroke, risk factor modification can be targeted at groups and individuals who are at risk. Table 1.1 lists the preventable and nonpreventable risk factors for stroke. Many of the risk factors are shared with other forms of cardiovascu-lar disease, so the modification of stroke risk factors also decreases the risk of cardiac-related morbidity and mortal-ity.

units.title: Cardiac Rehabilitation for Stroke Patients
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Cardiac and vascular diseases share many risk factors with ischemic stroke. In an effort to decrease recurrent stroke, there is a movement to develop exercise and educational interventions that mirror traditional cardiac rehabilitation programs. Another driver for the modified cardiac reha-bilitation programs for stroke is the recognition that the most common cause of death in stroke survivors is actu-ally cardiac disease. 106 Studies of the potential benefits of modified cardiac rehabilitation programs for stroke are underway in different trials in Europe and North Amer-ica.

units.title: INTROCUCTION TO ACUTE STROKE REHABILITATION
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: The neuro-ICU may be the starting point of occupational therapy (OT) evaluation and treatment. Many patients are evaluated by an occupational therapist within 48 hours of a stroke. The ICU environment is often fast paced with the focus on monitoring the individual patient’s medical status. The primary goals of any neuro-ICU are to stabilize the patient medically, progress the patient neurologically, and support the patient and family through this neurologic crisis.

units.title: THE IMPORTANCE OF EARLY INTERVENTION
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: There are many common complications associated with a prolonged ICU stay, which include but are not limited to deconditioning, muscle weakness, contractures, skin impairments, depression, anxiety, and reduced quality of life. 53 Early OT, engaging in ADLs and mobilization, can increase a patient’s level of consciousness, enhance overall mental well-being, and foster functional indepen-dence. 139,161 Occupational therapists provide a variety of treatments in the ICU, including, but not limited to, evaluations, splinting, positioning, cognitive retraining, self-care, and functional mobility training.

At teaching hospitals, a team of residents may also make medical decisions regarding the patients.

units.title: BOX 1.4 Initiating Treatment

Such reasons may be a change in mental status, development of a deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, or expansion of the stroke.

units.title: Telemetry
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Telemetry detects both the heart rate and rhythm and displays this reading on the monitor. An ECG is read by placing 12 electri-cal leads to read heart rate and rhythm; bedside telemetry uses either three or five leads. The primary nurse sets both heart rate and rhythm parameters on the monitor. If the rate and rhythm become abnormal, an alarm will sound.

units.title: Foley Catheter
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Foley Catheter A Foley catheter is indwelling and is used to drain urine from the bladder. The therapist should avoid clamping the catheter; doing so could result in a backup of urine in the bladder. The bag, which collects the urine, needs to be at a lower level than the patient’s bladder for the urine to flow in the correct direction.

units.title: External Ventricular Drain
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management

This procedure is used when the ICP is elevated, and the drain may be clamped for short periods of time by nursing only. Because of specific calibration, function of the drain, and accuracy in measurement, the head of the bed must be elevated to a specific level.

units.title: Spinal Drain
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management

The lumbar drain should be set to drain below the level of the leak. When the drain is open and is draining CSF, the spinal drain is set at a determined level next to the bed.

units.title: Graded Sitting and Standing Activities
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Graded Sitting and Standing Activities Supported Sitting in Bed. For the supported sitting in bed position, the head of the bed should gradually be raised in approximately 30- to 40-degree increments to avoid an orthostatic hypotensive response. As the patient tolerates the change in degrees of elevation, the therapist should continue to monitor vital signs. If there appears to be no change in the patient’s blood pressure, the therapist should continue to elevate the head of the bed to approximately 80 degrees.

units.summary: Evaluate the potential cause if edema is present. Discuss with nursing whether the swelling may be associated with the presence of a blood clot or an IV infiltrate. In the ICU, the preferred method for treating edema is positional elevation because compression garments or ace wraps may not be appropriate because of various IVs and line access needed by nursing.

units.title: SHOULDER MANAGEMENT
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: Many patients may experience upper extremity edema, pain, humeral head subluxation, or impingement after a stroke (see Chapter 20). Many of the upper extremity interventions provided in the ICU or acute stage are pro-phylactic measures to prevent these problems. To protect the shoulder against potential pain and subluxation, the team should be educated in proper roll-ing techniques and bed mobility so they can avoid pulling on the extremity. The team should be instructed to roll the patient by placing the hands on the trunk rather than pulling on the extremity.

units.summary: INCREASING SPATIAL AWARENESS BY ARRANGING THE ENVIRONMENT Although the ICU environment may be more restrictive than a rehabilitation setting, there are subtle yet important interventions that can be implemented to increase spatial awareness. Strategically place items of common use, such as the television remote control, on the involved side while providing cues to assist the patient in locating them. Stra-tegically place food items on the meal tray during feeding to encourage scanning and locating desired items to eat.

units.title: SKIN PROTECTION AND PREVENTION OF BREAKDOWN
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
SKIN PROTECTION AND PREVENTION OF BREAKDOWN
units.summary: Skin breakdown and development of pressure ulcers are common complications associated with an ICU or acute admission. After stroke, patients are at risk for develop-ing pressure ulcers because of prolonged bed rest and immobility. Other risk factors include poor circulation, poor nutrition, edema, low level of arousal, confusion, and incontinence. 4 Pressure management and skin protection should become a part of each treatment session.

section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: For patients who are unable to communicate verbally, whether because of mechanical ventilation or aphasia, alternative methods of communication are necessary. Exam-ples may include Nurse, Doctor, Pain, Thirst, and so on, to which the patient can then point.

units.summary: Training in ADLs is an integral part of OT treatment. It is important to engage patients in self-care tasks as soon as they are medically stable. Energy expenditure is often an issue for low- level patients, so grading the self-care task is as important as the choice of activity. Acute patients may also be limited by IVs, lines, and artificial ventilation.

units.title: FAMILY TRAINING
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
units.summary: The primary purpose of family training in the ICU or acute setting is to allow for the patient to engage in as many therapeutic activities as possible immediately after the neurologic event. Family members should be empow-ered to assist their loved ones to achieve their therapy goals. Occupational therapists may spend as much time educating the family as they do treating the patients. When training family members, the therapist should demonstrate the tasks and then provide an opportunity for the family members to attempt the tasks.

units.title: Unheaded source content
section_path: Improving Participation and Quality of Life through Occupation
units.summary: To participate fully in a life that has meaning, indepen-dence, and choice, the individual engages in “occupa-tions.” Occupation has been defined as the “ordinary and familiar things that persons do every day.” 22 Occupations have purpose, and perhaps most importantly, they have meaning for the person engaged in them. When individu-als engage in occupations, they are engaged in activities that are directed by goals or are purposeful, are per-formed in situations or contexts that influence them, can be identified by the doer and others, and are meaning-ful. 20 Occupations should be considered neutral, that is, they are neither positive nor negative; for some individu-als, smoking cigarettes or other risky or illness producing activities are valued occupations. 62 Occupations usually are classified into general cat-egories, the most common classifications fall into the domains of work (or productivity), play or leisure, and self-maintenance (also referred to as self-care and instru-mental tasks).

units.summary: Those activities that are necessary for maintenance of the self within the environment constitute another major clas-sification of occupation. Often included in this category are activities related to personal care (eating, grooming, and hygiene), getting around (mobility), and communicat-ing. 3,5 For a person to be self-reliant in any community, a level of competence is required that enables the accom-plishment of tasks beyond those of basic self-care. For this reason, an additional category of instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs) in the OTPF includes communication management including phones and computers, child and pet care, meal preparation, home establishment and main-tenance, laundry, shopping, financial management, driving and community mobility, health and medication manage-ment, and spiritual activities (see Chapters 5 and 6).

BARRIERS TO PARTICIPATION AND QUALITY OF LIFE
units.summary: BARRIERS TO PARTICIPATION AND QUALITY OF LIFE Once the practitioners identify problems with partici-pation and quality of life, they must address barriers to resumption of activities. Such barriers can be divided into several subgroups, including disability in basic and com-plex IADLs, decreased cognition, impaired motor func-tion and balance, limited mobility, urinary incontinence, poor speech and language function, depression, decreased resource utilization, environmental inaccessibility, and diminishing social and community support. Each is dis-cussed to highlight how rehabilitation can address the issues that may limit an individual’s participation after stroke.

units.summary: Rehabilitation seeks to help the person with disabilities achieve the highest possible degree of performance. The modalities of inpatient rehabilitation treatment are no different from acute care therapy or outpatient therapy; however, the tasks progress to be more difficult. Once the client has mastered a task in a therapeutic context, the conditions are altered to more real-life situations. Inher-ent in this progression is that the client is the leader.

units.summary: The advantage to home health therapy is that the inter-vention takes place in one setting where the skills will be applied as they are being learned. One of the obvi-ous goals of home health is to identify the physical bar-riers to the client’s success in the home environment. However, identification of the cognitive and perceptual barriers that limit performance in the home setting is key. In addition, clients may perform better in a famil-iar environment.

units.title: Outpatient Therapy
section_path: Improving Participation and Quality of Life through Occupation
BARRIERS TO PARTICIPATION AND QUALITY OF LIFE
units.summary: A good outpatient program involves a multidisciplinary team working with the client to achieve maximum inde-pendence in all aspects of life the client indicates as impor-tant. Outpatient therapy forces the client to maintain a schedule of therapies, get ready in time for the appoint-ment, arrange transportation to and from the appoint-ment, and follow through with home programs that are jointly designed with the therapists. To get to therapy, the client must have the physical endurance to participate in the preparation, the travel, and the therapy itself. The cognitive process involves initiation, planning, attention, organization, and sequencing.

units.title: Systems Model of Motor Control
section_path: THEORETICAL ASSUMPTIONS AND MODEL UNDERLYING THE OT-TOA
units.summary: In the past 30 to 35 years, new models of motor con-trol have evolved from the ecological approach to per-ception and action 31,87 and from the study of complex, dynamical systems in mathematics and the sciences. 35 The new models emphasize the interaction between persons and their environments and suggest that motor behavior emerges from persons’ multiple systems interacting with unique tasks and environmental con-texts. 65 “Thus, the systems model of motor control is more interactive or heterarchical and emphasizes the role of the environment more than the earlier reflex- hierarchical model.” 57 In the systems model, the nervous system is viewed dif-ferently from earlier reflex-hierarchical models. Instead of being the primary system controlling movement, the nervous system now is considered only one system among many systems that affect motor behavior.

units.title: Ecological Approach to Perception and Action
section_path: THEORETICAL ASSUMPTIONS AND MODEL UNDERLYING THE OT-TOA
Ecological Approach to Perception and Action
units.summary: The ecological approach “emphasizes the study of inter-action between the person and the environment during everyday, functional tasks and the close linkage between perception and action (i.e., purposeful movement).” 57 Gib-son described the role of functional goals and the environ-ment in the relationship between perception and action. He stated that direct perception involves the active search for affordances 32 or the functional use of objects for a person with unique personal characteristics. 91 Therefore, Gibson’s concept of affordances recognizes the close linkage between perception and action in terms of what the information available in the environment means to a specific person. 32 Bernstein 9 also recognized the importance of the envi-ronment and personal factors other than the CNS in motor behavior.

units.title: Dynamical Systems Theory
section_path: THEORETICAL ASSUMPTIONS AND MODEL UNDERLYING THE OT-TOA
units.summary: The study of dynamical systems originated in the disci-plines of mathematics, physics, biology, chemistry, psy-chology, and kinesiology and has been applied to the professions of OT, physical therapy, nursing, adapted physical education, and some areas of medicine. 15,57 Such study has influenced the development of a systems model of motor control as well. Dynamical systems the-ory proposes that behaviors emerge from the interaction of many systems and subsystems. Because the behavior is not specified but is emergent, it is considered to be self-organizing.

units.title: Experience-Dependent Neural Plasticity
units.summary: Our ability to adapt and change in response to our envi-ronment and personal circumstances and contexts is dependent on the adaptive capacity of the brain, other-wise known as neuroplasticity. 50,67 According to Kleim and Jones, 50 the ability of neurons and other brain cells to change their structure and function in response to a variety of factors, including behavioral training, is what underlies our ability to learn new behaviors and relearn behaviors that have been lost due to disease or injury. They suggest that neural plasticity is driven by changes in behavioral, sensory, and cognitive experiences and that promoting this type of “experience- dependent neural plasticity” is instrumental in reorganizing the brain after damage. 50 Based on an extensive review of neuroscience literature, they have identified 10 key principles of “experience-dependent neural plasticity” that can be used to guide rehabilitation approaches and optimize functional outcomes.

section_path: Create an Environment That Uses the Common Challenges of Everyday Life
units.summary: Create an Environment That Uses the Common Challenges of Everyday Life Therapists need to be creative in creating environments within their clinical settings that provide typical chal-lenges. Some facilities have purchased more real-life envi-ronments such as Easy Street, and other facilities have remodeled their clinics to simulate environments in which patients typically have to interact. Some have created small apartments to create a more realistic environment, in contrast to a typical hospital room, in which patients can interact before being discharged.

units.title: Remediate a Client Factor (Impairment) if It Is the Critical Control Parameter
section_path: Remediate a Client Factor (Impairment) if It Is the Critical Control Parameter
units.summary: Remediate a Client Factor (Impairment) if It Is the Critical Control Parameter When therapists identify person factors in the cognitive, psychosocial, or sensorimotor systems as possible critical control parameters, then they should attempt to remediate those factors, assuming it is possible. For example, Flinn 27 identified decreased strength as one critical control param-eter that interfered with occupational performance tasks for a person after stroke. Thus, she attempted to remedi-ate this sensorimotor variable through the use of exercise and increased use of the involved extremity for functional tasks. For this person, the use of exercise was meaningful because she saw a clear connection between her exercise program and her ability to use her involved arm and hand for everyday tasks.

units.title: For Persons with Poor Control of Movement, Constrain the Degrees of Freedom
section_path: For Persons with Poor Control of Movement, Constrain the Degrees of Freedom
units.summary: For Persons with Poor Control of Movement, Constrain the Degrees of Freedom Persons learning a new task initially restrict the degrees of freedom at their joints by self-imposing some form of freezing of body segments. 41 As a result, their perfor-mance appears stiff and uncoordinated. With practice, the performance becomes smoother and more coordinated as the restrictions on the degrees of freedom decrease. Unfortunately, some persons with CNS damage are not able to constrain the degrees of freedom at their joints.

units.title: For Persons Who Do Not Use Returned Function in Their Involved Extremities, Use Constraint-Induced Therapy
section_path: For Persons Who Do Not Use Returned Function in Their Involved Extremities, Use Constraint-Induced Therapy
units.summary: For Persons Who Do Not Use Returned Function in Their Involved Extremities, Use Constraint-Induced Therapy A growing body of literature supports the beneficial effects of constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) for persons after stroke with active wrist extension and active finger extension. 12,64,95 The original CIMT involves intensive therapy (i.e., about 6 hours/day for 10 days in a 2-week period) while the less-involved arm is constrained by a sling or glove. As a result, participants are forced to use their involved extremity to complete functional tasks, and thus CIMT, counteracts the learned nonuse seen in many persons after stroke. CIMT is consistent with two assumptions of the OT-TOA: “functional tasks help orga-nize behavior and experimentation with various strate-gies leads to optimal solutions to motor problems” 58 (see Chapters 16 and 20).

units.summary: This chapter describes an OT- TOA for persons after stroke and describes the theoretical basis for and assump-tions of the approach, based on contemporary motor con-trol, motor learning, and motor development literature. The chapter also provides a top-down evaluation frame-work that emphasizes the importance of evaluating role and occupational performance tasks first and then the selective assessment of personal and environmental fac-tors. In addition, the chapter describes the application of treatment principles to various patient problems and, finally, includes a case study describing the application of the OT-TOA to a specific person after stroke. In addition to his son who farms, he has another son and daughter, who are married and live within a 2-hour drive.

units.summary: The ADL Taxonomy, 38,40 similar to the COPM, 25 is an occupation-focused interview guide that can be admin-istered early in the intervention process, when the cli-ent is asked about what ADL tasks he or she performs and perceives as strengths and problems of occupa-tional performance. The ADL Taxonomy differs from the COPM in that it focuses on smaller actions that are part of ADL tasks, and its design minimizes the risk of the client being allowed to identify problems that are not occupation focused (e.g., improved ability to use right hand). The design of the ADL Taxonomy allows for the use of a variety of formats for recording the client’s reported strengths and problems, but one of the most common is conceptualized as a divided circle in which each area of daily life tasks has its own slice (Fig. All slices are then divided into the actions included in each task domain according to a hierarchy of difficulty.

units.summary: Geriatric Day Rehabilitation Unit: Client Living in Comfort (Assisted) Living In rehabilitation departments in Sweden, as well as in North America and other world regions, it is common to work with interdisciplinary teams. 10,30,38 This means that several pro-fessions are involved throughout the entire rehabilitation process, and members contribute to the team with their spe-cific expertise using profession-specific evaluation and inter-vention methods. The use of a collaborative interdisciplinary approach, in which the client is viewed as an integral member of the team, allows the team to better obtain a full picture of the client’s needs and provide appropriate interventions. Such an approach requires that the team members collabo-rate closely and assist each other in solving problems that arise during the rehabilitation process.

units.summary: Establish Client-Centered Performance Context Because of a waiting list, Astrid did not start coming to the geriatric day rehabilitation unit until 4 weeks after her discharge from the inpatient unit (4.5 months after her stroke). At her first visit, her new occupational thera-pist, Maria, began the process of establishing the client- centered performance context by reading through Astrid’s medical record, which included the background informa-tion from her stays in the stroke unit and the inpatient geriatric rehabilitation unit. Maria then met Astrid and carried out an initial OT interview. Astrid came to the interview with her ex-husband, Emil.

units.title: Motivational Dimension
section_path: Enhancing Performance of Activities of Daily Living Tasks
units.summary: Astrid’s interests include being together with friends; she is especially motivated to invite her friends to her apart-ment and wants to be able to do that independently. She also wishes to be able to eat a meal using customary uten-sils because it bothers her that others see her using only her fork while eating (in Sweden, it is customary to use both a knife and a fork during a meal, with the knife held in the right hand and the fork held in the left hand during the entire eating process). Because of this, she does not want to eat in the dining room but instead chooses to have the staff prepare meals for her in her apartment, where she eats alone. Astrid values being independent and doing as much for herself as possible.
summary_sentences: Astrid’s interests include being together with friends; she is especially motivated to invite her friends to her apart-ment and wants to be able to do that independently.

She also wishes to be able to eat a meal using customary uten-sils because it bothers her that others see her using only her fork while eating (in Sweden, it is customary to use both a knife and a fork during a meal, with the knife held in the right hand and the fork held in the left hand during the entire eating process).
Because of this, she does not want to eat in the dining room but instead chooses to have the staff prepare meals for her in her apartment, where she eats alone.
Astrid values being independent and doing as much for herself as possible.

units.title: Task Dimension
section_path: Enhancing Performance of Activities of Daily Living Tasks
units.summary: The tasks Astrid mentioned that are relevant to her past and current situation include personal ADLs (dress-ing, toileting, showering, grooming, and eating), social activities (e.g., socializing with her family, socializing and having coffee with her friends), instrumental ADLs (preparing coffee, preparing simple meals such as oatmeal or sandwiches, shopping), and leisure (reading the news-paper, watching TV, resting). Tasks that were relevant to her life before her stroke but that now are irrelevant because of her lack of interest or are now too difficult for her to perform include walking in the forest and picking berries and mushrooms; attending the theater, concerts, and movies; gardening; house cleaning; and managing her finances (banking, paying bills). Astrid is a typical Swedish woman, and her cultural beliefs, values, and customs as well as where and how she performs her daily life tasks are similar to those of other persons of the same age living in northern Sweden.

units.title: Societal Dimension
section_path: Enhancing Performance of Activities of Daily Living Tasks
units.summary: Astrid has several resources available and that she now uses, including the staff at the comfort living complex who are available to help her 24 hours per day; her ex-husband, who is legally responsible for her finances; home help ser-vice personnel, who come once a week and clean her apart-ment; and the interdisciplinary team at the geriatric day rehabilitation unit. She also has full access to any needed health care services provided by the Swedish health care system. The Swedish health care system will pay for her to take a taxi (mobility service) to the geriatric day rehabilita-tion unit twice a week and will pay for her rehabilitation services at the unit until she meets her rehabilitation goals. This generally includes paying for adapted equipment and assistive technology that might be prescribed.

units.summary: Develop Therapeutic Rapport and Work Collaboratively with the Client When Maria met Astrid and Emil, they started to develop therapeutic rapport and identify the persons to include in the client constellation and subsequent collaborative rela-tionship during the intervention process. Although Emil was a source of support for Astrid, he did not have prob-lems with occupational performance in relation to Astrid, so the “client” was determined to be only Astrid. Emil’s role was to confirm what Astrid tried to say and to pro-vide her with moral support. In fact, Astrid managed the interview to a great extent by herself and only occasion-ally looked to Emil for support.

She has a well-established daily routine and is motivated to be as inde-pendent performing daily life tasks as is possible (e.g., cooking, self-care).

units.summary: Identify Client’s Reported and Prioritized Strengths and Problems of Occupational Performance The second outcome of the OT interview Maria imple-mented during her first meeting with Astrid and Emil was that Maria learned about what Astrid perceives to be her strengths and problems of occupational perfor-mance and which task performances Astrid wants to prioritize for further evaluation and intervention. Maria chose to use the ADL Taxonomy to guide this part of the OT interview because she thought that doing so would provide Astrid with a structure that would sup-port her in identifying and prioritizing what she viewed as her most important problems with daily occupational performances. Because Astrid has both aphasia and some memory loss, Maria believed it would be too difficult to use the COPM.

units.summary: Observe Client’s Performance of Prioritized Tasks and Implement Performance Analyses Now that Maria had learned what daily life tasks Astrid reported as problems and wanted to prioritize, Maria’s next step in the OT intervention process was to observe Astrid perform some of those tasks. Maria, therefore, shared with Astrid that she would like to observe Astrid perform two of the tasks she was most concerned about during their next session together. She also clarified that doing so would enable her to better understand Astrid’s problems with occupational performance so that they could then determine together what interventions might be most appropriate. Because many task options were included in the AMPS manual that were culturally relevant and that matched ones Astrid had prioritized, Maria further clarified, “I would like to use a standardized evaluation tool, the Assess-ment of Motor and Process Skills, or AMPS, when I observe you.

units.summary: Observation of Prioritized Task 1: AMPS Task C-2—Hot Cooked Cereal and Beverage for One Person When Astrid and Maria set up the environment before her performance of the first AMPS task, Maria ensured that Astrid was completely familiarized with the clinic kitchen, including what tools and materials were available, where they were located, and how any equipment she might use was operated (e.g., water taps, electric appliances). As part of this process, Astrid, with help from Maria when needed, rearranged the kitchen so that objects were placed in loca-tions as similar to how she would have them at home as was possible. units.title: Define and Describe Task Actions the Client Does and Does Not Perform Effectively

Define and Describe Task Actions the Client Does and Does Not Perform Effectively
units.summary: Define and Describe Task Actions the Client Does and Does Not Perform Effectively Maria reasoned that defining and describing what actions Astrid had and had not performed effectively required that she go through four steps. In the first step, she would score the AMPS items for each task Astrid had performed. In the second step, Maria would select the AMPS items that best reflected Astrid’s strengths and problems with occupational performance. In the third step, Maria would group these AMPS items into clus-ters and write summary statements that she would use to document Astrid’s specific baseline levels of occupational performance.

units.summary: Step 1: Score the AMPS Items for Each Observed Activity of Daily Living Task Performance When Maria scored Astrid’s quality of ADL task perfor-mance, she used the criteria in the AMPS manual to score each AMPS item = 4, 3, 2, or 1. 16,17 More specifically, the ADL motor and ADL process skills Astrid performed effectively were scored 4 (competent) or 3 (question-able, but no apparent disruption). units.title: Step 2: Select the AMPS Items That Best Reflect the Client’s Observed Quality of Activity of Daily Living Task Performance
section_path: Enhancing Performance of Activities of Daily Living Tasks
Step 2: Select the AMPS Items That Best Reflect the Client’s Observed Quality of Activity of Daily Living Task Performance
units.summary: Step 2: Select the AMPS Items That Best Reflect the Client’s Observed Quality of Activity of Daily Living Task Performance Maria then reviewed the scores she had given Astrid on each task and selected three AMPS items that best reflected Astrid’s strengths: Stabilizes (she was stable when sitting in her wheelchair, never demonstrating any momentary loss of balance), Endures (she never demonstrated any obvious evidence of physical fatigue), and Sequences (she performed the steps of both tasks in a logical order). Aware that she should limit the number of AMPS items to those that best reflected Astrid’s problems with occu-pational performance, Maria chose 12, two more than the recommended 10: Aligns (persistently leaning back in her wheelchair), Positions (positioning herself too far from the refrigerator and diagonally to the counter), Reaches and Bends (increased physical effort bending forward while reaching for task objects), Grips (task objects slipping out of her grasp, “grip slips”), Manipulates (fumbling the knife and measuring cup), Coordinates (“grip slips” and fumbling task objects when using two hands; not using two body parts to stabilize task objects), Handles (delays before stabilizing task objects and not always using two body parts to stabilize task objects), Moves (effort mov-ing her wheelchair), Transports (transporting task objects one at a time), Heeds (completing somewhat different tasks than she had said she would perform), and Chooses (choosing ingredients that were different from those she said she would use).

units.title: Criterion-Referenced Interpretation
section_path: Enhancing Performance of Activities of Daily Living Tasks
units.summary: When Maria reviewed Astrid’s AMPS Results Report, she started by looking at where Astrid’s linearized ADL motor and ADL process ability measures were located along the respective AMPS scale (see Fig. It was clear to Maria that Astrid’s ADL motor and ADL process ability mea-sures were well below the criterion-referenced cutoffs that indicate that the person demonstrated at least some degree of clumsiness or increased physical effort (i.e., below the ADL motor cutoff at 2 logits) or some degree of ineffi-ciency (time-space disorganization) (i.e., below the ADL process cutoff at 1 logit). But Maria was more interested to know the criterion- referenced range of quality of ADL task performance commonly observed among persons whose AMPS mea-sures are at the same location along the AMPS scales as were Astrid’s ADL motor and ADL process ability measures. For example, Maria noted that Astrid’s ADL motor ability measure was in the range along the ADL motor scale where most people are observed to have moderate to marked clumsiness or increased physical effort or fatigue.

units.summary: Subgoal 1: When Performing Kitchen Tasks, Astrid Will Move Her Wheelchair and Transport Task Objects with Only Minimal Increased Physical Effort and Mild Inefficiency After Maria and Astrid agreed on an intervention plan, Maria initially changed the seat cushion in Astrid’s wheel-chair to one that was not so thick. When Astrid tried it, she was immediately able to propel herself forward both effec-tively and quickly by using her feet, but she did not like it and wanted to change back to her higher cushion. Maria then suggested and Astrid tried out a wheelchair that had a lower seat, but that too was unsuccessful.

units.title: Subgoal 3: Astrid Will Safely and Independently Hold and Stabilize Task Objects When Preparing Simple Meals

Subgoal 3: Astrid Will Safely and Independently Hold and Stabilize Task Objects When Preparing Simple Meals
units.summary: Subgoal 3: Astrid Will Safely and Independently Hold and Stabilize Task Objects When Preparing Simple Meals At the end of their session, Maria and Astrid began to address Astrid’s third subgoal. Maria had observed many occupational performance issues related to holding and stabilizing task objects during just two AMPS task obser-vations. Astrid had needed assistance to open the jar of orange juice; many task objects (e.g., knife, serving spoon, cheese slicer) slipped from her grasp when she attempted to hold them in her right hand; and she did not always sta-bilize task objects, resulting in the sandwich and the pan of hot oatmeal almost falling onto the floor or into her lap.

units.title: Putting It Together: Engaging in Acquisitional and Compensatory Occupation
section_path: Enhancing Performance of Activities of Daily Living Tasks
Putting It Together: Engaging in Acquisitional and Compensatory Occupation
units.summary: Putting It Together: Engaging in Acquisitional and Compensatory Occupation Over the next 2 weeks (four sessions), Astrid practiced making open-faced cheese sandwiches with cucumbers or tomatoes, pouring herself a glass of juice, making oat-meal, and preparing yogurt with muesli (another break-fast she often eats). Within 2 weeks, Astrid could make her own sandwiches provided she used presliced cheese and vegetables that Maria had prepared for her; she ate her sandwiches for her afternoon snack at the geriatric day rehabilitation unit. When she practiced preparing hot oatmeal, she persisted in demonstrating problems with not stabilizing task objects, so Maria placed more emphasis on occupational skills training focused on prac-ticing and learning to effectively stabilize task objects using her right hand.

units.summary: Reevaluate for Enhanced and Satisfying Occupational Performance Now that Astrid had had an opportunity to practice mak-ing sandwiches and preparing oatmeal, Maria felt it was important to reevaluate Astrid’s quality of occupational performance and document her progress. Reevaluation using the AMPS also enabled Maria to clearly define what task actions were now effective and which ones remained ineffective and needed to be targeted through further intervention. When Maria reevaluated Astrid’s quality of ADL task performance, she observed the same two tasks that she had observed the first time she evaluated Astrid.

units.title: Continued OT Services
section_path: Enhancing Performance of Activities of Daily Living Tasks
units.summary: Continued OT Services When Astrid and Maria met again, it was the end of the seventh week that Astrid had been coming to the geri-atric day rehabilitation unit. After meeting with Astrid and discussing the results of the second AMPS observa-tion and revisiting Astrid’s goals, Maria planned to share her findings with the entire rehabilitation team. Maria thought that it was time for the team to review Astrid’s common rehabilitation goals and develop an ongoing intervention plan. Over the final 3 weeks that Astrid came to the outpa-tient geriatric day rehabilitation unit, she continued to participate in ongoing OT services related to her goals.

units.title: Eating
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis
units.summary: The patient should be positioned with feet stabilized on the floor to offer the necessary support and maintain comfortable upright posture when eating. Aspiration precautions (see Chapter 29) should always be observed to ensure safety with meals. The weaker arm should be positioned on the table with good alignment to promote proper posture as well as attention to the arm. The follow-ing adaptive equipment can be considered to increase ease and efficiency during feeding.
