units.title: Showering and Bathing
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis
units.summary: Safety is an important consideration during bathing, and factors such as transfer techniques, seating and position-ing, amount of assistance required, and control of water temperature should all be evaluated. Nonslip mats or adhesive decals should be placed inside and outside the tub or shower. A tub transfer bench and grab bars can increase safety with transfers and stability during bath-ing (see Chapter 7). The patient should be seated with back support and feet stabilized.

units.title: Unheaded source content
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis
units.summary: There are a number of different techniques and approaches for dressing with hemiparesis. The indi-vidual needs of each patient should be considered as well as the presence of caregivers who may be assist-ing the patient. Regular practice with dressing during OT intervention has been shown to lead to significant improvements in performance. 21 Resources such as the Occupational Therapy Toolkit™ 7 provide handouts for one-handed dressing techniques that can be helpful for patients and caregivers to carryover techniques learned in therapy.
summary_sentences: There are a number of different techniques and approaches for dressing with hemiparesis.
The indi-vidual needs of each patient should be considered as well as the presence of caregivers who may be assist-ing the patient.
Regular practice with dressing during OT intervention has been shown to lead to significant improvements in performance.

units.title: Pants and Underwear in Bed
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis
units.summary: Bend the weaker leg toward the body using the stron-ger arm or leg to bring the foot within reach. Pull the underwear or pants over the weaker leg and allow the leg to straighten into the clothing. Place the stronger leg into the clothing and pull the pants up as far as possible. Place one or, if possible, both feet on the bed and bridge to lift the pelvis.

section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis
units.summary: Depending on the needs of the individual, as well as the layout of the client’s space, many modifications can be implemented in order for an individual with hemiplegia to participate in kitchen tasks safely. Some products can be ordered through medical supply companies; however, many companies are now making products that are readily available to a general population. The following are guide-lines that can be applied as appropriate to each individual.

units.summary: Energy conservation and work simplification techniques can also be applied to instrumental ADLs (IADLs). Patients can prioritize, organize, and limit work in order to save time and energy. In general, patients should allow increased time for task completion and take frequent, short rest breaks. Work surfaces should be positioned at a height that allows for maximal efficiency to avoid exces-sive reaching and bending.

units.title: Unheaded source content
units.summary: The performance of supine activities is often associated with the acute stages of the rehabilitation process. Bridg-ing, rolling, and movement from side lying to sit are basic functional mobility tasks that are necessary to the provi-sion of nursing care and movement of the client from a bed to a wheelchair. However, these mobility sequences are also important in enabling the client to participate in a wide range of life areas. For example, consider the indi-vidual who chooses to lie on a beach to enjoy the sun and surf.

units.title: Analysis of Movement
units.summary: Analysis of Movement In the functional mobility task of bridging, the back and hip extensors support the body against the forces of gravity. The arch formed when the upper back and feet are in contact with the supporting surface is maintained by the activation of muscles located on the underside of the arch. Use of the arms or legs increases the demands placed on the trunk muscula-ture. When an arm or leg is raised (as in attempts to dress), the muscles located above the arch (the oblique abdominal muscles) must become active to support the limb.

units.title: Treatment Strategies
units.summary: Treatment Strategies Bridging is an important position that the patient should be instructed to assume early in the intervention process. Bridging is a mobility function necessary for the use of a bed pan, reduction of pressure on the buttocks, and move-ment within the bed (bed scooting). 52 A patient with hemiplegia may have trouble in assum-ing the crook-lying position and forming a bridge because of a variety of underlying causes. The lack of selective muscle activity on the affected side, caused by the use of mass patterns, prevents the patient from combining the necessary hip components of flexion and adduction.

units.title: Rolling to the Hemiplegic Side: Selected Problems and Treatment Strategies
section_path: Rolling to the Hemiplegic Side: Selected Problems and Treatment Strategies
units.summary: Rolling to the Hemiplegic Side: Selected Problems and Treatment Strategies Patients with hemiplegia frequently roll over using an extensor pattern to initiate the movement sequence because of lack of flexor control of the trunk and the early return of extensor activity. These patients rely on the unaffected side to push against the supporting surface, resulting in an arching of the axial spine as the body is thrust forward in the direction of the roll. Davies 27 suggested that rolling activities can be used to promote active flexion of the trunk and achieve sub-sequent improvement in active control of the trunk mus-culature. The need exists to balance the concentric and eccentric contractions of the trunk muscles in proportion to the change in force exerted by gravity as the patient changes position.

units.title: Selected Problems
units.summary: Selected Problems Movement from the side lying to seated position becomes a challenge for the patient after stroke because of the combined effects of limited muscular activity and mal-adaptive compensatory strategies. Patients lack appro-priate postural alignment and stability. 21,27 The lack of flexor control of the trunk and early return of extensor activity interfere with the patient’s ability to grade con-centric and eccentric muscle activity effectively relative to the changing forces of gravity. 27 If inadequate con-trol of the trunk musculature is evident, the patient must rely on compensatory strategies that may include over-use of the unaffected arm or leg or exaggerated use of head movements.

units.summary: Treatment Strategies Many methods are suggested to retrain the patient in the supine- to- sit movement sequence. One method suggests that patients with hemiplegia be taught initially to roll toward the affected side to decrease the amount of effort required and to reduce maladaptive strategies such as pulling and pushing to achieve the seated position. 20 Others suggest that patients with hemiplegia be instructed to rise from both sides early in treatment to prevent associated reactions.

units.title: Side Lying to Sit toward the Affected Side
section_path: Side Lying to Sit toward the Affected Side
units.summary: Side Lying to Sit toward the Affected Side The therapist assists the patient in lifting the hemiplegic leg over the side of the bed; the head, neck, and upper tho-rax are brought forward, requiring the neck to flex laterally. Concurrently, the nonaffected arm must be brought across the body and placed on the bed. The unaffected leg also must be lifted over the side of the bed as the patient pushes down with the hand. The movement of the unaffected leg as the patient simultaneously pushes with the hand adds a momentum strategy to this movement sequence; the weight of the leg assists the patient in attaining a seated posture.

units.title: ACTIVITIES IN SITTING
units.summary: The ability to maintain a seated position and perform ADLs safely and efficiently is a goal many occupational therapists seek with their patients (see Chapter 17). In the acute stages after stroke, the therapist should begin to work on control of sitting and standing with the patient as soon as possible to promote the ability to manage the upright position and increase overall visual input in func-tional positions.

units.title: Analysis of Movement
units.summary: For controlled movement in sitting, the ability to bear and shift weight anteriorly, posteriorly, laterally, and in a rotary pattern must be present. This suggests that the concentric and eccentric abilities of the trunk flexors and extensors and the ability to activate these muscle groups selectively relative to the task demand must be present. For example, for controlled anterior weight shift through the pelvis, the need for concentric contraction of the low back extensors and an associated eccentric contraction of the trunk flexors (abdominals) is evident. In a posterior weight shift through the pelvis, the need for concentric contraction of the trunk flexors and an associated eccen-tric contraction of the trunk extensors is evident.

units.title: Selected Problems
units.summary: Many patients dis-play difficulty with voluntary trunk control in sitting after a stroke. Messier and colleagues 61 looked at trunk flexion in sitting poststroke and noted decreased displacement of the center of pressure and lower extremity weight bear-ing through the feet. They believed that this was probably indicative of minimal anterior tilt of the pelvis and most of the trunk motion initiating from the upper trunk. 61 There is electromyography (EMG) evidence to sup-port alterations in trunk muscle activity after stroke.

units.title: Selected Problems
units.summary: Selected Problems Patients with neglect who attempt to transfer often suc-ceed in transporting only half the body onto the support-ing surface. Additionally, the left foot may be neglected, and the patient may be oblivious to proper left foot place-ment before transferring. Many patients require considerable help to maintain a flat foot on the floor. This may be because of unilateral inattention, poor sensation on the affected side, shortened trunk muscles resulting in asymmetrical sitting, and short-ening of the calf muscles on the affected side.

These patients’ actions are unpredictable and often run counter to those expected after instruction from the therapist.

units.title: Analysis of Movement
units.summary: The ability to stand is a goal many patients with hemi-plegia want to achieve because the drive to be upright is strong. Patients should be provided the opportunity to practice standing and shifting their centers of gravity in all directions and reaching for functional objects in the environment. The trunk responses needed for controlled sitting (i.e., selective lengthening and shortening depend-ing on the requirements of the task) also are needed for controlled standing; however, these trunk responses are carried out over a much narrower base of support.

units.title: Selected Problems
units.summary: Standing may prove challenging for patients with severe hemiplegia who have only one side of the body available to use for movement; moving with one half of the body is stressful work. The slow, laborious effort of standing and attempting to move in this position causes an increase in posturing and skeletal muscle activity. Movements often are lacking in spontaneity and must occur at a conscious level for the patient. Postural deviations noted in sitting in these patients become even more exaggerated in standing.

For some patients, accomplishing this requires all of their attention and energy.

units.title: Falls Prevention
units.summary: It has been identified that falls in elderly adults have been associated with underlying precipitants, such as intrinsic factors (related to physiological changes, pathologic con-ditions, and adverse medication effects) and situational factors (length of stay in institutional settings, time of fall-ing, and availability of caretakers). 69 These factors apply similarly to the stroke population as well. Falling can be a major complication during stroke reha-bilitation. Nyberg and Gustafson 65 studied the incidences, characteristics, and consequences of falls in an inpatient rehabilitation setting.

units.title: Feedback
section_path: ADJUNCT TECHNIQUES TO ENHANCE SKILL ACQUISITION
units.summary: Patients rely on feedback for performance of all mobility tasks. For example, before initiating a transfer, a patient uses visual information about the appropriate position of the limbs before movement begins. As the patient begins to rise from the seated position, the somatosensory system pro-vides information about the forces exerted and the ongoing changes in limb position. On completion of this task, the results of the sequence provide additional feedback.

units.title: Manual Guidance
section_path: ADJUNCT TECHNIQUES TO ENHANCE SKILL ACQUISITION
units.summary: Manual guidance is a technique frequently used during the rehabilitation process, which is often described as assisting the patient to “feel” the appropriate movement pattern or to position the patient in a desired posture using physical handling techniques. The degree of man-ual guidance provided and when it is supplied remain controversial subjects. Two types of manual guidance have been identified in the literature: passive move-ment and spatiotemporal constraint (physical restric-tion); both forms are often incorporated during mobility training. 47,48,60 For example, during the mobility task of rolling toward the affected hemiplegic side, the paretic arm is often passively moved and placed in a safe position in preparation for the patient to move his or her body over the prepositioned arm.

units.title: Blocked and Random Practice
units.summary: Blocked and Random Practice Blocked practice in functional mobility retraining is the rote practice of mobility functions in sequence. For exam-ple, the patient initially practices rolling to the unaffected side, then to the affected side, and then to the seated posi-tion. Repetition of experiences and a degree of mastery must occur at each level before the patient proceeds to the next level of skill. This method of structuring practice ini-tially may assist the patient in gaining proficiency during the practice session but is not effective in preparing the patient to engage in self-care tasks in which changes in the position of the body occur randomly in response to task requirements.

units.title: Variable Motionless Tasks
units.summary: Bed mobility becomes a variable motionless task if the therapist is not present to regulate certain features of the environment. Patients preparing to get out of bed inde-pendently may find the pillows and bed linens in disar-ray, making movement difficult; the bed guard rails are lowered, the top of the bed remains slightly elevated, and the height of the bed may be too high. Simultaneously, the patient may be receiving verbal encouragement to “hurry up.” Without the therapist present to structure the envi-ronment, the patient may experience difficulty and may use compensatory strategies incompatible with the res-toration of performance component deficits. The patient may hook the unaffected leg under the affected leg and use the hands to pull up to a seated position.

units.title: Open Tasks
units.summary: Many advanced mobility skills meet the criterion of an open task in which the spatial and temporal parameters of movement are determined by events occurring in the envi-ronment. Open tasks require more precise timing of move-ment, and the patient is challenged to anticipate and react to unexpected events. A sit-to-stand maneuver on a moving train, plane, or bus is an example of an open task. Practice of this kind of task should occur in the actual environment whenever possible.

units.title: Unheaded source content
units.summary: The type of gait of a person who has had a stroke depends on where in the brain the insult has occurred and which systems are affected, such as motor, sensory, balance, coordination, perceptual, and visual systems. If a motor area in the cortex or a motor track is involved, hemiple-gia or hemiparesis is manifested in the contralateral limbs. The location of the infarction within these areas deter-mines whether the arm or the leg is more impaired. Not all patients after stroke are hemiplegic or hemiparetic, nor do all hemiparetic patients have the same degree of motor deficits.

units.title: Cerebellar Strokes
units.summary: A person who has an infarct in the cerebellum caused by occlusion or hemorrhage of a vertebral or a cerebel-lar artery may exhibit completely different gait deviations than a hemiparetic patient. The cerebellum is composed of three parts or lobes: the flocculonodular lobe, the ante-rior lobe, and the posterior lobe. The flocculonodular lobe also is called the vestibulocerebellum because most of its input is from the vestibular nuclei in the pons. The anterior lobe also is known as the spinocerebellum because most of its input is from the spinocerebellar tracts via the inferior cerebellar peduncle and the superior cerebellar peduncle.

units.title: Contraversive Pushing or Pusher Syndrome
units.summary: An unusual motor behavior that patients with hemiple-gia sometimes display in the clinic is ipsilateral pushing. The patients tend to push away from the unaffected side in any position. Davies 34 described the syndrome in 1985 and called it the pusher syndrome. The original description of the pusher syndrome was based solely on a practitio-ner’s observation and was most often thought to be asso-ciated with left hemiplegia.

units.title: Proprioceptive Deficits
units.summary: Loss of sensation after a stroke can compound motor deficits. In particular, loss of proprioception can greatly impede motor recovery after stroke. 42 Proprioception is conveyed to the cerebellum and to the cerebral cortex. Information about joint position and muscle activity is sent to both, but the information projected to the cerebel-lum is not recorded as conscious perception.

units.title: Visual Deficits
units.summary: Visual impairments from strokes also can affect gait. The most common visual deficit in patients with hemiplegia is homonymous hemianopsia, 128 which occurs when an infarction involves the optic tract, the lateral geniculate body, or the optic radiation to one occipital cortex. A branch of the internal carotid artery, the anterior choroi-dal artery, supplies most of the optic tract and the optic radiation, with some coverage by branches of the middle cerebral artery and the posterior cerebral artery. 128 The visual cortex is supplied mainly by the posterior cerebral artery but also is supplied by some middle cerebral artery collaterals.

section_path: Four-Point Contralateral Gait Pattern Using Two Devices
units.summary: Four-Point Contralateral Gait Pattern Using Two Devices The devices used in a four-point contralateral gait pattern could be canes or crutches. The therapist might choose this type of gait for patients after stroke who have func-tional use of all four limbs but have impaired balance. They require bilateral support but are able to advance each device (two points) and each leg (two points) individually and reciprocally.

units.title: Five-Point Gait Pattern Using One Device
section_path: Five-Point Gait Pattern Using One Device
units.summary: Therapists may train patients with a walker if they have functional control of all four extremities but require greater trunk control than that afforded by a cane. For example, certain patients who have had cerebellar strokes may never recover adequate postural stability to be able to use two canes. A walker allows the patient to use five points of contact: the four legs of the walker and one of the patient’s legs. The patient advances the walker simul-taneously with one leg and then places all four of the walker legs firmly on the floor at the same time as the patient’s foot.

units.title: GUARDING TECHNIQUES
units.summary: The goal of gait training after a stroke is to have the patient walk as efficiently, safely, and independently as possible. To promote optimum functional ambulation, it is important for the patient to experience postural insta-bility and to relearn the way to correct these imbalances. With this in mind, the therapist must be as close to patients as necessary to prevent them from falling or injur-ing themselves and yet not inhibit them from learning the way to right themselves. Therapists must allow patients to take some risks without jeopardizing the patients’ safety or their own safety.

units.summary: ASSESSING THE CLIENT’S WORK ABILITIES AND LIMITATIONS Employment tests must be derived from a job analysis and physical demands analysis that targets critical or impor-tant job duties, work behaviors, or work outcomes. 31 Evaluations used to make work decisions must possess the following characteristics in this hierarchical order: (1) it must be safe to administer; (2) it must give reliable val-ues that are quantifiable; (3) it must predict risk of future injury or illness; and (4) it must be practical. Predicting risk of future injury is a type of validity, which means that the test measures what it claims to measure.

units.title: AFTER THE ASSESSMENT
section_path: ASSESSING THE CLIENT’S WORK ABILITIES AND LIMITATIONS
units.summary: If the client does not possess the ability to return to work after the assessment but wants to return to work and there is potential to do so, a treatment plan can be initiated. The profession of OT defines the occupation of work as (1) employment interests and pursuits, (2) employment seeking and acquisition, (3) job performance, (4) retire-ment preparation and adjustment, (5) volunteer explora-tion, and (6) volunteer participation. 2 Much of the work rehabilitation that has occurred in the professions of occupational and physical therapy over the past 25 years has been directed at returning people with work-related musculoskeletal disorders to their jobs through services such as work hardening, work conditioning, and post- offer preemployment testing. Historically, people who have strokes are at or above working age, so return to work has not been a major focus of treatment.

units.summary: DESIGNING TREATMENT TO ADDRESS RETURN TO WORK AFTER STROKE Stroke can impair a wide range of functions that result in limitations in a client’s ability to meet these generic worker requirements. This may be directly tied to physical, physi-ological, cognitive, emotional, social, sensory, or motiva-tional changes after stroke, or it could be a combination of a constellation of limitations. Interventions to address some of these generic worker requirements may be novel to clinicians who treat in traditional outpatient settings.

units.title: WHERE CAN OT ADDRESS RETURN TO WORK AFTER STROKE?

WHERE CAN OT ADDRESS RETURN TO WORK AFTER STROKE?
units.summary: WHERE CAN OT ADDRESS RETURN TO WORK AFTER STROKE? When the client is medically stable, discussions regard-ing return to work may be appropriate. Depending on the severity of the stroke, this may be while the client is hospitalized, in a day treatment program, in outpa-tient rehabilitation, in a community program, or in an employer- based return- to- work program. The occu-pational therapist’s role in these settings may vary.

section_path: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living
units.summary: For most individuals, the world becomes a larger place when one acquires a driver’s license. Driving a motor vehicle allows people to move beyond their neighborhood, community, state, province, or country to visit, explore, and join activities outside the home and immediate envi-ronment. Although public transportation in communities provide some of the same destinations, driving a motor vehicle allows for the spontaneity and freedom to move beyond the boundaries of train, subway, or bus stations. After a driver’s license has been acquired, there is an expectation that a person will be always be able to drive, and although there may be other methods of transport available, driving is the most accepted form of community mobility in the United States.

units.title: The Impact of the Baby Boomers
section_path: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living
The Impact of the Baby Boomers
units.summary: The generation born between 1945 and 1964 is affection-ately known as the Baby Boomers. News media, politicians, insurance companies, and advertisers have spent significant resources and time researching this generation because the numbers of individuals in the age group overwhelmingly outnumber other cohort groups. Currently, as the Boom-ers move into later stages of adulthood, the unique aspects of this generation will continue to change OT practice over the next several decades. For example, there will be a shift from the Depression-era seniors, fearful to spend too much money on near necessities, to the Boomers, who overspend on luxuries.

units.title: Occupational Therapy Roles in Stroke Rehabilitation
section_path: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living
Occupational Therapy Roles in Stroke Rehabilitation
units.summary: Occupational Therapy Roles in Stroke Rehabilitation As discussed throughout this text, the role of occupational therapists in evaluation and intervention with stroke survi-vors differs by setting as well as the severity of the stroke. After the stroke event, the survivor is typically treated ini-tially in acute care (see Chapter 1), where the therapist is concerned with evaluation of client factors and performance skills to prevent further deterioration (e.g., spasticity, con-tractures) and enhance recovery from functional disabilities. Moving quickly into the subacute phase, evidence is clear that interdisciplinary stroke rehabilitation improves the outcomes of stroke survivors when rehabilitation resources, including OT, are devoted to these stages of recovery.

units.title: The Profession of Driver Rehabilitation
section_path: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living
units.summary: The profession of driver rehabilitation is a multidisci-plinary field that plans, develops, and implements driver rehabilitation services for individuals with disabilities. The driver rehabilitation specialist is also a general term that encompasses a diverse group of providers. Because the requirements for certification and education for the field are vague and inconsistent from state to state, the back-grounds of providers who use the initials DRS include engineers, driving instructors, and health care profession-als. It is important to understand that the driver rehabili-tation field developed soon after the proliferation of the automobile.

units.title: BOX 10.1 Definitions for Select Commonly Used Terms in Driver Rehabilitation
section_path: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living
BOX 10.1 Definitions for Select Commonly Used Terms in Driver Rehabilitation
units.summary: BOX 10.1 Definitions for Select Commonly Used Terms in Driver Rehabilitation Fitness to drive: a driver characteristic, defined by the absence (or the extent to which) of any functional (sensory, perceptual, cognitive, or psychomotor) deficit or medical condition that significantly impairs an individual’s ability to competently operate a vehicle while conforming to the rules of the road or that significantly increases crash risk Driving competency: the demonstration of fitness to drive that meets criteria recognized by a body responsible for driver licensing Driving skill: the demonstration of vehicle control decisions at operational and tactical levels in a range of traffic and environmental conditions that a driver may be exposed to in everyday experience Driving ability: the necessary sensory, perceptual, cognitive, or psychomotor skills needed to control a motor vehicle for a designated range of traffic and environmental conditions plus a knowledge of rules of the road that meets jurisdiction requirements Clinical driving evaluation: a health care professional obtaining, interpreting, and documenting data to determine fitness to drive through assessment of sensory, perceptual, cognitive, or psychomotor abilities using specific tools or instruments. On-road assessment: a driving evaluation in a motor vehicle to examine a person’s driving abilities and skills at the operational, tactical, and strategic levels using a method of scoring or determining attainment levels Comprehensive driving evaluation: a complete assessment of an individual’s driving knowledge, skills, and abilities by a health care professional that includes (1) medical and driving history; (2) clinical assessment of sensory, perceptual, cognitive or psychomotor abilities; (3) on-road assessment, as appropriate; (4) an outcome summary; and (5) goals and recommendations for inclusive mobility plan including transportation options Behind the wheel: performing driving maneuvers using a vehicle or simulated vehicle for purposes of instruction/training on public roads or off-road settings On road: driving on roadways that are private or streets, roadways, or highways Driving test: an examination of driving maneuvers and knowledge of the rules of the road performed in a motor vehicle on a public highway or street Off road: a component of the on-road assessment that is conducted on roadways or areas that are not publicly managed as roadways (e.g., private road, parking lot, closed course). It should be noted that in some areas or disciplines, this refers to the clinical assessment done before the on-road assessment.

units.title: The Driver Rehabilitation Specialist and Occupational Therapist
section_path: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living
The Driver Rehabilitation Specialist and Occupational Therapist
units.summary: The Driver Rehabilitation Specialist and Occupational Therapist A DRS who is also an occupational therapist typically performs a comprehensive driving evaluation to determine an individual’s driving knowledge, skills, and abilities. The comprehensive driving evaluation is defined as “a complete assessment of an individual’s driving knowl-edge, skills, and abilities by a health care professional that includes: (1) medical and driving history; (2) clinical assessment of physical, cognitive, vision, and/or percep-tion abilities; (3) on-road assessment, as appropriate; (4) an outcome summary; and (5) goals and recommendations for inclusive mobility plan including transportation options.” Specifically for older adults with medical conditions such as stroke, the individualized plans may include recom-mendations for rehabilitation of skills (e.g., increase scan-ning skills through designed intervention), compensation through training (e.g., learn to drive a roundabout, learn to use hand controls), compensation through adaptation of the vehicle (e.g., using a steering knob for one-handed turning), cessation of driving, or a combination of these. A wide range of options and innovations makes it possible to compensate for physical disabilities through technol-ogy.

units.title: Levels of Service for Driving
section_path: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living
units.summary: As described, the profession of driver rehabilitation is evolving with the changing needs of clients, state licens-ing authorities, and families and the fast-paced changes of technology. To complicate matters, frequently, physi-cians are asked about driving and may not know about the services of driver rehabilitation or that a general practice occupational therapist can screen for driving risk. Under-standably, consumers are confused or complain about cost because they do not understand the level of service that is needed for completing a medically based comprehensive driving evaluation. Consumers may not understand why the licensing authorities may simply withdraw a license based on a diagnosis and where to go for help if that happens.

Evidenced-Based Assessment Tools for Driving Fitness
units.summary: Evidenced-Based Assessment Tools for Driving Fitness Assessment tools currently used by DRS for determin-ing fitness to drive span all functional areas, and selection in each of the areas shows significant diversity. 24,42 Over the past 10 years, research has attempted to determine which tool has the best predictive validity and reliability for driving performance. Some tools have been used for many years (e.g., Trail Making A and B, Mini Mental Sta-tus Examination, Useful Field of View), and others are relatively new or new to the application of driving (e.g., AMPS), but all fall short of being the only tool that can be used for prediction of driving performance.

units.title: Interventions to Facilitate Returning to Driving
section_path: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living
SCREENING AND EVALUATION PROCESS FOR DRIVING AND COMMUNITY MOBILITY
Interventions to Facilitate Returning to Driving
units.summary: Interventions to Facilitate Returning to Driving As discussed earlier, driving is a highly valued IADL, and clients may not ask if they can return to driving in order to avoid the answer no. Families or caregivers may not recog-nize that it is an issue or may also avoid the repercussions of dealing with a spouse, parent, or sibling who will need assistance with transportation for an indefinite period of time. Because of possible reluctance on the part of the cli-ent or family, it is critical for the occupational therapist to bring up the issue of mobility with the client as well as the primary caregiver.

Evidence of Interventions for Improving Fitness to Drive
units.summary: Evidence of Interventions for Improving Fitness to Drive There have been some recent systematic reviews about interventions used to improve fitness to drive after a stroke. In a recent Cochrane review, 36 George et al. inves-tigated the literature to determine if “any intervention, with the specific aim of maximizing driving skills improves the driving performance of people after stroke.” The primary outcome was on-road performance; assessments of vision, cognition, and driving behavior were considered sec-ondary outcomes.

units.title: Interactive Driving Simulators
section_path: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living
SCREENING AND EVALUATION PROCESS FOR DRIVING AND COMMUNITY MOBILITY
units.summary: An interactive driving simulator is defined as a computer- controlled environment that represents selected aspects of the driving experience considered to be representational of real-world driving and allows objective measurements of users’ responses to designed driving tasks and scenar-ios and the users’ responses influences subsequent events within the limits of the parameters of the simulation pro-gram through accelerator, brake, and steering compo-nents. There is a wide range of simulators, from desktop computer programs with one screen to the totally immer-sive ones in which the person sits in a motor vehicle with a widescreen projection of a driving scene. Despite the diversity, for functional clinical use, a handful of models have been designed and developed specifically for clinical occupational therapists. With technology costs decreas-ing, companies have worked hard to develop ready-made systems for therapists to literally put in the key and use.

units.title: Adaptive Equipment and Vehicle Modification for Driving
section_path: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living
SCREENING AND EVALUATION PROCESS FOR DRIVING AND COMMUNITY MOBILITY
Adaptive Equipment and Vehicle Modification for Driving
units.summary: Adaptive Equipment and Vehicle Modification for Driving As a general practice occupational therapist, adaptive equipment, demonstration, and practice for transferring in and out of a vehicle should be priorities for all stroke clients who are returning home. The client and family may not be planning a trip, but the client will be in all like-lihood returning to his or her home via a motor vehicle (personal, family, friend, or taxi) and will have follow-up appointments with physicians and therapists. Techniques of transfers do not necessarily differ from other types of transfers, but tools such as the Handybar, which provides a portable support on either side of the vehicle, or a car caddie attaches to the frame of a vehicle and can be used to offer balancing support.

units.title: Working with Pregnant Women Poststroke
units.summary: Working with a woman who is trying to decide whether to become pregnant or who is in the first trimester of pregnancy is a challenge for the OT practitioner, who has to imagine both how pregnancy may impact the client’s mobility and how her limitations may affect her ability to care for the baby. It is helpful for women to understand that physical difficulties from a stroke need not close off the option to have a child. During pregnancy, mobility generally is affected from the latter part of the second tri-mester, when the center of gravity has changed, to deliv-ery. 10 This change in the center of gravity will most likely affect walking; standing up; and transferring in and out of bed, cars, and so on.

units.summary: Facilitating Relationships between Babies and Parents Poststroke Without appropriate supports, a stroke occurring late in pregnancy or postpartum can be devastating to a mother, family, and infant–parent relationship. Because hospital-ization creates a separation between mother and child, it is critical to consider the need to promote attachment dur-ing the subacute phase of rehabilitation. The occupational therapist should have attachment activities as part of the treatment plan.

units.title: Facilitating Physical Care by the Parent
section_path: Facilitating Physical Care by the Parent
units.summary: Being able to provide physical care to the baby is one of the essential elements in parenting. For a caregiver who has had a stroke to pursue the dream of caring for a baby, he or she may need baby care equipment, appropriate durable medical equipment (DME), and adaptive tech-niques. Transitional tasks refer to tasks that are necessary before accomplishing or between basic baby care tasks. Therefore, it is important to begin intervention with these tasks: (1) holding, (2) carrying and moving, (3) transfers, and (4) positional change.

units.title: Carrying and Moving
units.summary: Carrying and Moving TLG has recommended a four- wheeled walker, also known as a rollator, for safely moving the baby around the house. This walker has been used successfully with caregivers with hemiplegia (in whom half of the body is paralyzed) and with those with ataxia (problems with coordination) because it keeps both baby and parent phys-ically stable. This piece of equipment consists of a baby carrier securely attached to a walker seat. The baby carrier can be a bouncy seat or a booster seat, although the for-mer is more difficult to attach.

(1) Choose or arrange surfaces that are high enough to avoid back strain.

units.title: Bedtime
units.summary: Bedtime TLG gets more calls about issues with bedtime than any other topic. For most clients, the greatest difficulty occurs in the course of the transfer activity of putting the baby in bed. The parent can often enjoy the ritual of dressing his or her child in night clothes, reading a book, cuddling, and perhaps singing a song, but because most cribs are inac-cessible, the soothing bedtime activities feel incomplete, resulting in frustration for parent and child alike. Some commercially available infant beds allow the child to sleep with the parent, but these have flaws.

units.summary: Childproofing Home visiting is essential to address childproofing. It is necessary to try several types of devices to see which one is successful. The process is an opportunity to assess visual and visual neglect issues, apraxia, sequencing, and motor planning.

units.summary: In addition to baby care equipment, the caregiver may need assistive mobility technology, such as a power wheelchair, scooter, or four-wheeled walker. Unfortunately, the caregiver may face difficulties acquiring appropriate mobility equipment because there may be no coverage if he or she can walk within the household or inad-equate coverage of costs (e.g., for a motorized wheelchair).

units.title: Feeding: Combining Adaptive Baby Care Equipment and Techniques
section_path: Feeding: Combining Adaptive Baby Care Equipment and Techniques
units.summary: Feeding: Combining Adaptive Baby Care Equipment and Techniques Feeding is one of the most important aspects of care in the formation and maintenance of a parent–child relationship. Being able to breastfeed can be impor-tant for the relationship between mother and baby and can give the mother self-confidence and hope that she can con-tinue her role as a mom. If the mother’s stroke was caused by high blood pressure, she may need blood pressure medication or blood thinners, which could affect breast milk and, therefore, breastfeeding. Before breastfeeding, it is important to consult with physicians regarding pos-sible harm to the baby from medications being used.

units.title: DIAPERING
units.summary: In diapering a child, application of the parent–child collab-orative technique is essential. Most babies can be “trained” to do the “bottoms-up” technique. Parents can teach their baby to lift his or her bottom by lifting the baby’s bottom with the working arm and saying, “Up, up” simultaneously. With time, many babies will then lift their bottoms when cued with the words “up, up” or “butt up.” With infants who are premature or still mostly in the flexed position, the caregiver can rest the baby’s bottom on the caregiver’s functional palm and lift the child onto the diaper.

units.title: Car Seats
units.summary: Car Seats Latching safety straps of car seats is essential, but fastening them can be difficult even for people with two hands. It is important for the caregiver to experiment with a variety of brands in order to find the easiest to use. The chest strap must be narrow enough to be grasped and closed with one hand. Engaging the straps is easier if the crotch strap is short and stable so that it does not wobble.

units.title: Cognitive Issues
units.summary: Cognitive impairment is present in the majority of patients with stroke, so it is crucial to identify any impair-ment and assess the impact on parenting. 3 The caregiver may lose many aspects of cognitive functioning such as the ability to speak, read, or follow directions (completely or partially), and other impairments may occur. Cognitive assessment can pinpoint the cognitive difficulties and strengths so that interventions can be developed to compensate for parenting difficul-ties. The occupational therapist must determine which specific parenting tasks may be problematic and which impairments lead to these difficulties.

units.title: Emotional Issues
units.summary: When parents have significant difficulties with commu-nication, both cognitively and emotionally, there can be a profound effect on parenting, and teamwork among occupational therapists and mental health practitioners is crucial. However, it is important to keep in mind that all parents need support; all parenting is interdependent. Many people now live away from their immediate family, which can be stressful for both the parent and partner. If a partner who has been providing assistance goes back to work, it is important that the parent who has had a stroke has enough support or is safe and confident to care for the baby by him- or herself.

units.title: Care by Others
units.summary: Other stroke survivors may receive help from their in- laws or their parents. Grandparents may be concerned about both their own child and the new baby and want to decrease the stress on everyone. When grandparents live nearby, they may step in with good intentions but may not give the new parent sufficient opportunity to learn how to take care of the baby. The insufficient contact between parent and baby can impede the attachment and adapta-tion process and intensify depression and grieving in the parent.

units.title: Discipline from Crawling through Toddling
units.summary: For caregivers who have had a stroke to discipline suc-cessfully, it is important to teach the parent and child to collaborate. Parent–child collaboration helps facilitate development of the baby and creates a special bond. To restore and maintain the parent–child relationship, it is crucial to support enjoyable interaction between them (e.g., identifying roles and play in which the parent can be effective, offering adaptations to support positive mutual experiences). Children tend to be more collaborative and act out less when they have fun with the parent and see them in effective roles.

units.title: CASE STUDY 5
units.summary: Alicia had a stroke and returned home when her child, Ramon, was 1 year old and just learning to walk. The occu-pational therapist taught Alicia to entice Ramon to come to her. Having an arsenal of enticing items, such as a bottle, toy cell phone, or toy car, is essential to engage the baby and make the baby want to crawl over to the parent. Because Ramon liked to crumple paper and chew on it, he was shown a piece of paper, which was shaken to make noise; he was told, “Look, look at the paper!” When Ramon came over to get his paper, Alicia was able to lift him onto the couch where she was sitting by using a one-handed technique, bringing her hand down Ramon’s back and lifting him up from under his crotch.

units.title: Temper Tantrums
units.summary: Temper Tantrums When a toddler throws a temper tantrum, it is usually impossible to have the child go to the parent, but there are other techniques. Most parents with a stroke cannot pick up kicking and screaming children and take them to their room. However, the belief that taking a misbehaving child to his or her room is the only appropriate response is due to visual history that prevents caregivers from see-ing alternative approaches. It is important to remember that the point of the separation is separation.

units.title: Transportation
units.summary: Transportation In a national survey and in national and regional task-force reports, parents with disabilities have reported that the availability of transportation had more of an impact on being able to parent with a disability than any other issue. 8,13 Because many people who have experienced a stroke can no longer drive, they are often left relying on paratransit services for individuals with disabilities. Unfortunately, many problems are involved in using this service, especially for parents with disabilities transporting their children. One such difficulty is that paratransit does not provide car seats for children.

units.title: Recreation
units.summary: Recreation Being able to take child to a playground is a common out-ing for parents; however, recreation is an area fraught with problems for parents with physical or cognitive disabili-ties. The task force reports and national survey of parents with disabilities have identified access problems during recreation: “Public recreational sites such as playgrounds and parks are either inaccessible altogether or only acces-sible for young children with disabilities—rarely for a par-ent/adult with a disability.” 8 Parents also reported needing assistance in recreation with their children. Parents with attention problems or difficulties with the authority required to manage behavior in public places may need mental health services to facilitate interaction and possibly an ongoing adult companion during outings. When a par-ent with a physical or cognitive disability goes out in the community with a toddler, it is important to have a walk-ing harness.

units.title: Parenting Older Children
units.summary: Because a stroke can occur at any time, it can happen when a parent has school-age children. If a parent has had a stroke before the child’s birth, the parent’s disability is integral to the child’s experience of the parent. For an older child whose parent has a stroke, the changes in the parent are typically experienced as loss of the parent as the child has known him or her, and grieving about this loss can take the form of depression or acting out. Provid-ing continuity in contacts between the parent and child, including during hospitalization, can be helpful so that loss is less complicated by separation.

units.summary: Jim and Mary had two older children in junior high and high school when a surprise pregnancy occurred. Soon after Sharon was born, Jim had a left hemisphere stroke, resulting in aphasia and right hemiplegia. Jim was not the only one in the family who had depression; his wife and older children also did. They thought they had lost their father and husband who had had a great sense of humor and enjoyed the outdoors.

In each phase, definite physical changes occur in both sexes. During the excitement phase, physiologi-cal reactions occur because of somatosensory or psycho-genic stimulation.

units.summary: Occupational therapy purports to be holistic and client cen-tered. By assuming this role, occupational therapists focus on client independence, the assumption or reassumption of life roles and responsibilities, the bolstering of self-esteem, and the professional commitment to the quality of life (QoL) experienced by the client. Mohammed (2012) indicates that although the profession is committed to improving the cli-ent’s life status, we do not regularly or comfortably address the ADL of sexual activity with any regularity. Sexuality long has been considered an appropriate area for OT intervention.

units.title: Team Approach
section_path: EFFECTS OF STROKE ON SEXUAL FUNCTION
units.summary: Although occupational therapists must be involved in sexual health care, effective sexual rehabilitation, similar to all rehabilitation, requires a team approach. The rehabilitation team must address all the individual’s problems in a holistic way, and all team members should be knowledgeable about sexual issues and treatment options. 47,82 If each member of the treatment team is educated and skilled in this area, the patient can choose the team member with whom he or she is most com-fortable to address sexual issues. In addition, each team member has different expertise from which the patient may benefit.

section_path: EFFECTS OF STROKE ON SEXUAL FUNCTION
units.summary: Permission Permission is the most basic and most frequently required intervention. Permission consists of reassuring patients that their actions and feelings are normal and acceptable. All occupational therapists should strive to perform permission-level sexuality interventions. Recog-nizing that sexual behavior varies widely and not project-ing one’s own values or morals onto the patient are most important.

units.title: Specific Suggestions
section_path: EFFECTS OF STROKE ON SEXUAL FUNCTION
units.summary: Specific Suggestions If a patient is experiencing a sexual problem, limited infor-mation may not be enough to solve it. The next level of intervention is specific suggestions aimed at solving the specific problem. This type of intervention requires more knowledge, time, and skill from the therapist but is appro-priate for some occupational therapists (Box 12.1). The therapist should meet with the patient (and partner, if appropriate) in a comfortable, private setting and obtain a sexual problem history.

units.summary: Intensive Therapy To perform this level of sexuality intervention, the therapist should fulfill the criteria for permission, limited information, and specific suggestions and do the following: the therapist must understand the sexual problem fully before making specific suggestions. After obtaining the sexual problem history, the therapist should develop treat-ment goals in collaboration with the patient. These goals may address learning the effects of stroke on sexual func-tion; adapting to changes in sensory, motor, or cognitive function; adapting to psychosocial and role changes; and improving sexual communication.

If the sexual prob-lems predate or are not related to the onset of disability, the patient may require referral.

units.title: Contraception and Safer Sex
units.summary: Most stroke patients are past the childbearing years; how-ever, contraception remains an issue for those who are still fertile. Menses may be affected after a stroke, although studies are inconclusive. 49 However, the exploration of contraceptive methods may be necessary, depending on the patient’s impairments. The functional abilities needed to use condoms, a diaphragm, or a cervical cap include fine motor abilities, motor praxis, and intact cognitive and perceptual function.

units.summary: LEISURE ACTIVITIES DURING OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY Occupational therapists working with patients who have had a stroke are concerned with the way these individuals spend their time. Often, leisure and play interventions are considered secondary during the rehabilitation process as therapists focus on self-care and instrumental activities of daily living. However, leisure activities can be equally meaningful to patients as they redefine their life roles.

units.summary: Characteristics of Caregivers in the United States The typical caregiver may be described as a married woman with some post–high school education or a college degree and a full-time employee earning less than $50,000 per year. The median age of a caregiver is 48 years old and of a care recipient is 79 years old 26 (see Table 14.1). On the other hand, spousal caregivers are split evenly between male and female, with a median age of 64 years.

units.summary: The majority of research on caregiving after stroke and other conditions has focused on the negative psychological and emotional burden experienced by caregivers. How-ever, an analysis of population-based studies found that caregivers, when compared to noncaregivers, had reduced mortality and increased longevity. 77 Some research-ers argue that to find ways to buffer caregivers from the negative effects, the positive aspects of caregiving should receive more examination.

units.title: Caregiver Burden
section_path: OVERVIEW OF CAREGIVING INTHE UNITED STATES
units.summary: Another predictor of depression and anxiety in caregivers is a high level of caregiver burden. 91 Caregiver burden, a subjective state reflecting the individual caregiver’s per-ceptions, is a widely accepted feature of many caregiving studies that measure the effects of caregiver stressors and emotional symptoms. 13 Zarit and colleagues defined care-giver burden as “the extent to which caregivers perceive the adverse effect that caregiving has on their emotional, social, financial, and physical functioning.” 98 In caregiv-ing for adults with any condition, Adelman and colleagues found that caregiver burden was greater in caregivers who were female, had less education, resided with the care recipient, had depression, were socially isolated, incurred financial stress, spent more time caregiving, and lacked the choice to be a caregiver. 1 There were similar findings for caregivers of stroke survivors.

units.title: Evaluating the Caregiver
section_path: OT ROLE WITH CAREGIVERS OF PERSONS WITH STROKE
units.summary: Caregiver assessment is an essential first step in acknowl-edging, valuing, and understanding the caregiver. It has been defined as a “systematic process of gathering infor-mation about a caregiving situation to identify the specific problems, needs, strengths, and resources of the family caregiver, as well as the caregiver’s ability to contribute to the needs of the care recipient.” 36 Among leaders in care-giving research, there is a consensus on the fundamental principles to guide caregiver assessment policy and prac-tice (Box 14.1). 34 There are differing opinions on when a caregiver assessment is warranted. Adelman and colleagues 1 sug-gested that caregivers receive a referral for assessment of burden if they have around-the-clock responsibilities for recipients with high health needs or if they are dealing with an impending care setting transition.

units.title: BOX 14.1 Seven Fundamental Principles for Caregiver Assessment
section_path: OT ROLE WITH CAREGIVERS OF PERSONS WITH STROKE
BOX 14.1 Seven Fundamental Principles for Caregiver Assessment
units.summary: BOX 14.1 Seven Fundamental Principles for Caregiver Assessment Because caregivers are a core part of health care and long-term care, it is important to recognize, respect, assess, and address their needs. Caregiver assessment should embrace a family-centered perspective, inclusive of the needs and preferences of both the care recipient and the family caregiver. Caregiver assessment should result in a plan of care developed in collaboration with the caregiver that indicates the provision of services and intended measurable outcomes.

units.title: Intervention with the Caregiver
section_path: OT ROLE WITH CAREGIVERS OF PERSONS WITH STROKE
units.summary: According to the Improving Stroke Caregiver Readiness Model, after matching the needs of the stroke survivor with the caregiver commitment and capacity, a plan for inpatient preparation of the caregiver must be developed to make the transition to home as smooth as possible. 62 Caregiver preparation may include activating resources (financial, social), readying the home environment (installing ramps, grab bars), providing skills training for stroke survivor care at home (transfers, medication man-agement), training for the case management role (coordi-nating care, negotiating with insurance, managing work schedules or leave), and planning for caregiver self-care (respite, counseling). Rehabilitation services outside of inpatient settings have been shown to benefit both the stroke survivor and the care-giver. Home health services have been found to have mod-est positive effects on caregivers’ mood, levels of strain, and knowledge of stroke.

units.title: SUMMARY
section_path: OT ROLE WITH CAREGIVERS OF PERSONS WITH STROKE
units.summary: Stroke is a leading cause of long-term disability and is one of the primary health conditions that caregivers identify as the reason why their care recipient requires assistance. 12 The broad and complex nature of stroke may include physical, cognitive, emotional, or behavioral impairments. Thus, caregivers of persons who have had a stroke face daunting challenges. Although there is some recognition of their value in providing long-term care and in reducing medical costs, caregivers remain a “shadow workforce.” 14 To bring caregivers out of the shadows and value their contribution to the health of our clients who have had a stroke, we must understand who the caregivers are, the tasks that they perform, and the effect that caregiving has on their lives.

units.title: Depression
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Among the most significant considerations in understand-ing the characteristics and consequences of stroke is the relationship of depression to onset, recovery, and reha-bilitation. Because of the neurophysiological changes and reaction to the consequences of stroke, depression has major implications for the course of recovery. Despite the causes of depression, assessment and treatment of depres-sion affect psychological, functional, and medical health. The relationship between cerebrovascular disease and depression has long been studied.

units.title: Anxiety Disorders
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: A significant comorbidity exists between poststroke depression and anxiety. 7,20,41 Anxiety disorders can emerge during any phase of recovery. Although compelling evidence suggests that anxiety is often a reaction to loss of anticipated or actual functional ability, 20 other evidence links early onset to a previous history of psychiatric conditions. 41 Regard-less of whether it accompanies depression or manifests on its own, anxiety occurs in 18% to 24% of stroke patients and persists in 38% to 76% of those who experience it.

units.title: Dementia
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Poststroke dementia, also known as multi-infarct demen-tia or vascular dementia, has been diagnosed in many individuals, although the consistency of diagnostic criteria has not been applied. 112 A systematic review of poststroke dementia, spanning 60 years, underscores the difficulty in assessing prevalence because study methods vary. Regard-less, dementia occurs in 10% of those with a first stroke and in more than 30% of those with recurrent stroke. 104 This is especially important because the risk for dementia even 10 years after stroke is higher than in the nonstroke population.

units.summary: Early detection of individuals at risk for psychological dis-orders is critical, and it has been suggested that all patients should be screened for depression, anxiety, and apathy within the first 2 weeks after stroke. 118 This is especially critical because lengths of hospital stays have decreased after the acute event. Because these conditions can emerge later on in the recovery process as well as many years later, continued attention is warranted. Many methods have been used to identify psychological conditions, but recent attention has been paid to the sensitiv-ity and specificity of such measures.

units.title: BIOLOGIC INTERVENTION
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: A number of factors are associated with the cause of psy-chological conditions after stroke. Social and psychologi-cal stressors play a major role in the development of these conditions, as do anatomic lesions. Despite the debate regarding the primary cause of psychological conditions, leading some to conclude that no evidence supports a single theory on the origin of psychological conditions in persons with stroke, 154 no debate exists regarding the importance of taking a biopsychosocial approach in under-standing and treating stroke because psychological condi-tions take their toll on recovery and functional ability. Medication is not sufficient to counter the effect of stroke on daily function, 22 but it is a critical weapon in the treatment of psychological conditions.

COPING WITH ILLNESS, RECOVERY, AND REHABILITATION
units.summary: COPING WITH ILLNESS, RECOVERY, AND REHABILITATION The relationship between psychosocial factors and sus-taining a stroke is compounded by the roles that emotion, personality, and culture have in how one copes with trau-matic illness. Defense mechanisms, which serve to protect the individual from the overwhelming emotions that may arise, may add to one’s difficulty in coping with illness and disability. 91 Defense mechanisms typically used include denial, which negates the reality of what is happening and has happened; avoidance, in which the individual is aware of what is happening and has happened but avoids the implications; regression, in which one exhibits increased emotion or increased dependent behavior not characteris-tic of one’s developmental level; compensation, in which one becomes adept in an area to counter an inability of another area; rationalization, which provides reasons or excuses for not being able to accomplish tasks or goals; and diversion of feelings, in which unacceptable feelings are altered into socially appropriate behaviors.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
IMPACT OF STROKE ON THE FAMILY
units.summary: When a disabling illness occurs, it impacts the individual’s entire family and social network. 77 Family members, who are accustomed to relating to one another in specific ways and through specific roles, are now expected to cope with the immediate health needs and subsequent rehabilitation needs of the family member who has had the stroke. Entire families undergo role and status change, and family mem-bers are likely to experience depression and anxiety. 149 In fact, depression in the primary support person is higher than in the general population.

units.title: CONSIDERATIONS FOR THE RECOVERY PROCESS
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: For many stroke patients, recovery is a long and arduous process. Returning to a quality of life that is satisfying requires dealing with consequences that may impact not only physical functioning but cognitive, social, and emo-tional functioning as well. 144 These factors are neither stagnant nor predictable, but they influence quality of life. Characteristics related to personality, self-worth, hope, optimism, internal locus of control, and adaptive coping interact and can facilitate or impede recovery.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Throughout this chapter, reference has been made to how psychological conditions and psychiatric disorders impact recovery and rehabilitation. Personality traits, 92 levels of stress, 57,86 anxiety, and depression 102 have been linked with stroke recovery. Depression and anxiety have perhaps the greatest impact on recovery and rehabilitation, with depression being linked with deficits in physical function 22 and with deficits in impairment in daily living. 21,22,105 The presence of anxiety reduces functional ability and dimin-ishes social networks as well.

units.title: The Therapeutic Relationship
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Areas identified within this chapter—personality traits; cultural attitudes and beliefs; psychological and cognitive consequences of stroke; emotional reactions to illness, disability, and recovery; and social context and support— affect physical, psychological, and social functioning and the potential for independence. This information has a direct bearing on the occupational profile developed and on the intervention strategies carried out. Given this, it is paramount to consider every interac-tion between the patient and therapist as a context for assessment and intervention. 113 The relationship that develops presents an ongoing opportunity to consider personal and social needs, clarify and refine goals, and address the ambient emotional conditions affecting prog-ress.

units.title: Evaluation
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Evaluating the psychological conditions in an individual with stroke should be part of every therapist’s ongo-ing assessment procedures. In addition to using specific measurement tools that target psychological and cogni-tive functions, the therapist should seek to answer a series of questions via interview of the patient and family and through observation. This process may be a challenge, particularly if speech, language, or visual spatial impair-ments are evident. The mental status examination provides the initial and the ongoing evaluation of mental states.

units.title: Patient-Centered Care
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Recognizing and addressing the symptoms of emotional and psychological issues should be part of all treatment approaches and in all phases of care. Attention to self- esteem by building competencies, setting realistic goals, and planning for the future is an important consideration. Specifically focusing on role transition 28 is also critical because role satisfaction contributes to one’s sense of self. Surprisingly, occupational therapists, despite knowing that practice includes addressing community participa-tion, have traditionally not attended to this area when pro-viding treatment.

units.title: Family-Centered Care
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Any discussion on intervention must include family- centered care because stroke affects not only the patient but also the patient’s immediate and extended social net-work. 77 Hence, emotional reactions, coping strategies, social and community support, and participation are fam-ily issues. The emotional responses family members have when a loved one has a disabling condition were discussed earlier and parallel the emotions the patient has. 39 Just as the family members hope to have all functional capacities restored in their loved one, they also want their family to return to “normal.” 39 Lawlor and Mattingly 77 remind us that family occupa-tions help define family relationships and their well-being.

units.title: EVIDENCE-BASED PRACTICE
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Approaches to Motor Control Dysfunction: An Evidence-Based Review
units.summary: Evidence-based practice is an important aspect of education, clinical practice, and research in occupational and physi-cal therapy. Its importance stems from the need to choose the best (most effective and current) available intervention techniques, which is a fundamental ethical responsibility of occupational and physical therapists. Sackett coined the term evidence-based medicine and defined it as “the conscien-tious, explicit, and judicious use of current best evidence in making decisions about the care of individual patients. The practice of evidence-based medicine means integrating individual clinical expertise with the best available external clinical evidence from systematic research.” 35,36 Evidence-based rehabilitation is the application of the principles of evidence-based medicine to clinical questions in the field of rehabilitation.

units.title: Implications for Practice
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

units.summary: The systematic review confirms that the Bobath approach is less effective as compared with functional TOT, CIMT, and RT. In the past few years, proponents of the Bobath approach have made an attempt to integrate traditional techniques with the language of newly emerging knowl-edge in motor control and motor learning. This can be seen in a recent text describing the theoretical basis of neurodevelopmental treatment. 15 The amalgamation of traditional techniques with new theoretical knowledge is not useful theoretically (since established Bobath tech-niques are not consistent within the new paradigm of motor control and learning) or for clinical practice (since numerous studies have demonstrated the superiority of newer approaches).

units.title: CURRENT APPROACHES: TASK ORIENTED APPROACH
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Approaches to Motor Control Dysfunction: An Evidence-Based Review
units.summary: The Task Oriented Approach (TOA) is based on a systems model of motor control and theories of motor learning. The approach attempts to understand the challenges faced by the nervous system to control movements. This field of motor neuroscience represents a multidisciplinary approach to understanding motor control and learning from the perspectives of neurophysiology, biomechanics, and behavioral sciences. Within this framework, motor control is understood as an attempt by the nervous sys-tem to adapt movements to constraints imposed by the mechanics of the motor apparatus (including length, mass of limbs, and intersegmental forces of moving segments), constraints imposed by the environment (open or closed environment), and constraints imposed by the behavioral context.

units.title: Implications for Practice
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Approaches to Motor Control Dysfunction: An Evidence-Based Review
units.summary: Since 2015, there has been very good evidence that RTP, TOT, or RTT, involving the use of structured practice of functional tasks, is effective in improving UL func-tion. Evidence from one notable RCT seems to contract the findings of the systematic reviews. However, the trial demonstrated that dose equivalent OT, which involves practice of functional skills, may be similar to protocols used in TOT. Taken together, these studies highlight the importance of contextually appropriate task-specific prac-tice of functional skills.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

units.summary: 9 reviewed 38 individual RCTs with 1561 participants whose stage of recovery from stroke ranged from 1 day to 10 years. Sixteen studies were conducted in the acute and subacute stages, 13 were conducted in the chronic stage, and 9 included participants at any stage of recovery. The amount of time for constraining the less impaired limb varied across studies and ranged from 20% to 90% of waking hours. While there were differences in the intervention across studies, participants were pro-vided with structured, intense practice of functional UL tasks.

units.title: Implications for Practice
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Approaches to Motor Control Dysfunction: An Evidence-Based Review
units.summary: Since 2015, there is accumulating evidence for the ben-efits of CIMT or mCIMT in improving arm and hand function. The combination of restraining the unimpaired UL and structured, intensive practice of functional skills is beneficial in the chronic stage of recovery follow-ing stroke. There is emerging evidence that CIMT and mCIMT is safe, feasible, and beneficial in the acute stage of recovery. However, CIMT or mCIMT is not more effective when compared with dose-equivalent interven-tion that includes training of meaningful functional tasks.
summary_sentences: Since 2015, there is accumulating evidence for the ben-efits of CIMT or mCIMT in improving arm and hand function.
The combination of restraining the unimpaired UL and structured, intensive practice of functional skills is beneficial in the chronic stage of recovery follow-ing stroke.
There is emerging evidence that CIMT and mCIMT is safe, feasible, and beneficial in the acute stage of recovery.
However, CIMT or mCIMT is not more effective when compared with dose-equivalent interven-tion that includes training of meaningful functional tasks.

units.summary: 43 reviewed 44 RCTs to examine the effects of RT on UL motor control, UL capacity, ADL, muscle strength, and muscle tone in comparison with nonrobotic therapy. The review separately examined the effectiveness of two different types of robotic systems: exoskeletons, defined as external structural devices that are designed to apply assistive forces on one or more joints, and end- effectors, defined as systems with a single attachment designed to guide the most distal part of the UL. The total number of participants in this review was 1362, making this one of the most comprehensive reviews. Most studies included participants who were more than 3 months of their stroke event.

units.summary: 16 conducted an RCT to compare the effi-cacy of a proximal robot (InMotion-arm) and distal robot (InMotion-wrist) in improving motor control in people at the chronic phase of recovery after stroke. The study recruited 44 participants who were more than 6 months from their stroke, had residual arm and hand function, and did not demonstrate excessive spasticity or neuropsycho-logical deficits. Participants were randomly assigned to a proximal robot group, distal robot group, or conventional rehabilitation. The proximal robot provided assistance during two-dimensional shoulder and elbow movements with the forearm supported while participants interacted with a video game interface.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

units.summary: One limitation of the TOAs described above is that they have been tested with patients who have some active movement (particularly wrist and finger exten-sion) in the paralyzed UL. In order to initiate inter-vention for patients with little or no active movement following a stroke, mirror therapy (MT) has been pro-posed as an alternative intervention as a precursor or supplement to TOAs. MT was originally proposed to help with phantom limb sensation following limb loss and has been applied to stroke rehabilitation. 1,33 MT is based on neurophysiological studies that demonstrate that performance of an action and observation of the same action activates similar cortical areas.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

units.summary: Virtual reality (VR) has a history in recreation and gaming before it was adapted for use in training settings, such as simulated flight training and simulated procedural training for surgery. As VR technology became more affordable and user-friendly, it has been adapted for rehabilitation. 45 The application of VR to stroke rehabilitation is predicated on the fact that it allows for intense practice of simulated functional tasks. VR is defined as “use of interactive simulations created with computer hardware and software to present users with opportunities to engage in environments that appear and feel similar to real-world objects and events.” 45 In VR, patients interact with virtual environments and objects, which can provide the user with feedback using either a head-mounted device, projection screen, or flat screen.

units.summary: Rib Cage The rib cage is formed by the sternum, costal cartilage, ribs, and the bodies of the thoracic vertebrae. The rib cage protects the organs in the thoracic cavity, assists in res-piration, and provides support for the upper extremities. During inspiration, the ribs are elevated, and during expi-ration the ribs are depressed. Although each rib has its own ROM (occurring pri-marily at the costovertebral joint), rib cage shifts occur with movement of the vertebral column.

units.title: Postural Malalignment
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

units.summary: Postural Malalignment Stroke patients commonly assume postural malalignments that first must be identified via observations and palpa-tions. After identification, the causative factors must be determined before determining the most appropriate intervention (Table 17.3). Prolonged postural malalignment results in muscle shortening on one side of the trunk and muscle over-stretching on the opposite side. For example, a posterior pelvic tilt with lumbar flexion results in shortening of the anterior musculature and elongation (overstretching) of the posterior muscles.
