Managing Stiffness and the Degrees of Freedom Problem
units.summary: Managing Stiffness and the Degrees of Freedom Problem Mohr 43 states, “Normal control in any body part demands the ability to dissociate (separate) different parts of the body.” She gives the examples of dissociating the head from the body, one side of the body from the other, and the upper trunk from the lower trunk. Instead, patients often appear stiff, have nonfluid movements, and move their body segments as a unit. Examples of dissociation during functional tasks include upper trunk rotation with lower trunk stability while reaching for toilet paper, counterrotation of the trunk dur-ing ambulatory activities, and upper trunk rotation with concurrent lower trunk lateral flexion to increase the range of reach beyond the arm span when reaching for a phone positioned on the left side of a desk with the right hand. Difficulty with dissociation/postural stiffness may result from soft-tissue tightness, bony contracture, or efforts by the patient to decrease the degrees of freedom in the trunk 48 during functional activities.

units.title: Subjective Interview
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Seated Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Therapists should question patients about their perceived stability limits. Stability limits have been defined as the “boundaries of an area of space in which the body can maintain its position without changing the base of sup-port.” 50 Patients’ perceived stability limits may or may not be consistent with their actual limits. If patients’ perceived lim-its of stability are greater than their actual limits, they are at risk for falls. If their perceived limits of stability are less than their actual limits, they may be reluctant to attempt tasks with progressively greater demands on their postural system (e.g., lower extremity dressing without assistive devices and picking up objects from the floor without a reacher).

units.title: Trunk Control Test
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Seated Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: The Trunk Control Test 15 examines four functional movements: roll from supine to the weak side, roll from supine to the strong side, sitting up from supine, and sit-ting on the edge of the bed for 30 seconds (feet off the ground). Each of the four tasks is scored as follows: 0, unable to perform with assistance; 12, able to perform but in an abnormal manner; and 25, able to complete move-ment normally. The Trunk Control Test has been shown to be sensi-tive to change in assessing recovery of stroke patients, to correlate with the Functional Independence Measure, and to predict motor Functional Independence Measure items at discharge better than motor Functional Independence Measure scores. found that the Trunk Control Test significantly correlated with length of stay, discharge motor Functional Indepen-dence Measure scores, gait velocity, walking distance, and the Berg Balance Scale.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Seated Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Trunk Impairment Scale (B) This tool consists of seven items. Abdominal muscle strength and verticality items were derived from the Stroke Impairment Assessment Set, and the other five items con-sist of the perception of trunk verticality, trunk rotation muscle strength on the affected and the unaffected sides, and righting reflexes both on the affected and the unaf-fected sides. The seven items are scored on a four-point scale, with 0 indicating poor performance and 3 indicating best performance 30 (Box 17.1 and Table 17.7).

Postural Assessment Scale for Stroke Patients
units.summary: Postural Assessment Scale for Stroke Patients The Postural Assessment Scale for Stroke Patients includes items related to trunk control. Overall, the scale contains 12 four-point items graded from 0 to 3. Items include sitting without support, standing with and without support, standing on the nonparetic leg, standing on the paretic leg, supine to affected side, supine to nonaffected side, supine to sit, sit to supine, sit to stand, stand to sit, and standing and picking up a pencil from the floor. The Postural Assessment Scale for Stroke Patients has been found to be highly valid and reliable during the first 3 months after stroke.

units.title: Chedoke-McMaster Stroke Assessment
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Seated Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Chedoke-McMaster Stroke Assessment The Chedoke-McMaster Stroke Assessment is used to assess physical impairment and disability in clients with stroke. It has two components including the Impairment Inventory (which determines the presence and severity of physical impairments in the six dimensions of shoul-der pain, postural control, and arm, hand, foot, and leg quantified in a seven-point staging system) and the Activ-ity Inventory (which measures the client’s functional abil-ity). The Activity Inventory has two components: the Gross Motor Function Index (with items including mov-ing in bed and transferring to a chair) and the Walking Index (with items including walking on rough ground and climbing stairs).

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Seated Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Fugl-Meyer Assessment The Fugl-Meyer Assessment 29 evaluates five areas: joint motion and pain, balance, sensation, upper extremity motor function, and lower extremity motor function. The balance subscale includes seven functions related to postural con-trol: sit without support, protective reactions on affected and nonaffected sides, stand with support, stand without support, stand on nonaffected leg, and stand on affected leg. Mao and colleagues 42 compared the psychometric properties of the balance subscale of the Fugl- Meyer Assessment, the Berg Balance Scale (see Chapter 18), and the Postural Assessment Scale for Stroke Patients. They concluded that all three tests showed acceptable levels of reliability, validity, and responsiveness with the Postural Assessment Scale for Stroke Patients showing slightly bet-ter psychometric characteristics.

units.title: Observations of Trunk Alignment/Malalignment
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Seated Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: For the purposes of this chapter, observations concern the seated posture. The patient’s trunk should be exposed as much as possible, and the patient should be asked to “sit up nice and straight and gently rest your hands in your lap.” (Table 17.8 outlines the ideal alignment of the trunk and extremities and common asymmetries observed after stroke during static sitting.) Following the evaluation of postural malalignments during static sitting, the therapist should begin to hypoth-esize the cause of these malalignments. Causes may include increased skeletal muscle activity on one side of the trunk, inability to recruit muscle activity or weakness, soft-tissue shortening, fixed deformity, body scheme dis-order, and inability to perceive midline. The therapist must remember that observed pos-tures may be caused by more than one impairment (see Table 17.3).

The examiner asks the patient to indicate when he or she feels the trunk is in a vertical position. The examiner then records the degree of trunk angle deviation from the vertical line drawn from the midpoint of the Jacoby line. 1 = The angle is <30 degrees and ≥20 degrees.

Trunk Rotation Muscle Strength on the Affected Side
units.summary: Trunk Rotation Muscle Strength on the Affected Side The patient is asked to roll the body from the supine position to the unaffected side. The arms should be crossed in front of the chest and legs kept extended. The patient is asked to roll his or her body without pushing the floor with his or her limbs or pulling on the bed clothes. Isometric contractions for stabilization and other muscles than external oblique (e.g., pectoralis major) activation during rolling are allowed.

units.summary: Trunk Extensor Control The following four movement patterns are used to evaluate trunk extensor control during seated activities and bridging. To start this movement pattern, the patient assumes a flexed spine posture with a posterior pelvis tilt (the resting posture for many stroke survivors). The patient initiates the movement with the lower trunk and pel-vis 43 and assumes an extended spine posture with a neutral to slight anterior tilt, which accentuates the lumbar curve (Fig. The patient completes the movement pattern by a concentric contraction of the trunk extensors, which is the trunk pattern required for forward reach.

units.title: Assuming an Appropriate Starting Posture
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Seated Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Before initiation of tasks and retraining of trunk control, the trunk must be in a proper biomechanical alignment. Therapists should observe patients anteriorly, posteriorly, and laterally to detect deviations from normal alignment (see Table 17.8). Physically or verbally cueing patients to assume an appropriate starting posture should place them in a posi-tion of readiness for function-optimal symmetry in the trunk that is usually in midline, depending on the task (see Box 17.3). This neutral starting posture is similar to the position the trunk and lower extremities assume when a person begins a typing task.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

Maintaining or Increasing Trunk ROM through Mobilization and Movement
units.summary: Maintaining or Increasing Trunk ROM through Mobilization and Movement Concerning ROM in the trunk, Mohr 43 states, “If there is not full range in all trunk movements (flexion extension, lateral flexion, and rotation), it will be more difficult to gain full control of the trunk. Any lack of ROM in the trunk will lead to decreased function.” Although limited ROM in the extremities is com-monly evaluated and treated, the ROM in the spine often is overlooked. After acute strokes, patients lose the ability to shift their weight and make postural adjustments.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Seated Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Therapists may use various postures as an adjunct treat-ment during patients’ performance of functional tasks. Therapists should select postures based on specific patient needs. The chosen posture should accentuate and chal-lenge the movement and control patterns interfering with independent performance of life activities. If the patient is not engaging in a specific activity (self-care tasks, games, and adapted sports), the use of these postures in isolation is not encouraged.

units.title: Treating the “Pusher Syndrome” or Contraversive Pushing
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Seated Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
Treating the “Pusher Syndrome” or Contraversive Pushing
units.summary: Treating the “Pusher Syndrome” or Contraversive Pushing The “pusher syndrome” is a phrase coined by Davies, 17,18 who derived the name from what she felt was the most striking aspect of this syndrome: the patient pushes heavily toward the hemiplegic side in all positions and resists any attempt at passive correction (i.e., a correction that would bring the weight toward or over the midline of the body to the unaffected side). This phenomenon has been docu-mented in patients with both right and left hemispheric lesions. Further analysis has revealed that the brain struc-ture typically damaged in patients with pusher syndrome is the left or right posterolateral thalamus.

units.title: Engaging in Reaching Tasks
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Seated Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Therapists can use placement of objects in reaching activities as a way to place a variety of demands on the trunk. The key to eliciting a trunk response is to place the object slightly beyond the arm’s reach. Fisher 26 observes that when subjects with-out brain injuries reach, they anteriorly tilt the pelvis, slightly extend the upper back, and move the trunk in the direction of the arm. Patients with brain injuries do not incorporate trunk movements into arm movements and reach only to arm’s length as they maintain a slumped posture.

units.summary: Sitting Score with the patient seated, feet off floor, with both hands in lap. This will not be scored as “lateropulsion.” Position the patient with their trunk 30 degrees off true vertical toward their affected side, then score the patient’s response to your attempts to bring them back to vertical.

units.title: Handling
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

units.summary: Handling is a common technique used in the clinic. This intervention commonly is associated with neurodevel-opmental therapy 8 and may allow the patient to feel the desired movement pattern, gain range, assist weak move-ment patterns, and provide external support to prevent falls. To be effective, the patient must be aware of the goal associated with handling, and the therapist should use handling within the context of a functional task. In addi-tion, the handling from the therapist should be graded to allow the patient to perform as much of the movement pattern as possible.

units.title: Visual System
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

units.summary: Visual System The visual system (see Chapter 24) provides information regarding vertical orientation and visual flow. Visual or optical flow information, which describes movement of an image on the retina, is important input that aids detection of personal and environmental movement. Information provided by the visual system can be ambiguous and must be compared with other sensory information to determine accuracy. 6 For example, a person sitting in a stationary car next to another stationary car at a red light may receive optical flow information that indicates the other car is moving backward.

units.summary: Somatosensory System Somatosensory information is conveyed via cutaneous and subcutaneous receptors on the soles of the feet and pro-prioceptors located in muscles and joints. This informa-tion helps determine the relationship of the individual to the support surface and the relationship of one body seg-ment to another (e.g., lower limb position relative to the trunk). Evidence suggests that somatosensory information from all parts of the body plays an important role in pos-tural control.

units.title: Summary
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Standing Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Summary As indicated earlier, integrated sensory information from these three systems plays an important role in standing postural control. However, the CNS is able to “reweight” this sensory information (CNS increases reliance on one type of sensory input while decreasing reliance on another type) based on the constraints of the task and environ-ment. 6,60 For example, when visual cues are unavailable (eyes closed, dark room) or inaccurate (the environment is in motion), reliance on visual information is reduced, and the CNS will rely heavily on somatosensory and vestibular input. 6,60 The ability of the CNS to modify how sensory information is used is essential in allowing a person to maintain standing balance under varying task and envi-ronmental constraints.

units.title: Cognitive and Perceptual Systems
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Standing Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: In addition to sensory and motor processing, postural control is also influenced by cognitive and perceptual pro-cesses, such as the allocation of attentional resources 60,74 and the ability to perceive an upright orientation of the body with respect to gravity (aka subjective postural verti-cal [SPV]). 11 The role of attention in postural control was brought to light by studies utilizing dual- task paradigms (e.g., maintaining postural control while engaged in a complex cognitive activity). The results of these studies suggest that postural control is attentionally demanding and that attentional demands required for postural control vary as a consequence of the interaction between the person, task, and environment. 74 With respect to SPV, healthy indi-viduals are able to determine the upright orientation of the body with respect to gravity in standing within a very narrow range (normality values range from –1.7 to 2.3 degrees in the sagittal plane and from –1.6 to 1.2 degrees in the frontal plane) without the aid of vision.

units.title: Cerebral Cortex
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Standing Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Cerebral Cortex The cerebral cortex is thought to play an instrumental role in mediating postural control. Recent evidence suggests that cortical structures, such as the supplementary motor area, premotor areas, primary somatosensory cortices, prefrontal cortex, posterior parietal cortex, and the ante-rior cingulate cortex play an important role in modulating subcortical postural control centers (e.g., brainstem [BS] centers) in order to maintain upright standing posture and standing balance under varying task and environmental demands. 62,63 It is thought that these areas work in a coor-dinated fashion to integrate sensory information, moni-tor ongoing postural stability, detect stable from unstable postures, and generate coordinated postural responses to cope with potential and actual threats to standing balance. Thus, damage to the cerebral cortices can have a nega-tive impact on standing balance (see “Common Stand-ing Postural Control Impairments after Hemispheric Stroke”).

units.title: Cerebellum
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Standing Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Cerebellum The cerebellum is thought to be an important structure underlying postural control. 32,77 The cerebellum receives information from structures such as the cortex, basal ganglia, spinocerebellar tract (somatosensory informa-tion), vestibular nuclei, and vestibular pathways. Input is modulated, interpreted, and sent out to the cortex; basal ganglia; thalamus; fourth, fifth, and sixth cranial nerves; vestibular nuclei and pathways; and indirectly to the spi-nal cord, providing the regulatory input needed to modify postural muscle tone and postural response to cope with changing task and environmental demands. 77 Damage to the cerebellum can result in difficulties with both reac-tive and anticipatory standing postural control.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

units.summary: Basal Ganglia The basal ganglia are also involved in integrating infor-mation used for postural control. 70 The basal ganglia receive information from multiple sources, including the cortex and cerebellum, and then output information to the motor cortex via the thalamus. The basal ganglia work closely with the cerebellum and are believed to influ-ence sensory reweighting, postural flexibility (adapting to changing circumstances), and the sequencing of automatic postural reactions including the ankle, hip, stepping, and reach and grasp strategies previously discussed. 70 Dam-age to the basal ganglia may result in postural inflexibil-ity, impaired scaling of automatic postural responses, and an inability to modify postural responses according to the demands of a given task.

units.title: Brainstem
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Standing Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Brainstem The BS houses several centers (e.g., areas in the midbrain, vestibular and raphe nuclei, and the pontomedullary reticular formation) that are important for the regulation of postural muscle tone and postural responses and gen-eration of compensatory eye movements. 45 Many of these areas have reciprocal connections with the basal ganglia and cerebellum and are also modulated by the cerebral cortex. These nuclei output to lower motor neurons in the spinal cord via the vestibulospinal, raphespinal, and reticulospinal tracts, respectively. 45 Thus, damage to the BS can result in impairments in the regulation of postural muscle tone and the execution of appropriate postural responses.

Also, the spinal cord takes in somatosensory information and con-veys this information to higher centers).

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

COMMON STANDING POSTURAL CONTROL IMPAIRMENTS AFTER HEMISPHERIC STROKE
units.summary: COMMON STANDING POSTURAL CONTROL IMPAIRMENTS AFTER HEMISPHERIC STROKE Motor and sensory impairments after stroke may differ depending on the location and extent of the stroke (see Chapter 1). Thus, postural control impairments may differ based on these factors. Standing balance dysfunction after stroke may be caused by motor impairments (e.g., weak-ness, changes in muscle tone), sensory loss or impaired sensory reweighting, or cognitive (e.g., attentional impair-ment, impulsivity) and perceptual (e.g., visuospatial inat-tention, impairments in the perception of vertical, body schema) dysfunction.

units.title: Subjective Interview
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Standing Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: When conducting a subjective interview, the clinician must keep in mind that patients who have had an acute stroke may not be able to provide accurate information during the interview process due to cognitive and/or language impairments. Clinicians may need to use other sources of information, including family members, signifi-cant others, and information from the medical chart, to supplement, clarify, or verify information that a patient provides. Patients may improve in their ability to provide information as cognitive and language deficits improve. Patients often also demonstrate a greater awareness of their situation and surroundings as they improve and become more fully integrated into the home and commu-nity environments.

units.title: Component Assessment
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Standing Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: An evaluation of the visual, somatosensory, and vestibular systems is considered to be an important part of component assessment related to standing postural control. 6,60 An evaluation of the visual system typically includes visual acuity and an assessment of oculomotor function (reflexive and voluntary—see Chapter 24 for details). An evaluation of the somatosensory system should include an assessment of light touch, pressure, proprioception, and kinesthesia, particularly of the lower extremities. Finally, assessment of the vestibular system should be performed if deficits in this system are suspected (see Chapter 19).

units.title: Evaluating the Influence of Sensory Organization on Postural Control
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Standing Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
Evaluating the Influence of Sensory Organization on Postural Control
units.summary: Evaluating the Influence of Sensory Organization on Postural Control Assessing the ability of the CNS to evaluate, integrate, and appropriately weight sensory information is an impor-tant part of a component assessment of standing balance. Computerized tests of sensory organization are available commercially and often are combined with force plates that can measure motor responses to test conditions (to a degree). The sensory organization portion of the appa-ratus usually consists of a safety harness, a movable foot plate, and a movable visual screen that surrounds the sub-ject. Test conditions also have been simulated in the clinic by using 4-inch medium-density foam as a compliant sur-face and a visual “dome” that encompasses the patient’s visual field and is worn on the head.

units.summary: Using functional activities and emphasizing functional outcomes are basic principles of OT, and they are being embraced by many other disciplines. Hsieh and col-leagues 36 stated that using added- purpose occupation is motivating during performance. Currently, available information supports the use of repetitive functional tasks and engagement in activities as primary intervention tools for retraining standing balance. 1,3,26,33,44,53,65 In addition, adjuncts to task training such as exercise, 35 motor imag-ery, 17 and virtual reality training 50 have also been shown to be effective for improving balance (see Table 18.4).

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

Improving Postural Alignment and Retraining Effective Movement Strategies
units.summary: Improving Postural Alignment and Retraining Effective Movement Strategies As illustrated earlier, patients who have had a stroke often have an impaired ability to control their COM over their BOS in standing, resulting in an asymmetri-cal postural alignment, decreased ability to cope with external threats to balance, and difficulty generating anticipatory postural control responses. Wu and col-leagues 75 indicated that one functional goal in rehabili-tating persons with hemiplegia should be “to improve symmetrical characteristics of postural control.” The most common forms of treatment for asymmetrical weight bearing and poor standing postural control are to expose the patient to a variety of conditions that require the patient to control COM movements over the BOS.

units.title: Retraining Symmetrical Postural Alignment
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Standing Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Retraining Symmetrical Postural Alignment A variety of strategies can be used to help patients develop a symmetrical standing posture. For example, therapists often utilize verbal cues (e.g., “shift your weight a little more to the left”) or manual assistance (shifting patients weight through the pelvis) to help patients find their optimal postural alignment. 60 Once this alignment is achieved, the patient is encouraged to maintain it for a period of time. Therapists may also make use of feedback mechanisms to improve symmet-rical standing alignment.

units.title: Retraining Effective Movement Strategies
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Standing Postural Control: Supporting Functional Independence
units.summary: Retraining Effective Movement Strategies As discussed previously, part of a comprehensive bal-ance assessment is evaluating what patients do to main-tain their balance. Three strategies were outlined as normal movement strategies: ankle, hip, and strate-gies that change the BOS (i.e., stepping and reaching). Information from the component assessment allows the therapist to determine whether a strategy is being used, the amount of delay in strategy use (and therefore its effectiveness), and whether the strategy is appropriate. Therapists can use external perturbations (e.g., pas-sively moving the patient through the hips or using a moveable surface to cause weight shifting in various directions) in an attempt to retrain standing balance responses.

units.summary: Standing postural control is instrumental to our ability to engage in daily living activities and it is often com-promised after stroke. An understanding of the systems involved in postural control and the application of appro-priate assessment and treatment of standing balance dys-function is an important component of comprehensive OT treatment for stroke survivors. The subsequent case study provides an example of the implementation of these principles.

units.title: Inertial Mechanism
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Inertial Mechanism The mechanism of the vestibular labyrinth is based on the principle of inertia, that is, that an object remains at rest until an asymmetrical force acts on it, and then it contin-ues to move until another asymmetrical force acts on it to stop it. The semicircular canals are narrow (imagine a curved tube approximately the width of a hair on your head), so they provide a large amount of resistance to any fluid that fills it. The canals are then filled with a thick fluid known as endolymph. Endolymph has a high spe-cific gravity, so it has high inertia.

units.title: Innervation and Blood Supply
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Innervation and Blood Supply All of this hardware in the temporal bone is supplied by nerves and arteries. The vestibular labyrinth is innervated by the vestibular nerve, which is half of cranial nerve VIII. The superior branch innervates the superior and horizontal semicircu-lar canals and the utricle, and the inferior branch inner-vates the posterior canal and the saccule. The arterial supply to the vestibular labyrinth is similar to the innervation.

units.title: Lateral Medullary Syndrome
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The most common stroke of the vestibular system, first reported in the late 19th century, 31 is lateral medullary syndrome, also known as Wallenberg syndrome. 3 This syndrome is caused by a stroke of either the PICA or AICA. Because both arteries that supply the vestibular nuclei also supply other areas, lateral medullary syndrome is manifested by mixed sensory and motor loss, including vertigo, latero-pulsion, disequilibrium, ataxia, contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the trunk and limbs, and the following ipsilateral signs: facial numbness, Horner syn-drome (drooping of the upper eyelid, constriction of the pupil, and decreased sweating), and dysphagia. Involve-ment of the PICA also includes hoarseness and skew devi-ation of the eyes.

units.title: Cerebellar Infarcts
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Cerebellar lesions without involvement in the brain-stem can be caused by occlusion of the PICA, AICA, or vertebral artery. These patients are rarely seen for vestibular rehabilitation. According to noted authori-ties Baloh and Harker, acute episodes of vertigo, disequilibrium, and nausea accompanied by typical cerebellar signs of ataxia, disdiadochokinesia, and gaze nystagmus are often followed by edema of the cerebel-lum. 4 Cerebellar edema can be fatal because, when the cerebellum becomes compressed, the nearby brainstem structures can be damaged unless the area is surgically decompressed.

To complete this activity successfully, the patient must process appropri-ately the visual/perceptual information collected during the scanning process before initiating the reach pattern.

units.title: Weight-Bearing Task/Closed Chain Activity
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The weight-bearing task described requires the patient to use one arm as a postural support (i.e., extended-arm weight-bearing to support function) on a kitchen table while the other arm and hand wipe the table. As mentioned previously, motivation and purpose are required. The motivation may be hunger (so the table must be cleaned in preparation for a meal), extrinsic (e.g., visitors), or work related (e.g., table space is needed to balance the check-book or prepare a lecture). Because the weight-bearing arm is being used as a postural support, a variety of pos-tural adjustments occur in the arm.

units.title: SELECTED EVALUATION TOOLS
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Evaluation tools that are standardized, reliable, and valid can be overlooked no longer. Many therapists continue to use piecemeal evaluations that do not incorporate the use of functional tasks and rely too heavily on evaluation of impairments. Beyond validity and reliability, when choosing assess-ments, clinicians must consider time factors, level of motor function, the purpose of the evaluation (clinical, research, or both), and the environment in which the assessment will take place. Many available assessments such as the Fugl- Meyer Assessment, only evaluate the impairment level and do not include information regarding how the upper extremity is used during daily occupations.

units.title: Motor Activity Log (Self-Report)
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The Motor Activity Log (MAL) is a self-report question-naire (report by patient or family) related to actual use of the involved upper extremity outside of structured therapy time. Quality of movement (“How well” scale) and amount of use (“How much” scale) are graded on a 6-point scale. At present, there are 14-, 28-, and 30-item versions of the tool. Sam-ple items include hold a book, use a towel, pick up a glass, write/type, and steady myself, etc.

units.title: 36-Item Manual Ability Measure (Self-Report)
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The 36-item Manual Ability Measure (MAM-36) is a new Rasch- developed, self- report disability outcome mea-sure. It contains 36 gender-neutral, commonly performed everyday hand tasks. The patient is asked to report the ease or difficulty of performing such items. It uses a 4-point rating scale, with 1 indicating “unable” (I am unable to do the task all by myself), 2 indicating “very hard” (It is very hard for me to do the task and I usually ask others to do it for me unless no one is around), 3 indicating “a little hard” (I usually do the task myself, although it takes longer or more effort now than before), and 4 indicating “easy” (I can do the task without any problem).

units.title: ABILHAND Questionnaire (Self-Report)
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The ABILHAND questionnaire asks clients to use a 3-point scale (0 = impossible, 2 = easy) to rate how difficult it would be to complete 23 bimanual tasks (e.g., hammer a nail, wrap a gift, thread a needle, file nails, cut meat, peel onions, open jar, etc.). Grip strength, motricity, dexterity, and depression are significantly correlated with the ABIL-HAND measures.

units.title: Adult Assisting Hand Assessment Stroke
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The Adult Assisting Hand Assessment (Ad-AHA) Stroke is an observation-based assessment designed to measure how the affected hand is spontaneously used with the other hand when performing bimanual activities. The assessment was modeled after the original AHA that was developed for use with children with congenital hemi-paresis. It consists of the patient performing one of two selected tasks (i.e., Sandwich task or Present task) and task performance is video recorded and 19 items are scored on a 4-point ordinal scale. Both amount and quality of upper limb movements are assessed.

units.title: Assessment of Motor and Process Skills
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Assessment of Motor and Process Skills
units.summary: The therapists evaluate motor and process skills 76,77 within the context of basic ADLs and instrumental ADLs (IADLs). The quality of the person’s ADL performance is assessed by rating the effort, efficiency, safety, and inde-pendence of 16 ADL motor and 20 ADL process skill items, while the person is doing chosen, familiar, and life-relevant ADL tasks. There are more than 100 tasks to choose from, thus promoting a client-centered approach to assessment. Examples of evaluated motor skills include posture, mobility, coordination, strength, reach, manipu-lation, grip, lifting, effort, and energy expenditure (see Chapter 5).

units.title: Arm Motor Ability Test
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The Arm Motor Ability Test (AMAT) has been used to determine the effectiveness of constraint-induced move-ment therapy (CIMT) and includes 13 unilateral and bilateral tasks. Sample items include tying a shoe, opening a jar, wiping up spilled water, using a light switch, using utensils, and drinking. The therapist times task perfor-mance and rates movement quality on a 6-point scale. The test is appropriate for evaluating motor skills in high-level clients with active wrist and finger extension.

units.title: Wolf Motor Function Test
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The Wolf Motor Function Test (WMFT) has been used to document the outcomes related to CIMT and includes a variety of tasks such as basic reaching tasks (e.g., lift-ing arm from lap to table, extending elbow with and with-out a weight attached) and more functional activities that involve fine motor control (e.g., picking up a pencil, turn-ing a key in a lock). All tasks but one are unilateral and appropriate for both the dominant and nondominant arm. As many tasks do not require distal control, it is appropri-ate for people with a more involved upper extremity. The therapist times task performance and qualitatively grades movement.

units.title: Jebsen Test of Hand Function
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The Jebsen Test of Hand Function 113 includes the per-formance of seven test activities: writing a short sentence, turning over index cards, picking up small objects and placing them in a container, stacking checkers, simulating eating, moving empty large cans, and moving weighted large cans during timed trials. The original paper is based on data collected from 360 normal subjects and patients, including patients with hemiparesis resulting from a stroke. The mean times and standard deviations for nor-mal subjects (with their dominant and nondominant hand) are published in the paper. The test is standardized and reliable and does not have a practice effect.

units.title: The Functional Upper Extremity Levels
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The Functional Upper Extremity Levels (FUEL) is a new classification tool used to assess a person’s upper extrem-ity functional and physical performance after stroke. The FUEL includes seven levels of arm use that range from nonfunctional to fully functional. The tool includes a table that describes a description of how to classify the use of the affected arm during a task. While the FUEL uses examples of arm use during tooth brushing, it can be used for and activity that requires arm use as long as the defini-tions are adhered to.

Improved motor function is con-sidered a deviation from stereotypical synergies defined by Brunnstrom in this test.

units.summary: USE OF THE INVOLVED UPPER EXTREMITY TO SUPPORT TASK PERFORMANCE: SUGGESTIONS FOR INTERVENTION The foundation of occupational therapy is built on patients taking an active role in their own recovery by participat-ing in functional activities. The most current research on motor control supports the use of tasks performed in context- specific situations (see Chapter 3). Functional tasks in therapy include occupations that require upper extremity weight-bearing for postural support, reaching, carrying, lifting, grasping, and manipulation of common/natural objects.

units.title: Complex Rotation
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Complex Rotation The object is rotated, which requires isolated, independent movements of the finger or thumb. The object is turned between 180 and 360 degrees (e.g., turning a paperclip so that the correct end can be placed on a piece of paper). 234 demonstrated that using material- based occupation (e.g., picking up a pen and preparing to write one’s name) enhanced quality of movement performance more than imagery- based occupation (e.g., pretending to pick up a pen and preparing to sign one’s name) and exercise (e.g., moving the arm forward). Their data suggested that material- based occupation resulted in decreased reaction time, move-ment time, and movement units.

units.title: Weight Bearing to Support Function
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: The use of weight-bearing tasks has long been advocated in patients after stroke. Upper extremity weight bear-ing has been suggested anecdotally for achieving a vari-ety of therapeutic goals, including inhibiting hypertonus by moving the body proximally against the distal upper extremity 64 and stimulating upper extremity extension during protective responses. 25 Brouwer and Ambury 42 concluded that upper extremity weight bearing normal-izes corticospinal facilitation of motor units in stroke patients. They hypothesized that the mechanism respon-sible for their results was a sustained increase in motor cortical excitability through augmented afferent input.

units.title: BOX 20.4 The Australian Therapy Outcome Measures (AusTOMs) for Occupational Therapy: Upper Limb Use
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
BOX 20.4 The Australian Therapy Outcome Measures (AusTOMs) for Occupational Therapy: Upper Limb Use
units.summary: BOX 20.4 The Australian Therapy Outcome Measures (AusTOMs) for Occupational Therapy: Upper Limb Use The ability to use one or both upper limbs during activities of daily living include gross and fine manipulative skills and hand and arm use. This may comprise lifting and moving a heavy object while walking; picking up and using a pencil; grasping, using, and releasing objects such as keys, buttons, or taps; throwing and catching an object; and pushing, pulling, twisting, and turning objects.

units.title: Impairment of Either Structure or Function (as Appropriate to Age)
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Impairment of Either Structure or Function (as Appropriate to Age)
units.summary: Impairment of Either Structure or Function (as Appropriate to Age) Impairments are problems in body structure (anatomic) or function (physiological or psychological) as a significant deviation or loss. Impairments may be mental (cognitive/perceptual), sensory, cardiovascular/respiratory, digestive/metabolic/endocrine systems, neurologic movement, or musculoskeletal. A variety of impairments may affect ability to use upper limbs (if only one upper limb is affected, then rate the severity of impairments affecting this limb; if both are affected, then rate both). Considering all the impairments that an individual may have that affect upper limb use, assess the level of severity of these.

units.title: Electromyographic Biofeedback
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
SELECTED ADJUNCT INTERVENTIONS USED WITH A TASK-ORIENTED APPROACH
units.summary: Electromyographic (EMG) biofeedback shows promise and should be studied further for its potential use in treat-ing upper extremity dysfunction after stroke. Biofeed-back is provided by electronic instruments that measure and give information about neuromuscular or autonomic activity in the form of auditory or visual feedback signals. Tries’ review 207 of the literature included a variety of rationales for integrating this noninvasive modality, includ-ing training voluntary inhibition of spastic muscles and restoring muscle balance, into an upper extremity program. Tries 207 outlined specific techniques for scapula mobility and stability, humeral rotation, integrating scapular and humeral rotation with a forward reach pattern, and reinforcement of functional patterns in the elbow, forearm, and hand.

units.title: Electrical Stimulation
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
SELECTED ADJUNCT INTERVENTIONS USED WITH A TASK-ORIENTED APPROACH
units.summary: Electrical stimulation has been used in poststroke upper extremity rehabilitation for many years. Potential uses have included reduction of shoulder subluxation, reduc-tion of pain, improved motor control, and increasing use of the involved extremity. In general, the effects of electri-cal stimulation have been the most consistent at improving limb impairments such as ROM and reducing pain. The effects on function and ADLs have received less attention and have been inconsistent.

EMG- triggered stimulation detects underlying muscle activity when it reaches a threshold level prior to providing the stimulation. This type of stimulation assures that the intervention is not passive in nature.

units.summary: A relatively new intervention, this intervention appears to be cost-efficient and is able to be done independently. Yavu-zer and colleagues 237 describe the intervention as “During the mirror practices, patients were seated close to a table on which a mirror (35×35 cm) was placed vertically. The involved hand was placed behind the mirror and the nonin-volved hand in front of the mirror. The practice consisted of nonparetic-side wrist and finger flexion and extension movements while patients looked into the mirror, watching the image of their noninvolved hand, thus seeing the reflec-tion of the hand movement projected over the involved hand.

units.summary: During action observation (AO), clients watch another person performing common functional actions, most often via watching a video recording with the intention of imi-tating the observed actions. 79 tested this intervention by having patients carefully watch video footage showing 20 different daily routine tasks (actions) carried out with the upper limb. 79 The patient was presented only one task per day, starting from the easi-est and ending with the most complex action throughout 20 sessions, the whole treatment period lasting 4 weeks (5 sessions per week). Examples of observed actions include drinking from a glass, combing hair, opening a box, or eat-ing an apple.

units.summary: Until relatively recently, the impact of weakness (a negative symptom) on stroke patients is well established. 90,225 The motor control deficits in patients previously were attrib-uted exclusively to spasticity, which resulted in treatment focused on inhibiting the spasticity. Many therapists con-sidered upper extremity muscle tests for strength difficult to interpret because of common “synergy patterns.” Bour-bonnais and colleagues 36 demonstrated that the patterns of activity in the elbow flexor muscles were not consistent with established synergistic patterns. Weakness of the upper extremity musculature plays a major role in upper extremity dysfunction, most likely more than the posi-tive symptoms after stroke.

BOX 20.8 Physiological Changes Contributing to Weakness
units.summary: BOX 20.8 Physiological Changes Contributing to Weakness Gowland and colleagues 89 studied agonist and antag-onist activity during upper limb movements in stroke patients and concluded that treatment should be aimed at improving motor neuron recruitment rather than reduc-ing antagonist activity. In their study, patients who could not perform select upper extremity tasks had EMG values significantly and consistently lower than those of patients who were successful at the task. Indeed, recent empirical evidence highlights the rela-tionship between weakness and loss of function.

units.title: Spasticity
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

units.summary: Spasticity, which is a positive symptom according to the Jackson classification system, has been a subject of debate by various authors. Although an abundance of research has been done on spasticity, disagreements still exist about its definition, physiological basis, treatment, and evalu-ation. Glenn and Whyte 85 define spasticity as “a motor disorder with persistent increase in the involuntary reflex activity of a muscle in response to stretch. Four specific phenomena may be variably observed in the constellation of spasticity: hypertonia (frequently velocity dependent and demonstrating the clasp-knife phenomenon), hyper-active (phasic) deep tendon reflexes, clonus, and spread of reflex responses beyond the muscle stimulated.” In addi-tion, Babinski sign is characteristic, and hyperactive tonic neck or vestibular reflexes may be present.

units.summary: Passive ROM Soft-tissue and joint mobilizations are the treatments of choice for preventing contracture. The benefits of mobili-zation include maintenance of joint lubrication, 33 preven-tion of secondary orthopedic problems (impingements), maintenance of soft-tissue length, and possible reduction of spasticity by acting on the nonneural components of spasticity. Contracture is prevented by deliberate and frequent limb movement, with active movement being preferred over passive when possible. Perry 166 pointed out that it is essential to move the patient through complete ROM and not just the middle ranges.

units.summary: Positioning Positioning is another effective means of maintaining soft-tissue length and can be used to promote low-load, prolonged stretch. Therapists must address the posi-tioning needs of patients while they are in bed or wheel-chairs/armchairs (see Chapter 27) and anytime they are in a recumbent position. Effective positioning encour-ages proper joint alignment, variations in joint position, comfort, and the maintenance of stretch in areas at risk for contracture. Common areas of concern during patient positioning include head and neck alignment, trunk align-ment, glenohumeral joint alignment, scapula alignment, maintenance of abduction, external rotation, elbow exten-sion, and maintenance of length in the long finger flexors.

COMPLEX REGIONAL PAIN SYNDROME TYPE I
units.summary: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is classified as a reflex sympathetic dystrophy disorder or CRPS type I. The painful lesion that precipitates CRPS is a proximal trauma such as a shoulder, neck, or rib cage injury or a visceral source such as stroke. The syndrome begins with severe pain and progresses to stiffness in the shoulder and pain throughout the extremity. Other symptoms include moderate to considerable swelling of the wrist and hand, vasomotor changes, and atrophy.

units.summary: Stage 3 Patients rarely have pain and vasomotor changes, but they do have soft-tissue dystrophy, contracture (including a frozen shoulder and clawed hand), and severe osteoporosis. At this stage, shoulder–hand syndrome is irreversible. Tepperman and colleagues 204 concluded that meta-carpophalangeal tenderness during compression was the most valuable clinical sign of reflex sympathetic dystro-phy, with a predictive value of 100%. Vasomotor changes and interphalangeal tenderness had the next highest pre-dictive value at 72.7%.

BOX 20.14 Protocol to Prevent Shoulder–Hand Syndrome
units.summary: BOX 20.14 Protocol to Prevent Shoulder–Hand Syndrome The protocol shown below is for prevention of shoulder–hand syndrome in patients in the early stages of recovery after cerebrovascular accident (CVA). Both therapist and patient should follow the instructions and restrictions to passive movement for the first 4 months after CVA. Active movement, however, need not be restricted if the patient can move his or her affected fingers and arm, because active movement effectively diminishes hand edema and stiffness.

units.summary: Adhesive Changes Adhesive changes in the hemiplegic shoulder are consid-ered to result from immobilization, synovitis, or metabolic changes in joint tissue. Hakuno and colleagues 93 studied adhesive changes in hemiplegic shoulders and found that hemiplegia had a significant influence on the prevalence of adhesive changes in the shoulder. Adhesive changes were found in 30% of patients’ affected glenohumeral joints as opposed to 2.7% on the less involved side. Rizk and colleagues 177 examined 30 hemiplegic patients by arthrography of the shoulder and found that 23 patients had capsular constriction typical of frozen shoulder (adhe-sive capsulitis).

units.summary: Although pain syndromes have been discussed previously in the context of orthopedic injuries and CRPS, their impact on functional recovery is significant, 225 so this section specifically reviews the literature on hemiplegic shoulder pain. The incidence of shoulder pain in hemiplegic patients has been reported to be as high as 72%. 180 identified strong associations between hemiplegic shoulder pain and prolonged hospital stays, arm weakness, poor recovery of arm function, ADLs, and lower rates of discharge to the home. Those responsible for stroke patients have the onus to be aware of hemiplegic shoulder pain and to diagnose, relieve, and prevent this syndrome.

units.title: Loss of Glenohumeral Joint Alignment
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
SELECTED ADJUNCT INTERVENTIONS USED WITH A TASK-ORIENTED APPROACH
units.summary: Loss of Glenohumeral Joint Alignment Thus far, the loss of pelvic/trunk, rib cage, and scapula control has been reviewed. All of the aforementioned alignment changes have an effect on the stability and alignment of the glenohumeral joint. The mechanisms of glenohumeral joint subluxation remain controversial. As reviewed by Cailliet 46 and Basmajian, 19 the following factors assist in maintaining glenohumeral joint stabil-ity: the angle of the glenoid fossa when facing forward, upward, and outward; the support of the scapula on the rib cage; the seating of the humeral head in the fossa by the supraspinatus; possible support from the superior cap-sule; and contraction of the deltoid and cuff muscles when passive support is eliminated by slight abduction of the humerus.

units.summary: Loss of Distal Alignment Shoulder alignment problems directly affect the align-ment and control of the distal extremity. Boehme 25 states that rotational movements of the forearm “occur at the proximal end with the radius rotating on a vertical axis … the ulnar head is displaced, … the mechanics are made possible by concurrent external rotation of the humerus.” The typical alignment of the humerus after stroke is one of internal rotation, which blocks forearm rotation. Kapandji 116 states that when the elbow is flexed (a typi-cal posture), pronation is reduced to 45 degrees. Boehme 25 points out that when the wrist is bound by flexion and ulnar deviation (the typical posture of the CVA patient), control of forearm rotation also is blocked.

section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke

units.summary: Shoulder supports include any devices used to align, protect, or support an affected proximal limb. Shoulder supports include bed-positioning devices, adaptations to seating systems, and slings. The use of shoulder sup-ports, especially slings, has been debated in the litera-ture for at least 30 years. An earlier review concluded that “There is insufficient evidence to conclude whether slings and wheelchair attachments prevent subluxation, decrease pain, increase function or adversely increase contracture in the shoulder after stroke.” 5 This being said, current stroke gudielines 225 state that it is rea-sonable to consider positioning and use of supportive devices and slings for shoulder subluxation.

units.summary: The Haptic Master is a three-DOF robot that provides gravity assistance for the paretic arm while the user sits at a workstation to complete therapeutic tasks. A free- moving elbow splint attached to an overhead frame sup-ports the arm, and a passive mechanism supports the hand and allows for supination, pronation, and wrist flexion and extension. Force and position sensors enable interaction with virtual tasks such as reaching to a supermarket shelf or pouring a drink. The Haptic Master has been used for task-oriented training (TOT) in a three-dimensional vir-tual environment, as in the GENTLE/s project, 18 and during grasp and manipulation of real objects.

units.summary: The Armeo®Spring (https://hocoma.com), predecessor of the Armeo®Power described earlier, is a body-powered exoskeletal orthosis to support upper limb training after stroke. The robot size and spring tension are adjusted to provide a safe method of gravity assist to support the paretic arm and hand during interactive therapy games. The Armeo®Spring enables naturalistic movement across two-thirds or more of a normal workspace while the user attempts virtual reach and grasp tasks, such as moving items to a shelf or throwing a frisbee. DOFs can be con-trolled by the clinician to allow for whole-arm training or isolated practice of forearm and wrist motions.

units.summary: The MyoPro® myoelectric orthosis, successor to the Myomo e100 (http://myomo.com) is a portable, wearable device that assists with elbow flexion and extension and gross hand function during daily activities (Fig. It consists of a motorized elbow brace powered by recharge-able batteries and a control system that detects and ampli-fies surface electromyographic (EMG) signals generated by muscles of the paretic arm. Surface electrodes are placed over the bicep and triceps muscles to assist with elbow motions, and forearm flexor and extensor muscle groups to assist grasp and release. Forearm positioning is achieved by passively moving the forearm component of the orthosis to the desired degree of supination or prona-tion needed for task performance.

units.summary: The Hand Mentor (https://motusnova.com) is a com-mercially available repetitive motion device designed for home and clinical use (Fig. It uses a pneumatic arti-ficial muscle to extend the wrist and fingers and provides EMG biofeedback of muscle activation via light-emitting diodes displayed on a small screen. Its purpose is to inhibit flexor tone of the wrist and fingers, provide neuromuscu-lar reeducation, and increase ROM and strength of the paretic wrist and fingers. In two early single case studies, Hand Mentor training was combined with RTP to improve upper limb function in persons 7- and 22-months post stroke.

units.summary: Research on the use of bilateral arm training, in which both upper limbs perform the same movements simultaneously and independently, has shown bimanual practice to have a facilitating effect on paretic arm function after stroke, with movement of the nonaffected upper limb stimulating ipsi-lateral corticospinal projections to the paretic arm. While the neural correlates of bilateral arm training are not well understood, reported changes in cortical activation mea-sured by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), TMS, and EEG include significantly higher cortical acti-vation bilaterally 67 and a shift toward greater ipsilesional EEG activity in sensorimotor cortex after training. 31 Two rehabilitation devices have been empirically tested: the Bi- Manu-Track and Bilateral Arm Training with Rhythmic Auditory Cuing (BATRAC).

units.title: FUNCTIONAL ELECTRICAL STIMULATION
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Rehabilitation Technologies to Promote Upper Limb Recovery After Stroke
units.summary: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) is a method to facilitate limb movement after neurological injury, such as stroke or acquired brain injury, by apply-ing electrical current to paretic muscles. NMES may be applied under passive conditions to prevent muscle atro-phy and at low levels to provide sensory input through afferent pathways. 54 Functional electrical stimulation (FES) is a subcategory of NMES and is defined as elec-trical stimulation to facilitate muscle contraction during active, voluntary movement attempts. FES is a techno-logical advancement designed to facilitate motor recovery during functional activities, like holding a glass to drink.

units.title: Handmaster
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Rehabilitation Technologies to Promote Upper Limb Recovery After Stroke
units.summary: The Handmaster, marketed as the NESS H200 Hand Rehabilitation System (Bioness, Valencia, CA) is a non-invasive, advanced neuroprosthesis used for the treatment of upper limb paresis following stroke, traumatic brain injury, or C5–C6 spinal cord injury. It contains a custom- fit orthosis that uses FES to provide neuromuscular reedu-cation, sequentially activate muscle groups in the forearm, and elicit active grasp and release in the paretic hand. Research studies over the past 15 years have shown potential benefit of FES for persons with subacute and chronic upper limb paresis after stroke. RCT that examined dose effects in persons with moderate, chronic impairments (n = 32) revealed that 120 minutes/day of RTP augmented by the NESS H200 5 days/week for 8 weeks elicited large and consistent improvements on the FMA, Arm Motor Ability Test (function and quality scales), and ARAT scores.

units.summary: The SaeboFlex is a high-tech, dynamic orthosis developed to address the difficulty that many stroke survivors have in opening their paretic hand after stroke. This orthosis con-sists of a forearm cuff attached to a dorsal hand platform that anchors two spring attachments. Individual finger sleeves are placed over the distal phalanges and attached to the spring attachments via a high-tensile line to assist with finger and thumb extension (Fig. Several small trials have tested the feasibility of SaeboFlex training and found positive effects for persons with moderate to severe upper limb impairments after stroke.

units.summary: The rehabilitation technologies described in this chap-ter offer a wide range of treatment options for persons with upper limb paresis after stroke. Choosing the “right” technology for a particular patient during clinical practice involves an appreciation for key features of the device, the patient’s level of function, and therapeutic goals.

units.title: Key Features to Consider
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Rehabilitation Technologies to Promote Upper Limb Recovery After Stroke
units.summary: Key considerations when choosing technologies for patient treatment after stroke include the type of assistance and DOFs afforded by the device, whether it is portable or sta-tionary (e.g., requires treatment space for a workstation), and the amount of training needed to safely and effec-tively administer movement therapy. The device should be easily programmed to meet the patient’s needs as motor recovery occurs and allow for semiautonomous training, which can enhance therapist productivity while the patient engages in intensive movement therapy. Many robotic devices provide quantitative measures of motor functions such as movement speed, accuracy, and forces generated. These objective measures can complement activity and participation-focused clinical evaluations and can be used when documenting treatment plans and progress toward goals.

Reha-bilitation technologies can be easily programmed to ensure a certain level of success for patients with a wide range of motor abilities. This feature can enhance patient motivation and independent carryover of exercise programs.

units.summary: The edema that therapists treat is defined as an excess accumulation of fluid in the interstitium. It occurs on the capillary level (microcirculation level) when there is an imbalance of pressure between the arterioles, venules, and interstitium or an obstruction of the lymphatic sys-tem. 17,51 This is also known as an imbalance in Starling equilibrium. It is important to note the vascular system refers not only to the venous and arterial capillaries but also to the lymphatic capillaries.

Anatomic Overview of the Venous and Lymphatic Systems Related to Stroke Hand Edema and Its Etiology
units.summary: Anatomic Overview of the Venous and Lymphatic Systems Related to Stroke Hand Edema and Its Etiology The venous congestion and limb dependency theory is most relevant to the treatment techniques this chapter will present. Thus, it is important to take an anatomic look at the vascular system, which consists of both arterial and venous structures and the lymphatics. Both vascular struc-tures, the venule and lymphatic capillaries, remove excess fluid from the interstitium and can be simultaneously acti-vated in specific instances.

units.title: Dependency Edema Theory
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Dependency Edema Theory Dependency edema is due to a combination of the involved flaccid or hemiparetic upper extremity hanging in a dependent position, plus potentially the impairment of sympathetic controlled muscle function. Often consistent elevation, daily light retrograde massage, and a light compression glove and/or elastic stockinette tube on the arm will reduce this edema. However, even after diligently following these methods, edema can persist. How much does this persis-tent edema relate to prolonged trunk immobility, lack of scapular movement, and lack of thoracic pressure changes?

units.title: Combined Edema Theory

units.summary: When the lymphatic system acts as a safety valve or over-flow system for the venous system, it carries out of the interstitium both the small molecule products that the venous system usually absorbs and the large molecules only removed by the lymphatic system. The lymphatic system also has a maximum load capacity. When the sys-tem reaches this capacity, there will be lymphatic conges-tion. Clinically, lymphatic congestion presents as viscous and has a very slow rebound time from being pitted of 20 to 30 seconds or more.

units.title: Minor Trauma Edema (Inflammatory Subacute Edema) Theory

Minor Trauma Edema (Inflammatory Subacute Edema) Theory
units.summary: Minor Trauma Edema (Inflammatory Subacute Edema) Theory Minor trauma to tissue is often caused by the arm or hand being bumped, getting caught on something, or from overzealous and improper exercise by the client or care-giver. 8,18,30,33 This accidental trauma often occurs due to an impaired visual field or perception, neglect, lack of limb position in space awareness, decreased sensation, and from learned nonuse once motor function returns. Inflammation from trauma becomes a third component to persistent edema. On a microvascular level, trauma causes high capillary permeability leading to a wound healing sequence in the involved joints and tissue.

units.title: Sensibility Testing
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: There is an old saying, “an insensitive hand is a blind hand.” Hand insensitivity or decreased sensation facili-tates decreased use and possible injury to the extremity, which can be further complicated by unilateral neglect. The monofilament method tests for the degree of sen-sibility present and can indicate a sensory deficit rang-ing from decreased light touch to loss of protective sensation and to loss of deep touch. Various size mono-filaments on individual rods are slowly pressed against the tissue until the monofilament bends, and then the monofilament is slowly lifted from the skin. Once the monofilament bends, no further pressure can be exerted.

units.title: Rebound Test
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: This is a subjective test, but it gives an indication of whether or not congested edema is softening and decreas-ing from an area. The therapist places a 1-ounce weight or the weight of his or her thumb (enough weight to begin blanching the therapist’s fingernail) on the edematous area and counts to 10. This light pressure creates a pit in the edema. Then, the therapist counts the time the tis-sue takes to rebound to the height of the adjacent tissue.

units.title: • Swelling from a mastectomy
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Approximately 15% to 20% of clients develop lymphedema post mastectomy node removal. 42 However, because there is a decrease in the number of lymphatic structures, clients are always at risk to develop lymphedema. A stroke survivor with dependent edema involving the arm on the mastectomy side could poten-tially compromise the deficient lymphatic system and cause lymphedema. If this occurs, a therapist certified in manual lymphatic drainage techniques must be sought out to treat the lymphedema.

units.title: Elevation and Retrograde Massage
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Elevation and Retrograde Massage In the early stages of poststroke edema, elevation and light retrograde massage followed by use of an elastic glove on the hand and cotton/elastic stockinette tube on the arm, if needed, can be effective for reducing hand/arm edema. The rationale is that elevation decreases arterial hydro-static pressure and thus reduces the flowing of fluid into the interstitial spaces. 14,51 The elastic glove and stocki-nette give light pressure to prevent or lessen refilling of tissue. An active muscle pump is needed to intermittently compress venous and lymphatic structures to return fluid back toward the heart.

units.title: Manual Edema Mobilization
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Manual Edema Mobilization Manual edema mobilization (MEM) was first intro-duced by Artzberger in 1995 with subsequent publica-tions. 1–5,29,44 It recognizes that swelling that lasts longer than 1 week and presents as slow to rebound (i.e., 20 to 30 seconds or more to reach surrounding tissue height when pitted) indicates a congested lymphatic system. MEM teaches specific concepts to stimulate and quickly decongest the lymphatic system for post- orthopedic trauma and poststroke extremity edema. Treatment begins in the trunk, creating vacuum drawing periph-eral lymph proximally toward the trunk.

units.title: Bandaging Methods
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Bandaging Methods There are two types of bandaging systems: elastic (high stretch) and low elastic (low stretch). 14 Both look alike in thickness and color, but the low-elastic (low-stretch) ban-dages are usually 100% cotton and have no elastic fibers. 14 The Casley-Smiths point out that the initial lymphatic net will only pump when compressed against something solid such as between a contracting muscle and a solid counter-force (low-elastic bandage). 14 A tissue pressure differentiation, or pumping action, is created, facilitat-ing lymphatic absorption with muscle contraction against a counter-force (the lymphatic net is caught between the contracting muscle and the resistive bandage) and then relaxation of the muscle.

units.title: Continuous Passive Motion
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Continuous Passive Motion In 1990, Giudice published an article reporting hand edema reduction outcomes comparing 30 minutes of hand elevation and 30 minutes of hand elevation with continu-ous passive motion (CPM). Edema reduction was significantly greater with the combination of elevation and the use of the CPM machine. However, when the CPM was discontinued, the edema returned to its former rate. 25 More extensive use and evaluation of use of the CPM machine was reported by Dirette and Hinojosa in 1994.

units.title: Pneumatic Pump and Air Splints
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Pneumatic Pump and Air Splints Pneumatic intermittent compression pumps were first introduced to reduce venous leg edema, such as from varicose veins, and were then expanded to usage with the lymphedematous extremity. Leduc and colleagues reported that pneumatic pumps only force water back into the blood and do not remove excessive protein from tis-sues. 37 In 1999, Roper and colleagues reported on their study of 37 clients with stroke hand edema who received a 2-hour session twice a day of intermittent pneumatic compression for 1 month. They found no change in hand volume in the treated group.

units.title: Splinting
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Splinting There is some evidence that splinting reduces edema. Gracies and colleagues found that a custom-made Lycra garment with flexible plastic inserts when worn 3 hours a day provided a continuous stretch of spastic muscles and reduced edema. 26 There are some clinical arguments for the use of a wrist cock-up splint to reduce edema, to protect joints, and to minimize pain. 24 Burge and col-leagues conducted a randomized trial of a neutral func-tional realignment orthosis on 30 clients with subacute hemiplegia, with the orthosis group wearing it for 6 hours a day.

units.title: Exercise and Positioning
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Exercise and Positioning Research regarding post stroke development of SHS, CRPS, and elbow-hand syndrome repeatedly shows that the incidence can be reduced by half or more if inflamma-tion of tissue can be avoided. 7,8,30,33 Braus and colleagues reduced the frequency of SHS from 27% to 8% in their study by extensively educating everyone involved in cli-ent care on how to prevent trauma to the involved shoul-der and extremity. 8 Their regimen included immediately repositioning the hand/arm/shoulder if pain occurred; performing passive humeral motions of abduction and external rotation only after fully mobilizing the scapula; having not only the therapist perform the motion dur-ing treatment but also having other hospital services do so when handling the involved limb as part of their treatment, such as computerized tomography, electro-encephalography, or when relatives assist with care; and avoiding needle sticks in the involved hand/arm. 8 In their research article, Kondo and colleagues included a passive exercise protocol for both the therapist and cli-ent to follow to prevent SHS.

units.title: Electrical Stimulation
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Electrical Stimulation Over the past 25 years, there has been considerable interest in, evolving research on, and clinical usage of short- term electrical stimulation for neurologic stimulation poststroke for pain reduction, muscular stimulation, muscle strengthening, and tone reduction. Recognizing the role the venous and lymphatic sys-tems play for reducing edema and the effect the mus-cle pump has on these two systems to reduce edema, Faghri designed a research study using neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) to facilitate the muscle pump for edema reduction in the flaccid/paralyzed edematous poststroke hand. 22 His study showed that edema reduction with 30 minutes of NMES of the flac-cid/paralyzed wrist and finger flexors and extensors was significantly greater than 30 minutes of limb elevation alone. However, when the NMES was discontinued, the edema returned to its former volume in the limb.

units.title: Functional Activities
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Functional Activities Edema and the associated deficits it causes, such as reduced sensation and range of movement, may limit a person’s integration of the affected limb into normal tasks and may reinforce learned nonuse. Occupational therapists can grade and provide cueing in daily func-tional tasks to address the cognitive, perceptual, sensory, and motor aspects of performance and can facilitate use of the affected limb. Through task analysis, occupational therapists can highlight to a client what the client can do to maximize independence and reduce the impact of edema. Boomkamp-Koppen and colleagues found a sig-nificant relationship between edema and hand function when paresis was controlled in a statistical analysis.

units.title: Finger Spreader (Finger Abduction Orthosis)
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
REVIEW OF ORTHOSES COMMONLY USED FOR PATIENTS AFTER STROKE
units.summary: The finger spreader (finger abduction orthosis) is fabri-cated of foam rubber and positions the fingers and thumb in abduction. According to Bobath the purpose of the orthosis is to “obtain extension of wrist and fingers.… Abduction not only facilitates extension of the fingers, but also reduces flexor spasticity throughout the whole arm.… It has a better and more dynamic effect than the use of a (standard) orthosis and reduces the possibility of edema.” 2 One should note that Bobath’s rationale is not consistent with the current understanding of motor control and related neurologic principles. A sturdier version of this orthosis (fabricated of low- temperature plastic) was proposed by Doubilet and Polkow. 8 They recommended wearing the orthosis only during the day.

units.title: Firm Cone
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
REVIEW OF ORTHOSES COMMONLY USED FOR PATIENTS AFTER STROKE
units.summary: The firm cone can be fabricated of low-temperature plas-tic or purchased commercially; it is based on the tradi-tional theories of Rood. Rood’s theory (as interpreted by Stockmeyer) states that firm and prolonged pressure over the flexor surface of the palm and fingers results in an inhi-bition of the long flexors. A more current understanding of the mechanism of this orthosis from a biomechanical and functional perspective is that the cone is positioned to place stretch on the shortened long flexors and is graded progressively to increase stress to the soft tissues to pro-mote a more normal resting length.

units.title: Pressure Orthoses (Air Orthoses)
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
REVIEW OF ORTHOSES COMMONLY USED FOR PATIENTS AFTER STROKE
units.summary: The use of inflatable pressure orthoses as adjuncts to ther-apy was first advocated by Johnstone. 18 These orthoses are commercially available and exert continuous or intermit-tent pressure to the area to which they are applied. The pressure of the orthoses should not exceed 40 mm Hg. 36 According to Poole and colleagues, “inflatable orthoses have been used with patients who have had a stroke to reduce tone, facilitate muscle activity around a joint, facil-itate sensory input, control edema, and reduce pain.” 36 Their article includes a review of the neurophysiological rationales for the use of inflatable orthoses.
