units.title: Types and Efficacy of Dysphagia Interventions
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Types and Efficacy of Dysphagia Interventions
units.summary: Types and Efficacy of Dysphagia Interventions Recovery of swallowing function is likely due to a combi-nation of natural recovery and therapeutic effects. These effects include facilitation of available motions where structures and functions have been lost due to reduced sensation and altered muscle tone and volitional strength-ening of weak structures. Neuroplasticity is facilitated by these interventions 9 in ways that rehabilitation science has yet to fully understand.

units.title: Swallowing after Right Hemispheric Stroke
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Jones was admitted to the hospital with a right middle cerebral artery stroke, resulting in a left hemiplegia with dys-phagia. She had a nasogastric tube and was not referred for dysphagia evaluation until she was medically stable, a week after her admission. On evaluation, she demonstrated a left facial droop involving reduced muscle tone in the lip, cheek, and tongue. Drooling from the left side of her mouth was a problem because of reduced sensation.

units.title: Swallowing after Left Hemispheric Stroke
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Smith was admitted to the hospital with a left middle cerebral artery stroke and was referred for dysphagia eval-uation the day after admission. His oral movements and ability to follow commands were difficult to assess for-mally because of aphasia. Active and symmetrical motion of his lips, cheeks, and tongue were observed on attempts to speak. His gag reflex was intact, although palatal movement was not observed because of inability to phonate on command; he was unable to produce an automatic cough.

The therapist should collaborate with other professional such as architects, contractors, and interior designers to ensure that a safe functional home environment is constructed to meet the patient’s needs. Generally, modifications should be made in accordance with the guidelines established by the American National Standards Institute. 1 The American National Standards Institute publishes the document American National Standards for Buildings

units.title: General Comments about Doors and Landings
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
General Comments about Doors and Landings
units.summary: General Comments about Doors and Landings Standard door width should be a minimum of 32 inches. Several solutions to narrow door problems do not require replacing the entire frame and door with a wider doorway. Existing hinges may be replaced with swing-clear hinges if there is enough space behind the door for installation. Thus, the clear opening of the door may be enlarged by to 2 inches.

units.title: Hardware
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Hardware Lever door handles or doorknob adapters are preferable to round twist doorknobs. Slide bolts, which can be reached from a seated position, may replace deadbolt locks. Kick plates can be installed on doors to prevent gouging and scratches from wheelchairs and walking aids. They should be as thin as possible to allow clear door width opening.

units.title: Hallways, Living Room, and Dining Area
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
Hallways, Living Room, and Dining Area
units.summary: Hallways, Living Room, and Dining Area Hallways should be a minimum of 36 to 48 inches wide. Hallways and living areas should be free of clutter, scatter rugs, and protruding objects such as low tables, coat racks, planters, ottomans, as these could be trip hazards or limit wheelchair accessibility though out the home. Carpeting should be removed or tacked or taped down and nonslip and low- friction surfaces are recommended for safety. Furniture should be rearranged to accommodate a wheel-chair turning area of 5 square feet.

units.summary: Bedroom The bedroom should be free of clutter and scatter rugs. A minimum of 3 feet should be available on the side of the bed to allow for wheelchair transfers. Equal height of the bed and wheelchair is optimal for safe transfers. If the bed is too low, it may be elevated on blocks or a platform.

units.title: Bathroom
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Bathroom Doorway width may preclude bathroom access for the wheelchair user. Removing the door, installing a pocket or sliding door, reversing swing of bathroom door, or using a narrow rolling commode chair are options for entry to the bathroom for nonambulatory individuals. The optimal toilet seat height should be 17 to 19 inches, which allows for level transfers from a wheelchair and less bending for those who are ambulatory. Options for raising the height of the toilet include a raised toilet seat, an over-toilet com-mode, a drop-arm commode, or a toilevator.

units.title: Kitchens
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Kitchens The kitchen and work surfaces should be free of clutter and organized to allow access to daily used kitchen items. For instance, place commonly used small appliances within reach and items rarely used in higher cabinets. Countertops are generally 36 inches high, making accessibility difficult for wheelchair users. Alternative counter or work surfaces can be adapted by adding pullout cutting boards or placing a cutting board on top of a drawer that has been opened partially.

units.title: Moving around the Obstacles
section_path: Maximizing Outcomes for Specific Problem Areas Following Stroke
units.summary: Moving around the Obstacles General mobility and transfers will be difficult for the individual who has severe motor deficits. After a discus-sion of prognosis for motor return, it may be appropri-ate to recommend a safe mechanical transfer system for the primary caregiver to use within the home. historical perspective, standard lift systems were difficult to use because they generally required more than one per-son to operate and were difficult to maneuver in limited spaces. Modern advances in technology have resulted in effective, safe, and more affordable equipment available to mobilize the more physically involved individual.
